The one who has just been told that he is disgraced and hated asks to live on until every human being has been raised, so that not one of them is left without his attention.

### Can the prayer of a disbeliever be accepted?

The question comes from the verse "Calling upon Him ˹alone˺ is the truth" and its closing words, "The calls of the disbelievers are only in vain" (13:14). The usual reading is that a disbeliever's prayer is not answered. Yet here is Iblīs, the foremost disbeliever of all, and his request is granted. The difficulty is obvious, and the answer is straightforward.

In this mortal world, even a disbeliever's prayer can be answered. It was answered for Iblīs himself. In the life to come it will not be answered at all. The verse that speaks of calls being in vain belongs to the life to come and has nothing to do with this world.

So the grant given to Iblīs is not a kindness shown to his prayer and not an answer to a need. It is a decree, and the decree goes against him in the end, as the next verse shows.

### In short

- The request is for time and not for mercy, and the purpose attached to it is to keep misguiding the children of Adam until the last day.
- It was made at the worst possible moment, by one who had just been dismissed and disgraced.
- A disbeliever's prayer can be answered in this world, and this one was, but the answer in the life to come is no.
- What follows is a decree rather than a favour, and the decree turns against the one who asked.

15.text:
Allah said, "You are delayed ˹until the appointed Day˺."

### Phrase by phrase

**"You are delayed"** is the answer to the request, and the answer is a grant. The gloss reads the words as: you are given respite until the trumpet is blown. Another makes it plainer: the respite runs to the first blast of the trumpet, when every created being dies and the Creator alone remains. The same term is named in another verse as the day of an appointed time (15:36-37).

**"˹until the appointed Day˺"** is the limit set on the grant. The day is fixed and known to Allah, and it is not the day that Iblīs asked for.

### How long the respite was

The prayer he made asked for a lease of life running to the Day of Resurrection. The words of the answer say only that respite is given. Read against the question, that looks like a grant of exactly what was asked. What the verse does not state clearly is whether the term is the Resurrection as he requested, or something else. And there is a reason to think it is something else, because another verse puts the words "until the appointed Day" (15:38) in this very place.

The upshot is that his prayer was answered, and answered only in part. What he received was a fixed term preserved in Divine knowledge, and not the day of Resurrection or Qiyamah.

A report from as-Suddī supports this reading. Allah did not give Iblīs respite until the Day of Resurrection. He gave him a term whose hour is appointed, and that is the day when the Horn is blown for the first time, when every being in the heavens and the earth is stunned, and dies.

### Two days, and not one

The prayer that Iblīs made was for the time of the second blast, when the dead are raised. That is what is called al-Baʿth. Had the grant matched the request, Iblīs would have been alive at that moment. But the facts would not have allowed it. Nothing is alive at that moment except the Ever-Living and Self-Sustaining One, and that is the moment when the great promise stands fully manifested: "Every being on earth is bound to perish. Only your Lord Himself, full of Majesty and Honour, will remain ˹forever˺" (55:26-27). Iblīs was not to live to see it. So the term of the grant was changed to the day of the Horn, and it was given at that. Death then becomes the rule for the whole of creation. Iblīs dies with the rest, and when the others are raised he is raised too.

This also clears up a doubt that could arise from "Every being on earth is bound to perish" (55:26), which is closely tied to this prayer. The apparent contradiction is resolved.

The substance of it is that al-Baʿth and al-Waqt al-Maʿlum are two separate days. One commentary holds that they are indeed two separate days. From the first blast of the Horn until the entry into Paradise or Hell is one long day in which many things happen at different times. Because of what happens in it, that day can be named after any of those events. It can be called the day of the blast, the day of perishing, the day of resurrection and the day of recompense. On this account every difficulty in the passage falls away.

### In short

- The answer is a grant of respite, running to the blast of the trumpet when every created being dies.
- The prayer was granted only in part. What was given was a fixed appointed term, and not the day of Resurrection that was asked for.
- The raising of the dead and the appointed time are two separate days, and Iblīs was given the second and not the first.
- Because he would have been alive on the day when nothing is alive but the Ever-Living One, the term was changed, and the tension with "Every being on earth is bound to perish" (55:26) is resolved.

16.text:
He said, "For leaving me to stray I will lie in ambush for them on Your Straight Path"

### Phrase by phrase

**"For leaving me to stray"** is the ground on which everything that follows is built. The sense is: since You have sent me astray. Ibn ʿAbbās read it as "You misguided me". Others gave it as, since You ruined me, I will set myself in wait for the servants whom You will bring out of the offspring of the one for whose sake I was expelled. One gloss gives the force of the words as: for Your sending me astray.

**"I will lie in ambush for them"** means he will sit in wait against the children of Adam. The word is the word for a hunter at his post.

**"on Your Straight Path"** is the road itself. It is the path of truth and the way of safety, the path that leads to You, and the religion of Islam. Mujāhid said the straight path is the truth.

### The road he chose to ambush

The reply assumes that the object of the whole dispute is a road, and it assumes it so completely that the rest of the speech depends on it. The sense is that he will misguide them off that road so that they do not worship Allah alone, and the reason he gives is that he was sent astray himself. The path of truth and the way of safety are named as one thing, and to be sent astray from a road is to be sent astray from a destination.

The word also covers the religion. What is being ambushed is not a route on a map. It is a way of life, and the ambush is set across it.

### The ambush at every stage

Imam Aḥmad recorded from Saburah bin Abī al-Fakih that he heard the Messenger of Allah ﷺ say that Shaytan set himself in wait for the son of Adam upon all his paths. He took his post on the path of Islam and asked: will you enter Islam and leave the religion of your fathers? The son of Adam disobeyed him and entered Islam. So he took his post on the path of the migration, and asked: will you leave your land and your sky? The parable of the one who migrates is that of a horse in its strength and stamina. The son of Adam disobeyed him and migrated. So he took his post on the path of the struggle, the struggle against one's own self and the struggle with one's wealth, and asked: suppose you go out to fight and you are killed? Your wife will then marry another man and what you owned will be split up. The son of Adam disobeyed him and waged the struggle all the same.

The shape of the report is worth noticing. The ambush is not set at one point on the road. It is set at every point of it, and at each point the temptation is the one that fits that point. At the beginning the lure is the old ways. In the middle it is the comfort of staying where you are. At the end it is the price that will be paid. Each time the argument arrives dressed as a reasonable question.

The promise that comes with it does not vary. If a man among the children of Adam does this and then dies, the promise from Allah is that he enters Paradise. If he is killed, the same. If he drowns, the same. If a fall from an animal breaks his neck, the same. The list of ways to die is deliberately long, and the promise does not change with any of them.

### In short

- The speech rests on one grievance, that he was sent astray, and everything else is a response to it.
- The straight path is the path of truth and the way of safety, which is the religion itself, and the ambush is set across it.
- The ambush is set at every stage of the way, and the temptation at each stage fits that stage.
- The promise of Paradise does not depend on how a person dies, and the list of deaths is long on purpose.

17.text:
I will approach them from their front, their back, their right, their left, and then You will find most of them ungrateful."

### Phrase by phrase

**"I will approach them from their front"** means he raises doubts in them about the life to come. The content of the doubt is spelled out: that there is no Hell, no Paradise, no resurrection and no reckoning ahead of them.

**"their back"** means he makes them more eager for this life, telling them that the world lasts for ever, bidding them to pile up and hold back out of stinginess, and ordering them to corrupt.

**"their right"** is the side of religion. There he confuses those who are guided until they leave the guidance, and makes the road look fair to those already astray so that they stay astray.

**"their left"** is the side of pleasures and delights.

**"and then You will find most of them ungrateful"** is the count he takes at the end. Ibn ʿAbbās read the words as meaning those who single Allah out in worship. The opposite of ungrateful here is grateful in the sense of acknowledging the One God, so the claim is that most of them will not acknowledge Him.

### The four sides are not a boundary

The verse has him naming four directions: the front, the rear, the right and the left. The purpose is not to set a limit. The sense is that the attack comes from every side and from all directions together, and for that reason an attack from above or from beneath the feet does not contradict it at all. There is also a report that Shayṭān travels within a human being along the blood vessels, so that he comes to hold the whole body. That report does not contradict it either.

So the four are simply the four that can be named, and what they describe is the whole person. What is left out is not a small remainder. Two directions are left out, and a third direction is left out as well, the one inside the body of the man being addressed.

### What each side does

The four are not four attempts of the same kind. One works on the future, and its instrument is doubt about whether there is a future at all. One works on the present, and its instrument is the belief that the present will last for ever, which is what makes hoarding and corruption look reasonable. One works on religion, and its instrument is confusion for the guided and reassurance for the misguided. One works on appetite, and its instrument is pleasure.

Between them they cover a person completely, because each attacks a different part at the same time. Doubt about the future takes away the reason to obey. Belief in an endless present takes away the reason to give. Confusion about religion takes away the reason to choose. And pleasure takes away the desire for anything else.

### The guess that came true

On Iblīs's part the claim was no more than a guess. It nevertheless came out exactly right. The Qur'an says of him, "Indeed, Iblîs' assumption about them has come true, so they ˹all˺ follow him, except a group of ˹true˺ believers" (34:20). And it was never a matter of power, because he has no authority over them. The test is only to separate the one who believes in the Hereafter from the one who doubts it, and the Lord is watchful over all things (34:21).

A hadith on this subject teaches the believer to ask for protection from every side at once. Imam Aḥmad narrated that ʿAbdullah ibn ʿUmar said that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ used to recite this supplication often in the morning and when night came:

> O Allah, I ask You for well-being in this life and the Hereafter. O Allah, I ask You for pardon and well-being in my religion, my life, my family and my wealth. O Allah, cover my errors and quiet my fear in times of difficulty. O Allah, guard me from in front of me, from behind me, from my right, from my left and from above me. I seek refuge in Your greatness from being struck down from below me.

Wakīʿ explained the closing phrase, about being struck down from below, as a reference to earthquakes. Abū Dāwūd, an-Nasāʾī, Ibn Mājah, Ibn Ḥibbān and al-Ḥākim all collected this hadith, and al-Ḥākim said its chain is authentic.

### In short

- The four sides describe a totality rather than a boundary, and the directions left unmentioned are above, below and inside the man himself.
- Each side works on a different part of a person, and all of them work at once.
- The claim was a guess on Iblīs's part, and it proved true, save that he has no authority over the believers.
- The supplication asks for protection from in front, behind, right, left, above and below, which answers the verse's four sides with six.

18.text:
Allah said, "Get out of Paradise! You are disgraced and rejected! I will certainly fill up Hell with you and your followers all together."

### Phrase by phrase

**"Get out of Paradise!"** is the second expulsion, and it carries the curse with it. The statement brings together the cursing, the driving out, the banishment and the turning away from the highest stations.

**"You are disgraced and rejected!"** renders the two words that describe his condition. Ibn Jarīr said the first of them means disgraced, and the second means the one who is put at a distance, that is, banished and driven out. Ibn ʿAbbās gave the sense as belittled and despised. As-Suddī said hateful and expelled. Qatādah said cursed and despised. Mujāhid said driven out and banished. Ar-Rabīʿ bin Anas assigned banishment to the first word and belittlement to the second. One authority said that no being is known to be in this condition except one, and a well-known chain gives the sense of the first word as despised.

**"I will certainly fill up Hell with you and your followers all together."** is the sentence of requital. The "you" is Iblīs together with his offspring, and with people as well. In the address, those who are present carry more weight than those who are absent, and the sense of the whole line is the sense of a condition: whoever follows you will be punished.

### What the two words take away

Each of the two words is a denial. One says he has been made small. The other says he has been put far away. Together they remove both size and nearness, and once both are gone there is nothing in him that anyone could want. What is described is not a pain to be suffered somewhere. It is a standing condition, and the condition is contempt.

The second expulsion has an order of its own as well. The first command to leave the heavens was perhaps a proposal. This one is its implementation. The words "get out" are used again, and what has been added to them is the consequence: the Fire is to be filled.

### What the Fire is filled with

The rest of the passage sets out the purpose. The command is to go, and then the promise: "Be gone! Whoever of them follows you, Hell will surely be the reward for all of you—an ample reward" (17:63). Then comes the list of how the filling is done. "And incite whoever you can of them with your voice, mobilize against them all your cavalry and infantry, manipulate them in their wealth and children, and make them promises." And the line closes with the fact that undoes all of it: "But Satan promises them nothing but delusion" (17:64).

Every instrument in that list is either a kind of speech or a kind of pressure. The voice, the cavalry, the infantry, the wealth, the children and the promises all work on a person from outside. And the thing being promised is a delusion, so that what is finally filled is a Fire full of people who were talked into it by a lie.

The ground of it all is the last line of the same passage: "You will truly have no authority over My ˹faithful˺ servants. And sufficient is your Lord as a Guardian" (17:65). The instruments belong to Iblīs and the outcome does not.

### In short

- The two words used against him deny him both size and nearness, so that contempt is all that is left of his standing.
- The second expulsion carries out the first, and what it adds is the consequence, that the Fire is to be filled.
- The Fire is the reward of those who follow him, and the reward is described as ample.
- The means of filling it are the voice, the cavalry, the infantry, the wealth, the children and the promises, and every one of them is delusion.

19.text:
The scene moves into the garden itself. "˹Allah said,˺ “O Adam! Live with your wife in Paradise and eat from wherever you please, but do not approach this tree, or else you will be wrongdoers.”" The permission is wide and the prohibition is one point wide. Everything in the garden is open to the two of them except a single tree, and the verse names the consequence of going near it. The next three verses show what happened to that one narrow prohibition when the enemy went to work on it.

### Phrase by phrase

**"O Adam! Live with your wife in Paradise"** is the instruction to settle there. In the Arabic the pronoun "you" is repeated before the command to dwell, and the repetition is there to emphasise the subject of the verb and to attach what follows to it. The wife is Hawwāʾ (Eve), and the name is spelled that way in the reading given.

**"and eat from wherever you please"** sets out how wide the permission is. It covers all the fruits of the garden and any part of it the two of them might want.

**"but do not approach this tree"** is the single limit. The prohibition is not on eating only, since approaching is what is forbidden, and nearness to a forbidden thing is itself the danger. The tree has been described as wheat. In another place the warning is worded as eating from it, and the sense comes out the same.

**"or else you will be wrongdoers"** names the result. If they eat from that tree after the prohibition has reached them, they belong among those who transgress the limits and harm themselves.

### Why the story is told again

The story of Adam and Iblīs has already appeared in the fourth section of Surah Al-Baqarah, and detailed comments were given there on the same material. The retelling here is not a repeat for its own sake. Each place the story appears it is asked to carry a different weight, and this surah is using it as the frame for everything that follows about the enemy and about the children of Adam.

### What Adam was made of

Adam is called by four names: Adam, vicegerent, mortal, and man. He was named Adam because he was made from the surface of the earth, drawn from every region of it. That is why the Qur'an says: "And indeed, We created humankind from an extract of clay" (23:12). Every part of the earth was drawn on in the making of him. What went into him came from the briny places and from the sweet ones, from the hard ground and from the soft.

The point of that variety is what came out of it. Salt and sweetness were in the clay of Adam, and coarseness as well as softness, so the natures of his children came out differing. Among them are the sweet-tempered and the bad-tempered, the open and the closed, the generous and the stingy, the easy-going and the difficult, the black and the white. The extraction drew on every part of the earth, from the sweet and the briny to the soft and the hard.

Other verses describe the same clay from other angles. "He created humankind from ˹sounding˺ clay like pottery" (55:14). Pottery is dried clay that gives off a sound, and it is full of noise. The child of Adam, on this picture, is a noisy being. His head is full of commotion, and talk is what he clings to. "Indeed, We created them from a sticky clay" (37:11) points to a clay that clings to everything and mixes with everyone. "Indeed, We created man from sounding clay moulded from black mud" (15:26) points to a clay that is dark and black.

All of these were taught to Adam so that he would know his own measure and not step outside his rank. He was shown his own root, so that if he ever saw generosity he would not think it came from himself. He would know that eminence lies in nurture and not in soil.

And the two are not the same thing. Out of soil come wrongdoing, ignorance and harshness, and out of soil came the disobedience of Adam to his Lord (20:121). Out of nurture comes guidance freely given, repentance accepted and tenderness, and it was by His choice that Allah took Adam (3:33). The fruit that nurture bears is what the Qur'an says of a people: "He loves them, and they love Him" (5:54).

There is a story told to make this plain. Maḥmūd visited the house of Ayāz, and there he saw the property and the blessings and the gold and silver and jewels and silks and robes of honour that had been given to the man. In one corner hung an old patched cloak on a nail, and Maḥmūd asked what that was doing there. Ayāz said: that thing is what I am, in my helplessness and my lowliness. Everything beautiful, everything adorned, everything exalted and delightful in this house is yours. Looking at the cloak, I see how little I can do and I learn what I am worth. Looking at the rest, I see you, and knowing that it belongs to you makes me glad, and I lift up my head.

### In short

- The whole garden was permitted and one tree was not, and what was forbidden was even to go near it.
- The story has been told before, in the fourth section of Surah Al-Baqarah, and this surah retells it for a different purpose.
- Adam was named from the surface of the earth, and he was drawn from every region of it, sweet and briny, soft and hard.
- That mixture is why human natures differ so widely, and the lesson drawn is that eminence lies in how a person is nurtured and not in what he is made of.

20.text:
Then Satan tempted them in order to expose what was hidden of their nakedness. He said, "Your Lord has forbidden this tree to you only to prevent you from becoming angels or immortals."

### Phrase by phrase

**"Then Satan tempted them"** means he whispered to them and suggested to them what he wanted. The Arabic word for what he did carries the sense of a quiet speech that is not heard by others. What he wanted was to strip them of the favours and the fine clothing they were enjoying.

**"in order to expose what was hidden of their nakedness"** is the aim. The word for their private parts is built on a form that comes from the idea of covering, and the thing hidden was hidden by a covering of light. Before this, the two of them could not see each other's private parts.

**"He said, "Your Lord has forbidden this tree to you only to prevent you from becoming angels or immortals.""** is the lie itself. The sense he was working on is that if they ate from the tree they would gain both things at once, becoming angels and living for ever. The words are the words of a being uttering falsehood.

### The grammar of the lie

In the Arabic there is a construction at work in that sentence, and it is the same construction found in "Allah makes ˹this˺ clear to you so you do not go astray" (4:176), and in "He has placed into the earth firm mountains, so it does not shake with you" (16:15). In those two, the last clause gives the result that is being prevented. So the sentence of Iblīs means: so that you do not become angels or dwell here for ever. That is how the negation is to be read, and it is the opposite of what he wanted them to hear.

The same temptation is reported in another place, and the wording there is a question rather than a statement: "But Satan whispered to him, saying, "O Adam! Shall I show you the Tree of Immortality and a kingdom that does not fade away?"" (20:120). The offer there is immortality and a kingdom that never decays, and here it is angelhood and permanence. Read side by side, both are the same coin, and the coin is the promise of passing beyond the limits of a made thing.

### Where the tree stood

Paradise lay open to Adam and his spouse across all its vast expanses, and the good things in it were beyond counting. The two of them could use those things however they wished. Then, in the middle of more permitted things than anyone could list, one thing alone was forbidden. That narrow prohibition was the ground the enemy picked to attack from.

What he did was to belittle the wide world of legitimate gifts in their eyes and to inflate the importance of the one forbidden thing, presenting it in an attractive light and assuring them of the immense advantages hidden inside it. Adam and his spouse were worn down by his continuous urging, and they finally ate the fruit of the forbidden tree. What they got was the exact opposite of what they had been promised.

### How the same trick is worked on everyone

The strategy is not altered for anyone else, and it is worked for each person according to his own tastes and his own circumstances. One man is taught to hate health-giving food, and told that if he wants wonderful health he should take to drinking wines. Another has a position to defend, and is told that the most effective way of defeating his opponent is to begin destructive activities against him. Another has every opportunity to work on himself, and is told that the shortest road to success is protest and demands. Another has countless religious duties he could perform without any clash with the government of the day, and is made to believe that the system of Islam can only prevail if those in power are first unseated. The particulars change and the shape of the offer does not.

### The mark of care in the telling

The way the verse reports all of this is itself a mark of solicitude and a proof of generosity. The two of them sinned, and the verse turns the matter over to the whispering of Satan, and then adds the detail that the nakedness revealed was hidden from them. One reading spells out that their private parts were made to appear to them and not to others.

### In short

- The temptation was a quiet suggestion aimed at stripping them of what they had, and the aim was to expose what the covering of light had hidden.
- The lie was that the prohibition existed only to keep them from becoming angels or from living for ever, and the promise was immortality and a kingdom that does not fade.
- The attack was made on the one narrow point in a very wide permission, by belittling everything allowed and inflating the one thing forbidden.
- The same method is used on everyone, tailored to their tastes, and the shape of the offer never changes.

21.text:
And he swore to them, "I am truly your sincere advisor."

### Phrase by phrase

**"And he swore to them"** is the verse's whole weight. The Arabic verb behind the words is qāsamahumā, and it says that he swore to the two of them, and what he swore by was Allah. This is the act that makes the next verses intelligible. A lie had been told, and now the lie is put under an oath.

**"I am truly your sincere advisor"** is the content of the oath. The word for a sincere advisor is the word for one who gives good counsel out of goodwill, and he attaches it to himself in an unqualified way. Another rendering gives the sense as: I am a sincere adviser to you in this matter, and the oath is that the tree is the tree of immortality.

### Why the oath was needed

The claim in the previous verse was not a small one. What he was asking them to believe was that their Lord had forbidden the tree for a reason that had nothing to do with their good. Against that, the reputation he needed was the reputation of a friend.

So he swore. He swore by Allah, and he told them that he was created before them and therefore had better knowledge of the place. That is the whole argument: an older being, with longer experience of the garden, offering a piece of advice out of concern. The oath does not add any evidence to the claim. It adds only the appearance of a man who would not lie.

Qatādah commented on this verse and gave the same reading of it. The oath, as he described the matter, ran like this. I was made before you were made. My knowledge of this place is therefore better than yours. So follow me, and I will set you on the right road.

### The fact worth remembering

It is a fact that a believer in Allah can sometimes fall victim to deceit. That is the reason the story is set out in this much detail, verse by verse, with the whisper, the false claim and the oath laid one after another. The reader is not being told about two people in a garden. He is being shown the exact sequence of steps by which a being who believes in Allah is talked into doing what Allah forbade.

The two of them met afterwards, and that meeting is also reported. Adam asked him what had been done to himself, and what dust had been thrown up on the road he was walking. Iblīs gave back a question of his own. He said that he accepted having taken Adam off the road, and then asked who it was that had taken him off the road.

### In short

- The verse is the oath, and the oath was sworn by Allah, which is what gives the lie its weight.
- What the oath was asked to do was to establish him as a friend, since an older being offering help is harder to refuse than a stranger.
- He added the argument that he was created first and knew the place better, which is an argument from age rather than from evidence.
- The sequence is preserved in detail because a believer can be deceived, and the steps are what the reader needs to see.

22.text:
So he brought about their fall through deception. And when they tasted of the tree, their nakedness was exposed to them, prompting them to cover themselves with leaves from Paradise. Then their Lord called out to them, "Did I not forbid you from that tree and ˹did I not˺ tell you that Satan is your sworn enemy?"

### Phrase by phrase

**"So he brought about their fall through deception"** means he led them on to eat from the tree by guile, with falsehood and lies, until they ate from it. In another reading the phrase carries the sense that he brought them down, meaning that he lowered their station by his deception.

**"And when they tasted of the tree, their nakedness was exposed to them"** is the first result. The private part of each of them was revealed to the other, the front and the back alike, and every one of these parts is called shameful because exposing it puts a person to shame.

**"prompting them to cover themselves with leaves from Paradise"** is the second result. They began to piece the leaves together, that is, to stick them onto themselves, in order to cover up. Ibn ʿAbbās said the leaves they used were fig leaves. This statement has an authentic chain of narration reaching him. Mujāhid said they used the leaves of the garden, making them into a garment.

**"Then their Lord called out to them"** begins the question, and the question is addressed to Adam and to Hawwāʾ.

**"Did I not forbid you from that tree and ˹did I not˺ tell you that Satan is your sworn enemy?"** The interrogative is meant as an affirmation, so the sentence is a statement in the form of a question, and the answer to it is yes on both counts.

### What the change looked like

A report going back to Ubayy bin Kaʿb describes the moment. Adam stood as tall as a palm tree, and his hair was thick. Only when he committed the error did his private part become visible to him, and he had never seen it before. He took to running through the garden in his fright, and a tree caught hold of his head. He asked the tree to let him go, and the tree refused. Then his Lord called to him and asked whether he was running away from Him. He said that he was not. He said that he felt shame in front of his Lord.

The report reached Ibn Jarīr and Ibn Marduwyah through more than one chain, passing by way of Al-Ḥasan to Ubayy bin Kaʿb, and Ubayy related it as coming from the Prophet ﷺ. Making it Ubayy's own statement is the sounder of the two ways.

Another account of the covering comes from Wahb bin Munabbih. On his account a light lay over the two of them, and while it was there neither could see the other uncovered. Eating from the tree ended that, and the parts became visible. Ibn Jarīr reported the statement with a chain that is authentic. The same thought lies behind the words "stripping them of their raiment" (7:27).

### The rebuke and what it did

Whoever tracks his own appetite against the command of the Real is held back from the Real, and he does not reach the appetite either. That is what this verse shows. Adam the chosen had barely tasted the forbidden tree before the rebuke fell on him and his condition changed. The appetite was never satisfied, and the approval he had enjoyed was gone with it.

He looked again, and the crown was off his head and the robe was off his body. Before this he had seen himself seated on a throne of chosenness, resting back on the cushion of the vicegerency, dressed in the robes and ornaments of the garden. Now he saw himself shut out from all of it, uncovered and hungry, reduced to needing a single leaf from a tree. And the word came to him:

> O Adam, you were not able to enjoy all those blessings without suffering and toil. Now go to the house of tribulation and adversity and work, plant seeds, take pains, and be patient.

### Where the two of them differed

Afterwards the two of them met, and Adam put the question to Iblīs about what had been done to him. The answer given back was a question of its own. Both of them had turned away from the command, and there is a difference between the two. Adam slipped because of appetite. Iblīs slipped because of pride. Pride is the worse of the two. A sin that comes out of appetite leaves room for pardon. A sin that comes out of pride takes the faith down with it. And a report has come down on the point:

> Magnificence is My cloak and tremendousness My shawl. If anyone contends with Me in either of them, I will smash him.

The distinction is the answer to the whole passage. The two of them did the same thing in the sense that both disobeyed, and they did not do the same thing at all in the sense that matters, which is what the disobedience was made of.

Adam said of all of it: this is trifling if one day I am given access to this threshold again. He lamented the pain in his heart and placed his need and his incapacity on the palms of remorse, and he wept.

### In short

- The deception worked, and the first result was that the covering of light was taken away, so that each saw the other's nakedness.
- The second result was the leaves, which Ibn ʿAbbās named as fig leaves, and which they stuck on themselves to cover up.
- The question from their Lord is a statement in the form of a question, and it affirms both the prohibition and the warning about the enemy.
- Both of them disobeyed, and they differed in what the disobedience was made of: Adam slipped through appetite, which leaves room for pardon, and Iblīs slipped through pride, which loses the faith.

23.text:
They replied, "Our Lord! We have wronged ourselves. If You do not forgive us and have mercy on us, we will certainly be losers."

### Phrase by phrase

**"They replied"** is already the whole difference between the two of them. Iblīs, faced with a question, answered with an excuse. Adam and Eve, faced with the same kind of question, answered with a confession.

**"Our Lord! We have wronged ourselves"** is the confession, and the wording is exactly right. They did not say that they had wronged Allah. They said that they had harmed themselves by transgressing, which is what the wrong against Allah amounts to for a creature who can gain nothing for Him and lose everything for himself.

**"If You do not forgive us and have mercy on us"** asks for two things and treats both as necessary. To forgive is to overlook the transgression. To have mercy is to refrain from punishing it.

**"we will certainly be losers"** gives the consequence. The word is the word for being duped into receiving punishment, and one gloss adds what the loss covers, which is their share of the life of this world and of the Hereafter.

### What they did not do

They did not blame the tree and they did not blame each other. They did not blame the enemy, although the enemy was the one who had sworn a false oath to them. Every one of those answers was available, and not one of them was given. The confession is complete and unshared.

The contrast with the previous speaker in this surah is put directly in a report. ʿAbdur-Razzāq reported from Qatādah that Adam asked his Lord what would happen if he turned back and asked to be forgiven, and that the answer was that he would then be brought into Paradise. Shaytan, on the other hand, asked for time and not for pardon:

> As for Shaytan, he did not ask for forgiveness, but for respite. Each one of them was given what he asked for.

That sentence is the two stories laid side by side. One asked for time and got it, and the time went on the same work. One asked for pardon and got it, and the pardon was the start of a road back. Both requests were granted, and what each of them asked for is the measure of what he had learned.

### What was said about the confession

Ad-Dahhak bin Muzāḥim commented on these same words. The substance of his comment is what the verse itself says, that the two of them owned the wrong as their own doing and asked their Lord to cover it and to show them mercy.

### A prayer under the prayer

The words themselves are used as a prayer, and they have been read as the model of every sincere turning back. In full it runs like this:

> O God, if we weep, weeping for You is sweet. If we lament over You, our lamenting is appropriate. O God, what comes from dust other than error? What is born from defect other than disloyalty? And what comes from the generous other than loyalty? O God, we have come back with two empty hands. What would happen if You placed balm on the wounded? O God, You are the treasure of the poor, the travelling supplies of the distressed, the resource of the fleeing, the hand holder of the helpless. You created, so You saw the faulty jewel, but You selected it and bought it with all its faults. You lifted us up and no one said, "Lift up". Now that You have lifted up, do not put down. Keep us in the shadow of gentleness and entrust us to none but Your bounty. If You water, You Yourself planted. If You flatten the foundation, You Yourself raised it. I the servant am just what You fancied. Do not throw me down, for You lifted me up.

### In short

- The answer to the question is a confession and not an excuse, which is the difference between Adam and Iblīs.
- The wrong is stated as a wrong done to themselves, and both forgiveness and mercy are asked for, since either without the other leaves the matter unfinished.
- The loss they named covers their share of this life and of the next, so nothing is left outside the request.
- Adam asked for pardon and was given it, while Iblīs asked for time and was given that, and each received what he asked for.

24.text:
Allah said, "Descend as enemies to each other. You will find in the earth a residence and provision for your appointed stay."

### Phrase by phrase

**"Descend"** names Adam and his wife, and Iblīs, and the snake with them. Not every scholar lists the snake, and Allah knows best. The enmity is chiefly the enmity between Adam and Iblīs. Hawwāʾ (Eve) is with Adam in the matter. One reading takes the plural as covering Adam and Hawwāʾ together with all the offspring the two of them comprise, and another reading names the group as Adam, Eve, the serpent and the peacock.

**"as enemies to each other"** states the relation that the descent creates. Each of them is an enemy to the others on account of the wrong each does to the other.

**"You will find in the earth a residence"** means there will be for you a dwelling and a shelter down there. In another place the same descent is commanded in these words: "Descend, both of you, from here together ˹with Satan˺ as enemies to each other" (20:123).

**"and provision for your appointed stay"** means provision until death, that is, until the terms of their lives are fulfilled. Those terms are known and fixed. They are written in the first record, already set down by the Pen, and counted out by predestination.

### What the earth is for them

The story about the snake, if it is true, has the snake as a follower of Iblīs. Some scholars named the places on earth that the two of them were sent down to. These accounts are taken from Israelite tales, and only Allah knows whether they are true. And there is a rule that follows from it. If knowing those places were useful to people in their religion or in their lives, His Book would have named them, and His Messenger ﷺ would have named them as well.

What is given instead is the thing that actually matters. The earth is a dwelling place for the children of Adam for what remains of this earthly life. On it they live. On it they die and are buried. And out of it they will be raised for the Day of Resurrection, on which the first of creation and the last of it are gathered together and each is given what his deeds earned, whether that be reward or punishment.

### The war that began here

Both Adam and Satan were sent to the earth as each other's enemies, and the battle between them goes on until the Day of Doom. Satan never stops working to bring human beings onto his path and to strip them of God's grace, just as he himself was stripped of it. And man should set himself against him and spoil his plans. He should ignore his call and run to answer the call of God.

The fight takes visible shape in the way human beings divide into two groups. Some give in to the inducements of Satan and fall in with him. The others answer the call of God, and they take on the risk that all of Satan's companions will work to vilify them and defeat them. In every age the true devotees of the truth, who are always few, have been the ones who suffered the bitterest enmity of those who deny the truth. The reason lies in the enmity of Satan. He turns people against the believers, filling their hearts in one way or another with a burning hatred for them, until some of those people become his tools and begin to make life hard for the devotees of the truth.

### How the enmity shows itself

The original sin of Satan was the refusal to acknowledge the favour that had been given to Adam, and his effort now is to breed a temperament like his own in every man. He prods the younger ones to give no proper regard to their elders. In a deal between two parties, where one of them is bound to pay the other what is due, he persuades the first not to honour the pledge at all. When a servant of God brings the message of truth, he plants doubts of several kinds in people's hearts, so that they will not accept it. In a dispute between two parties, where one is ready to pay an amount that matches his circumstances, he slyly persuades the other party to refuse the offer and to demand more than the other can ever meet, so that the quarrel goes on and never dies.

That is how enmity between people comes to prevail everywhere. Two opposing groups form among human beings, and Satan takes care to see that the confrontation between them will never end.

### In short

- The descent is commanded for Adam, Hawwāʾ, Iblīs and those with them, and the enmity is chiefly between Adam and Iblīs.
- The earth is given as a dwelling and a provision for a term that has already been recorded and fixed.
- The reports that name the places of the descent come from Israelite tales, and what is useful for religion and life is what the Book and the Prophet ﷺ gave.
- The enmity began here and runs to the Day of Doom, dividing human beings into two groups and working through ordinary things like debts, quarrels and the message itself.

25.text:
He added, "There you will live, there you will die, and from there you will be resurrected."

### Phrase by phrase

**"There you will live"** means life on the earth, and the address is to Adam and Hawwāʾ and their descendants.

**"there you will die"** means that death too belongs to the earth, and the burial that follows it.

**"and from there you will be resurrected"** means that the earth is not only the place of dying. It is the place from which they will be brought out. In the Arabic the verb can be read in the active, "you shall come forth", or in the passive, "you shall be brought forth". Another verse gives the sense of the whole of it: "From the earth We created you, and into it We will return you, and from it We will bring you back again" (20:55).

### The three stages

The verse puts the whole of a human life into three clauses, and it gives each of them the same location. The earth is where people are made, where they live, where they die, where they are buried, and where they are raised. Nothing in that list happens anywhere else.

That is also what makes the sentence a comfort rather than a sentence. The descent in the previous verse is a departure, and this verse says what the departure is for. The one who leaves a garden is not sent nowhere. He is sent to a place laid out for him, with a term set for his stay, and with a last stage in which he comes out of it to give an account.

### In short

- Life, death and burial all belong to the earth, and so does the resurrection out of it.
- The sentence reads as a promise as much as a sentence, since the place of exile is the same place the return begins from.
- The verb can be read either as "you shall come forth" or as "you shall be brought forth", and the sense is the same either way.
- The whole of a human life is contained in three clauses, and all three of them name the earth.

26.text:
The story of the garden ends and the address changes hands. "O children of Adam! We have provided for you clothing to cover your nakedness and as an adornment. However, the best clothing is righteousness. This is one of Allah's bounties, so perhaps you will be mindful". Everything before this verse was told about two people. This verse is spoken to everyone who comes after them, and it turns the story they have just read into something they can wear.

### Phrase by phrase

**"O children of Adam!"** is the address, and the important thing about it is who is being addressed. This is not a message to Muslims alone. It goes to every child of Adam, and the width of the address is a pointer in itself. Covering the parts of the body that need covering, and wearing clothes at all, is a human need and a natural desire. Every community and every religion practises it, and none of them had to be taught it.

**"We have provided for you clothing to cover your nakedness"** names the first use of dress. The Arabic word behind "cover" comes from a root meaning to hide or conceal, and the word for nakedness is the plural of a word for a part of the body which, by nature, all human beings consider it shameful to uncover. So the sense of the words is that Allah has sent down for people a dress with which they can cover the parts of the body whose exposure brings shame.

**"and as an adornment"** names the second use. The word here covers whatever is worn for beauty and for dignity, and Ibn Jarīr said it takes in furniture and outer clothes as well. The point of naming it second is that a plain garment is enough to do the covering. Allah gave people more than that. What they were given includes things that make a person look well, and decent, neat and civilised.

**"However, the best clothing is righteousness"** names the third, and puts it above the other two. ʿAbdur-Raḥmān ibn Zayd ibn Aslam commented on these words that when a person fears Allah, Allah covers his faults, and that this is what the garment of taqwā means. In some of the readings (qirāʾāt) the word for garment is vowelised differently, so that the sentence reads as a further gift: We have sent down a third dress, that of taqwā. On the reading that is well known, the meaning is that everyone knows the first two garments, and that there is a third kind, the garment of taqwā, and that this is the best of all of them. Ibn ʿAbbās and ʿUrwah ibn az-Zubayr explained the garment of taqwā as right conduct, good deeds and the fear of Allah, and they placed the oneness of God at the head of it.

**"This is one of Allah's bounties, so perhaps you will be mindful"** closes the verse. The invitation is to understand what has been said and to take the instruction from it.

### How dress was sent down

The word used for what Allah did with clothing is that He sent it down, and this is worth a moment. The expression does not require clothes to come out of the sky ready to wear. The same word is used elsewhere of iron (57:25), which is dug out of the ground for everyone to see. What the word points to in both places is the way no human planning is the active agent in it. Cotton and wool and the like are the mother material of dress, and human ingenuity had no part in bringing them into being. They are simply a gift of the great creative power of Allah.

Human skill does begin to work after that, in making the materials up into clothes to fit a person's taste, his temperament and his need to be safe from heat and cold. And even the road to that skill was shown by Allah. So an eye that sees reality sees the whole of it as nothing but a gift sent down.

### The two uses, and which one comes first

Two uses of dress are identified in the verse, and the order they are given in is not an accident. The first is to cover the parts of the body that need covering. The second is protection from heat and cold, and the adornment of the body.

Placing the covering first tells the reader what the real purpose of human dress is. It also marks the line between human beings and the animals. The dress of an animal has been built into its body. What it does is protect the animal from heat and cold, or make it beautiful. No elaborate arrangement has been made for it to cover what a person would call his nakedness, though the shapes of particular parts of an animal's body have been placed so that they are not left wholly exposed. Some have a tail that acts as a screen, and others have something else in the way of a view.

The connection with the story that has just been told is direct. The first result of the satanic whispering was that the heavenly apparel of Adam and Hawwāʾ came off and left them uncovered, and they began hiding themselves with leaves. So the mention of dress here tells the reader what nakedness is. For a human being, to be naked, or to expose his shameful parts in front of others, is a sign of utter disgrace and of indecency at its worst. It is also the doorway to every kind of evil and disorder.

### The first attack, and the one still being made

It is worth noticing where the first assault of Satan landed. It came at this opening, and it came against human beings at the exact point where their dress had fallen from where it belonged. And the same thing is still going on. When Satan works through his accomplices to confuse people and waylay them, he picks a fashionable front for it. He calls it the trend, he calls it cool, and in the end he pulls people out of their houses into the streets naked or almost naked. What Satan has classified as modern advancement does not come about unless women are first stripped of their sense of shame and modesty and made to parade about nearly uncovered.

So the assault was answered by legislation, and it was answered at the earliest point available. The Sharīʿah took the matter with the seriousness it deserves, because it is responsible for planting, protecting and bringing to flower every good thing in its people. It therefore made the covering of the body the first duty after faith itself. The prayer, the fast and the duties like them all come after that.

### What the Prophet ﷺ taught about clothing

ʿUthman al-Ghanī reported a hadith of the Holy Prophet ﷺ. When a person puts on a new garment, he should say this as he puts it on:

> Praise be to Allah who has given me clothing with which I cover the parts of my body that need covering, and with which I look well in my life.

The same Companion reported another instruction. When a person puts on something new and gives the old one away as ṣadaqah, charity, to someone poor and in need, he comes under the protection and patronage of Allah in every state of his life and of his death. This is from the Musnad of Ahmad, and Ibn Jarīr is the one who reports the first of the two. In both of them the two considerations behind the creation of human dress are brought back to mind.

### Covering the body is natural

The story of Adam and the words of the Qur'an settle a further question. Wanting to cover the body and wanting to dress in something is built into a human being, and it has been there from the very beginning. There is a claim that the first man went about naked, and that the making of clothes came only after humanity had passed through a series of stages. That claim is plainly false.

### The garment that covers what the body cannot

The first two garments are visible things. The third is not, and it does more. A physical garment covers the parts of the body, protects against heat and cold, and gives beauty and embellishment. The garment of taqwā works in the same way for a person's inner life. It conceals his weaknesses and his moral shortcomings, and it delivers him from hardship here and from loss at the end. That is why it is the best of the garments anyone can put on.

There is a warning attached to it. A person who does evil and has no fear of Allah, and who does not care whether he acts rightly, will be disgraced in the end, however well he covers himself up. Ibn Jarīr reports from ʿUthman al-Ghanī, and the Holy Prophet ﷺ swore an oath on it. By Allah in whose hands rests the life of Muhammad, no deed a person does in secret stays private. Allah wraps it around him the way a sheet is wrapped, and then He announces it. If the deed was good, the announcement is good. If the deed was evil, the announcement is evil. A deed wrapped around a person like a sheet is a deed everyone can see. However quietly a man may act, the marks of it are made to show on his face and in his body. The Prophet ﷺ recited this verse to confirm it, with its mention of the dress that adorns and of the dress of taqwā that is the best.

### The purpose that a physical garment serves

The expression "the garment of taqwā" carries a further indication, and the book of tafsīr known as Rūḥ al-Maʿānī is where these readings of it are gathered. It means that the physical dress, which covers the body properly and also makes it beautiful, is really a route to the ability to be mindful of Allah. And once a person has that ability, it ought to show in the way he dresses. The parts of the body that must be covered should be properly covered, and a person should make sure that his modesty stays concealed. The body should not be left uncovered, and the garment should not be so tight that the parts look as though they were bare.

From there the requirements continue. The dress should carry no flavour of pride and arrogance. It should show modesty and humility instead. It should not be extravagant, and the material used should be cut to the need. The clothing of women should not be a man's clothing, and the clothing of men should not be a woman's, which is hateful and repugnant in the sight of Allah. And there should be no imitation in dress that copies other people, since that is a sign of drifting away from the settled norms of one's own community.

All of this runs alongside something more important, which is the need to put a person's character and his conduct right. That is the real purpose of dress, and the verse ends by inviting the reader to see it, since the whole matter is one of the signs of Allah and the point of a sign is to make a person willing to be told.

### The outward sign and the inward reality

God made the world on a pattern in which outward things are signs of something inward, and a person who thinks about what he sees outside can arrive at truths that are hidden. Human attire is one of those outer signs. The clothes a person has protect him, and they also improve his looks and his standing. That points to something about his inner life, which also needs a covering.

That covering is the righteousness that is born of the fear of God, and it stands for a person's inner self. On one side it protects a man from the attacks of Satan, and on the other it improves what is inside him and fits him for a place in the fine and beautiful world of Paradise.

What is this righteousness? It is fear of God. It is acknowledging the truth. It is holding to the same standard for oneself as for other people. It is treating oneself as a subject of God. It is behaving with modesty and humility. It is living for the Hereafter rather than wandering off after the world. A person who has built these qualities into himself has dressed his inner self, and while his body is under a garment of cloth, his soul is under the garment of taqwā. When his conduct is the opposite of all this, he is in effect laying his inner self bare.

### In short

- The address is to all the children of Adam and not to Muslims alone, because covering the body is a human need and a natural desire shared by everyone.
- Three garments are named: the one that covers, the one that adorns, and the garment of taqwā, and the third is the best of them.
- The word "sent down" does not require clothes to fall from the sky. It points to the mother materials of dress as a gift, not the product of human planning.
- Covering comes first among the uses of dress, and that is what marks human beings off from the animals and what the Sharīʿah made the first duty after faith.
- The garment of taqwā is right conduct, good deeds and the fear of Allah. It hides a person's weaknesses, and it is carried in the way he dresses, which must be modest, unostentatious and his own.

27.text:
The story is left behind and the warning becomes personal. "O children of Adam! Do not let Satan deceive you as he tempted your parents out of Paradise and caused their cover to be removed in order to expose their nakedness. Surely he and his soldiers watch you from where you cannot see them. We have made the devils allies of those who disbelieve". The verse names the enemy, describes what he did once, and tells the reader where the two of them stand now.

### Phrase by phrase

**"O children of Adam! Do not let Satan deceive you"** is the admonition, and the address returns to all the children of Adam as it was in the previous verse. The deceiving here is the making of disobedience look beautiful. The warning is that they should not let him do to them what he did to their two parents. The line is followed by a warning not to be tricked into either of two things: into dropping the covering of the body, or into dropping the garment of mindfulness.

**"as he tempted your parents out of Paradise"** is the example that gives the warning its force. He made the tree look worth eating from, and what followed was that the two of them were carried out of the garden. What he wanted, and what he got, was to move the father of mankind out of the dwelling of comfort and into the dwelling of hardship and fatigue, which is this life.

**"and caused their cover to be removed in order to expose their nakedness"** is the second thing he did. The robe that was torn off them was the robe of light. One reading gives the detail that their private part had been hidden from Adam before, and that uncovering it is what showed how deep the hatred ran. Another reading explains why the two of them cannot see him, and says that their breasts are his dwelling places.

**"Surely he and his soldiers watch you from where you cannot see them"** states the position the reader is in. The word for his soldiers means his company or his group, and a joined family group takes its name from the same root. The sense of the line is that the enemy and his accomplices do see you, and you do not see them. Other verses have made clear as well that the snare of Shaytan is far too weak to hold a person who keeps turning to Allah and keeps his guard up. What the end of this verse says, that the devils are made the friends and guardians of those who do not believe, also shows that the believers should find it no great difficulty to stay out of that net.

One gloss explains the invisibility in physical terms. They have ethereal bodies, or they are without colour. Another reading of it, given in Rūḥ al-Maʿānī, puts it in terms of general conditions and habit, which is to say that the statement describes the ordinary run of things. If a human being were to see them against the ordinary run, that would not count as a contradiction of it. That is what happened when the jinn came to the Holy Prophet ﷺ, asked him questions and embraced Islam, and this appears in authentic narrations of hadith.

**"We have made the devils allies of those who disbelieve"** is the closing statement, and it explains why the guard has to be kept up. The disbelievers did not simply fall into the net. The allies were given to them.

### How the guard is kept

Some righteous elders gave a simple answer to the problem of an enemy who sees us while we cannot see him. The way to defend against him is to come under the protection of Allah, since He sees these satans and watches how they move and act, and they cannot see Him.

The garden is the whole of the story, and it has already been told. Allah warns the children of Adam about Iblīs and those who follow him by setting out the old enmity he holds against the father of mankind. Iblīs schemed to get Adam out of Paradise and to uncover his private part after it had been hidden from him, and that is exactly what deep hatred does. And there is a verse that puts the exchange in its proper light: "Will you then take him and his offspring as protectors and helpers rather than Me, while they are enemies to you?" (18:50).

### In short

- The warning is put as a personal matter: do not let him do to you what he did to the two who came before you.
- He brought them out of the dwelling of comfort and into the dwelling of hardship, and he stripped away the covering that had kept them hidden.
- He and his company see the reader and the reader does not see them, which is what makes the danger real and the guard necessary.
- The defence named is to come under the protection of the One whom the satans cannot see, and the promise attached to taqwā is that his snare is weak for anyone who keeps turning to Allah.

28.text:
The verse takes up an argument the idolaters were making for themselves. "Whenever they commit a shameful deed, they say, "We found our forefathers doing it and Allah has commanded us to do it." Say, "No! Allah never commands what is shameful. How can you attribute to Allah what you do not know?"" The verse does not argue about which practice is being defended. It goes straight to the two defences that were being offered for it, and it takes them apart one at a time.

### Phrase by phrase

**"Whenever they commit a shameful deed"** names the act. The word Fāḥishah is the word for any evil act whose evil has reached the furthest limit and is loud and clear to ordinary sense and sound taste. According to most commentators the deed intended here is the walking round the House while naked, and the word also covers idolatry.

**"they say, "We found our forefathers doing it""** is the first defence, and it is an appeal to custom. It is a defence that a person of average sense can see through. A practice cannot be justified by the bare fact that one's ancestors followed it. If that were a sufficient reason, then the ancestors of every people on earth followed different and contradictory practices, and every wrong practice in the world would stand justified by it. The argument does not deserve an answer, and the Qur'an does not spend one on it here. Some narrations do answer it, and what they say is that an ignorant act committed by one's forefathers is worth nothing at all as a model.

**"and Allah has commanded us to do it"** is the second defence, and this one is a lie. They were laying on Allah a command He had never given. The answer to it is short: Allah never bids anything shameful. Commanding such a thing would run against His wisdom and against His being the purest of the pure.

**"Say, "No! Allah never commands what is shameful.""** is that answer, spoken to the Prophet ﷺ so that he can deliver it. What the practice amounted to was a despicable sin, and the claim that Allah had ordered it was the opposite of the truth.

**"How can you attribute to Allah what you do not know?"** is the rebuke, and the question is meant as a repudiation. What it charges them with is saying something about Allah on no evidence. That is rank effrontery in any case. When it is done in the case of Allah, it is a crime beyond the reach of imagination.

### What the practice was

Before Islam, one of the shameful customs Shaytan had planted among the people of the age of ignorance was this: nobody except the Quraysh was allowed to walk round the Kaʿbah in his own clothes. A man either borrowed a garment from a Qurayshi, or he made the circuit naked.

The Quraysh, who were known as al-Ḥums, wore their ordinary clothes for the ṭawāf. Anyone from the other Arab tribes who managed to borrow a garment from them wore that borrowed garment for it. Anyone who wore a new garment of his own discarded it when the circuit was finished, and after that nobody would wear it. Those who had no new garment, and who were not given one by al-Ḥums, had no way left but to go round with nothing on.

Mujāhid described the scene. The idolaters used to walk round the House while naked, saying that they did the ṭawāf the way their mothers had given birth to them. The women went round naked as well, and a woman would cover her sexual organ with something and say, as she did it, that some of it or all of it would appear today, but that whatever appeared of it was not permitted to anyone. In practice the women took care to make their circuit at night. The Quraysh could not possibly have clothed the whole of Arabia, so the outcome of the custom was that most people performed the ṭawāf naked, men and women alike.

The whole business was an invention of the idolaters, and they followed nobody in it but their own forefathers. Then they dressed the invention up as the law of Allah. That is the exact claim the verse refutes.

### The four kinds of cattle

Another form of the same argument appears in the matter of the cattle. The idolaters had taken four names out of the herds and declared them forbidden. These were al-Bahīrah, as-Sāʾibah, al-Waṣīlah and al-Ḥām. When they were challenged about it, they said again that they had found their fathers keeping to the practice and that Allah had commanded it. The answer given is that Allah does not command indecency, and that the forbidding of these animals was not a command of His at all.

What the two cases have in common is the way a human decision is moved backward in time until it looks like a tradition, and then moved upward until it looks like a revelation. The verse closes both doors at once when it says that Allah never commands what is shameful, and that nothing may be said about Him except what is known.

### A note on this verse and legal reasoning

One thing needs to be said clearly, because the verse could be misread. The recognised jurists, when they work out and state rulings by ijtihād from the verses of the Qur'an, are not doing what this verse condemns. Their reasoning works inside the words and the meanings that the Qur'an has given, and it rests on them. What the verse condemns is the opposite: a claim laid on Allah with no evidence behind it at all.

### How the enemy works on a person

The way Satan leads a man astray is by giving him wrong information. He makes the forbidden tree look like the fountainhead of every advantage. And he comes at a person by paths so innocuous that the man never suspects he is being misled. He knows the weak points and the delicate places in a person's moral armour, and he attacks exactly those places.

There is a further question in the verse about who he succeeds with. He succeeds with the people who cannot give an account of their faith when they are tested. He succeeds with those who do not think carefully about the signs of God, with those who turn down sound argument, and with those who cannot live up to what truth demands of them when it goes against their own inclinations. People of that kind do not recognise the truth as truth if it does not promote their interests.

### In short

- The verse answers the two defences the idolaters gave for a shameful practice, one from custom and one from a supposed command of Allah.
- The custom defended was the naked ṭawāf, imposed on every tribe except the Quraysh, and the four forbidden kinds of cattle were defended the same way.
- The appeal to forefathers proves nothing, since the ancestors of different peoples did contradictory things and every wrong practice in the world could be justified by it.
- The appeal to a command of Allah was a plain lie, and the rebuke is that they were saying things about Allah that they did not know.
- Satan misleads by misinformation delivered on innocent-looking paths, and he succeeds with those who cannot answer for their faith when tested.

29.text:
The command turns from what Allah never ordered to what He has ordered. "Say, ˹O Prophet,˺ “My Lord has commanded uprightness and dedication ˹to Him alone˺ in worship, calling upon Him with sincere devotion. Just as He first brought you into being, you will be brought to life again.”" Two verses earlier the wrong thing was being attributed to Allah. Here the right thing is set out in three parts, and the last part of it is a fact about the reader.

### Phrase by phrase

**"My Lord has commanded uprightness"** is the first part. The word used is al-qist, and it means justice, balance and moderation. In this place it refers to a conduct that has neither excess nor deficiency, one that neither falls short of the appointed limits nor goes past them. That is how the injunctions of the Sharīʿah work as a whole. So under this one word come all the acts of worship and obedience and every general injunction of the law. One of the early readings of the word takes it as the confession of Allah's oneness, that there is no god but Allah.

**"and dedication ˹to Him alone˺ in worship"** translates the instruction to set the face upright, and to do it at every place of worship. Most commentators take the place of worship here in the sense of prostration, so that the words mean a person should be upright and straight at the time of every prayer and every other act of worship. It can also mean that a person should take care to keep his orientation straight towards the qiblah. And it can reach further still. Keeping the orientation straight can mean putting everything one says and does under what Allah has commanded, holding to one stance that never varies and never drifts off elsewhere. Read that way, the instruction is not confined to the prayer. It takes in every act of worship, every dealing and every transaction.

**"calling upon Him with sincere devotion"** is the second of the two specific injunctions, and it belongs to the heart rather than to the body. It means worshipping Allah purely and alone, without making anything else a partner in the act in any capacity. The purity demanded reaches as far as what is called concealed shirk, the association of something else with the divinity of Allah. Under that heading come hypocrisy and showing off.

**"Just as He first brought you into being, you will be brought to life again."** is the third part. It was He who made you the first time, and it will be He who raises you again on the day of Qiyamah. For His perfect power this is not difficult at all. Perhaps it is to point to that ease that the verse says "you will return" and does not say "We shall make you rise". Bringing a person back requires no effort. Several commentators gave readings along these lines. Mujāhid read it as a promise of life after death. Al-Ḥasan al-Baṣrī read it as: the One who began you here will raise you on the Day of Resurrection. Qatādah said that He started their creation when they were nothing, that they perished afterwards, and that He will bring them back again. ʿAbdur-Raḥmān ibn Zayd ibn Aslam said that as He created you at the start, He will bring you back at the end. This last reading was preferred by Ibn Jarīr, who supported it with what he reported from Ibn ʿAbbās.

### The outward and the inward together

The two specific injunctions are placed side by side on purpose, and one of them concerns what a person does outwardly while the other concerns his heart. The indication is that both dimensions of a person have to be put right and held together in line with the Sharīʿah. Obvious obedience is not enough on its own without sincerity, and sincerity of the heart does not become sufficient on its own without following the Sharīʿah in what people can see.

This is where a common error is exposed. Some people treat the Sharīʿah, the outward adherence to the faith, and the ṭarīqah, the inward adherence to it, as two different roads to religion. Some of them even suppose that it is enough to put the inward dimension right, even if they do what contradicts the Sharīʿah. That is a glaring mistake.

### What justice means in practice

This is one of those short passages in which a great deal has been gathered together. The foundations of service are in it, and so are the signposts of practice and the realities of recognition. It teaches the faithful which character traits please their Lord, and what beautiful worship of Him looks like, and what beautiful living with His creatures looks like. What is commanded is justice, and that justice runs in three directions at once.

Towards the Real, it means putting the commands and the prohibitions to work, and being content with His decree in every state. Towards the creatures, it means living with good character, giving them what is fair in the various dealings between people, and not demanding fairness for oneself. Towards the soul, it means setting oneself against it, drawing it into discipline and struggle, and closing the door on appetite and comfort.

The same thought appears in another verse, where Allah commands justice and beautiful doing (16:90). And the mark of a passage like this one is that a great deal of knowledge has been gathered into very few words. A short verse elsewhere carries the same weight, where Allah says that He is with those who are mindful of Him and those who do good (16:128). Everything the Real gives to a servant is contained in the first half of that promise. Everything the servant does for Allah comes under the second. And everything that people owe to one another comes under the third.

### Why the mention of the life to come stands here

There is a benefit in the sentence about being brought back again standing where it does. It is what makes the injunctions of the Sharīʿah bearable. What makes a hard thing easy and a painful thing endurable is the settled conviction that another life is coming, with a Last Day in it and reward and punishment for every deed. Experience confirms it. A person is a hard case, and unless he is held by that apprehension no piece of advice will move him to do what is right, and no restriction of any law will keep him out of crime.

### What was said about the return

The Prophet ﷺ stood up and gave the people a speech, and in it he said:

> O people, you will be gathered to Allah barefoot, naked and uncircumcised. As We began the first creation, We shall repeat it. It is a promise binding upon Us. Truly, We shall do it.

The verse quoted is 21:104, and the report was collected in the two Ṣaḥīḥs. Ibn ʿAbbās commented on the return in another way. Allah began the creation of the sons of Adam as some believers and some disbelievers, just as He said: "He it is Who created you, then some of you are disbelievers and some of you are believers" (64:2). He will bring them back on the Day of Resurrection as He started them, some believing and some not. The hadith that supports this is the one al-Bukhārī recorded from Ibn Masʿūd, in which the Prophet ﷺ said:

> By He other than Whom there is no god, one of you might do the deeds of the people of Paradise until only the length of an arm or a forearm is left between him and it. Then what was written in the Book takes precedence, and he does the work of the people of the Fire and enters it. And one of you might do the deeds of the people of the Fire until only the length of an arm or a forearm is left between him and the Fire. Then what was written in the Book takes precedence, and he does the work of the people of Paradise and enters Paradise.

Held together with this reading, the Qur'an also says: "So set your face towards the religion, turning away from all else. That is the natural disposition Allah instilled in people" (30:30). And the two Ṣaḥīḥs record from Abū Hurayrah that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "Every child is born upon the fiṭrah, and it is only his parents who turn him into a Jew, a Christian or a Zoroastrian."

### In short

- What Allah commands is justice, which here means a conduct with neither excess nor deficiency, and it takes in every injunction of the law.
- The instruction to be upright at every place of prostration covers the outward act and reaches as far as holding everything one does under the command of Allah.
- Sincere devotion covers the heart, and it rules out concealed shirk along with hypocrisy and showing off. The two together mean the outward and the inward must both be put right.
- The return to life is certain, and it is mentioned here because the certainty of it is what makes the injunctions bearable in practice.
- Justice runs in three directions: towards Allah in obeying and accepting His decree, towards people in dealing fairly and asking nothing for oneself, and towards one's own soul in opposing it.

30.text:
The third verse names the two outcomes. "He has guided some, while others are destined to stray. They have taken devils as their masters instead of Allah—thinking they are ˹rightly˺ guided". The sentence is short and it separates two groups by name and by judgement. And the second group is not a group that knew it was lost. It is a group that believed it was on the right road.

### Phrase by phrase

**"He has guided some"** names the first group. What they were given is the knowledge and the felicity that Allah honoured them with, and they are the people of the right hand, the people of the right.

**"while others are destined to stray"** names the second. What has come down on them is denial and damnation, and they are the people of the left. The wording is exact: error was not merely something that happened to them. It was prescribed over them.
