Others explain it as what they say when they see the favour Allah showed them by giving them faith, so that they say that praise and thanks belong to Allah who guided them to the religion of Islam.

**"We would have never been guided if Allah had not guided us."** is the second half of the sentence. In the Arabic the words are built on a conditional construction with the answer to the condition left out, because the preceding clause already carries it.

**"The messengers of our Lord had certainly come with the truth."** is the third thing they say. The messengers brought truth itself, and with it the glad tidings and the reward.

**"It will be announced to them, “This is Paradise awarded to you for what you used to do.”"** is the cry that greets them in answer to their own words. This is the garden, and it is what they inherit for what they used to do and say of good in the life of this world.

### The bitterness that has to be cleared first

As-Suddī described how the removal is done on the way in. The people of the garden are brought to it and find a tree close to its door, with two springs running from beneath its trunk. They drink from one spring, and all hatred is drawn out of their hearts, because that is the cleansing drink. In the other they bathe, and the brightness of delight shines out of their faces. After that, none of them ever has unkempt hair or becomes dirty.

The first half of the verse is doing real work, and it is worth taking slowly. Believers will have crossed the bridge of Ṣirāṭ, and once their deliverance from Jahannam is certain they will be held back on a bridge that lies between the garden and the fire, so that ill will can be cleared out of them first. If one had a grudge against another, or ill feeling, or a heartache over a right that was lost, all of it will be settled between them and washed away there and then. So when they enter the garden they are free of malice and hatred and animosity and the other disorders of that kind. It appears in one tafsīr that this bridge is the last part of the bridge of Ṣirāṭ, the part closest to the garden, and ʿAllāmah as-Suyūṭī also chose that reading.

Then comes the matter of rights. Nothing can be paid in money for a right that was lost, since nobody there will have any. What is used instead is the currency of deeds. Abū Saʿīd al-Khudrī reported the hadith in al-Bukhārī on how that is done, and it is al-Bukhārī above all who carries it. The deed of the one who took the right is handed to the one whose right it was. And if the wrongdoer's deeds run out while rights are still outstanding, then the sins of the person whose right is unsettled are moved across to the account of the one who took it.

In a hadith the Holy Prophet ﷺ called the person who did good deeds in this world but was careless about the rights of people the greatest pauper, because the neglect lost him all his good deeds and left him standing there with nothing.

That is the general rule for settling rights and avenging wrongs in the fire. It is not necessary that everyone should meet that exact situation, and it is possible that ill feeling is removed without any settling of scores at all. Abū Hurayrah reported from the Prophet ﷺ that each of the people of the garden will be shown his seat in the fire and will say that Allah had guided him, and that this will make him grateful, while each of the people of the fire will be shown his seat in the garden and will wish that he had been guided, and that this will be his anguish. Some narrations describe what happens when people have crossed the bridge: they arrive at a stream and drink from it, and the property of that water is that it takes every trace of ill will out of their hearts. Al-Qurṭubī explains the verse about those who are given a pure drink (76:21) in the same way, that the grudges in the hearts are washed out by it.

ʿAlī al-Murtadā recited this verse once and then said that he hoped that he and ʿUthmān, Ṭalḥah and az-Zubayr would be among those whose hearts are cleansed of ill feeling before they enter the garden. Those men had disagreed with one another in their lifetime to the point of fighting, and the hope is that the verse covers them all the same.

### What their own words show

When they say that they would never have been guided if Allah had not guided them, they are stating a fact about everyone. Nobody enters the garden on personal effort alone. What makes it possible is the grace of Allah, and there is a further point in that. Even the effort a person makes is not within his own control. That too comes by the grace and the mercy of Allah.

Guidance itself is worth understanding properly. Rāghib al-Isfahānī explained hidāyah, guidance, as it is used across the Qur'an, and his point is that the word is a familiar one that has many degrees. Guidance is another name for finding the way that leads to Allah. Since the degrees of nearness to Allah are many, different and without end, the degrees of guidance are varied and different in the same way.

The lowest degree of guidance is deliverance from kufr and from shirk, along with īmān, faith. A person at that degree has had his direction changed, so that he is turned away from the path of error and towards Allah. After that there is the distance between Allah and His servants, and that distance is a journey with stages to travel. Every stage covered has its degrees, and those degrees are what guidance means. So guidance is a need that never lapses. At no point can a person say that he no longer needs it, and that includes the prophets and the messengers. It is for that reason that the Holy Prophet ﷺ not only taught his people to ask for the straight path but kept making that prayer himself, since the stages and ranks of nearness have no end. And it is for the same reason that entry into the garden mentioned in this verse is itself called guidance, because it is the last station of it.

### What the two destinations are like for the people in them

The position in the fire is that people who were friends in this world hate and curse one another. The air of the garden is the opposite. There every heart is open, and love and goodwill for others rise out of all of them.

There is a difference in memory as well. For the person in the fire, his past becomes a bitter recollection, and the life of the evil begins with a heart that is a graveyard of regret and frustration. For the good, the memory is pleasant. Their minds are full of the remembrance of God, the One they trusted, and they are glad to find that everything the bearers of the truth told them turned out to be exactly right. They recognise the grace of God in having blessed them and inspired them to stand with those who called them to accept the truth.

### The inner reading

There is also an inner reading of the passage, and this is the description of the followers of the path and the travellers on the road of reality. The Exalted Lord begins by making their hearts clean of caprice and of invented practice, so that they can step onto the road of the Sunnah and find their way to the plain text of the Book and to the Sunnah of Muṣṭafā ﷺ. They let go of their own imagination and their own understanding in the matter of the divine attributes, and they set aside the discernment of their own intelligence. They bow their necks in compliance, accept with their hearing, and set out on the road of surrender, and in that way they escape both from likening Allah to His creation and from declaring Him ineffective.

Then, a second time, He cleans their hearts of this world and of its defilement, so that the light of recognising Him shines in them and the eyes of wisdom open in them. He honours them with His gaze. He removes the love of creatures from their hearts, so that they are wholly with Him. They go forward in the reality of being alone with Him, and come back from secondary causes to the One who causes them. They see One, they hear One, and they reach One. Their tongues are busy with remembrance, their hearts with reflection and their spirits with love. They mention Him with the tongue, whisper with the heart, and rejoice in the spirit.

And here is the condition attached to all of it. Until the covenant that has no beginning takes hold of your hem, your heart will not accept this work. Until the Real joins with you, this path will not go along with you. Until the Real gazes on you, your heart will not want Him.

The announcement that this garden is inherited for what they used to do is spoken to soothe the heart of the servant and to increase the kindness shown to him. Otherwise the servant knows perfectly well that his own careless deeds do not deserve a threshold like that, and that those stations and degrees are not the wage for acts such as his. But through His bounty He makes the unworthy worthy and adorns what was displeasing, and in that He shows the servant His good godhood and His loving kindness.

### In short

- The verse names two things for the people of the garden: ill feeling of every kind is taken out of their hearts, and rivers flow beneath them.
- Ill will is cleared on a bridge between the garden and the fire, and the loss of rights is settled in the currency of deeds, as the two Ṣaḥīḥ collections record.
- Their words of praise are words about guidance, and nobody reaches the garden by personal effort alone, since even the effort comes by the grace of Allah.
- Guidance has many degrees, from deliverance out of kufr and shirk to the last station, which is entry into the garden itself, and no one outgrows the need for it.
- The verse is read as a description of hearts made clean of their own caprice, so that the road of the Sunnah and the plain text can be found.

44.text:
The two groups are placed where they can hear each other. "The residents of Paradise will call out to the residents of the Fire, “We have certainly found our Lord's promise to be true. Have you too found your Lord's promise to be true?” They will reply, “Yes, we have!” Then a caller will announce to both, “May Allah's condemnation be upon the wrongdoers"". The verse gives one question, one answer, and one verdict over both sides at once.

### Phrase by phrase

**"The residents of Paradise will call out to the residents of the Fire"** sets the scene. The call may be read as a statement of the truth or as a rebuke delivered to people who did not believe it.

**"We have certainly found our Lord's promise to be true."** is what the people of the garden say, and what they found true is the reward and the favour that had been promised to them. They have entered it, so the promise is now something they know by being in it.

**"Have you too found your Lord's promise to be true?"** is the question put to the other side. What is meant is the torment and the humiliation that had been promised to them.

**"They will reply, “Yes, we have!”"** is the answer, and it is short. The people of the fire give it when they have all taken their places. Another reading has them adding that they have found what was promised about the fire to be true.

**"Then a caller will announce to both"** describes a herald who proclaims between the two parties, making himself heard by both.

**"May Allah's condemnation be upon the wrongdoers"** is the proclamation. Another reading takes the word for the condemnation as meaning the torment of Allah, so that the announcement is that the torment rests on the wrongdoers, and that it stays with them. And another reading gives the sense of the proclamation: that the wrongdoers are to be removed from the mercy of Allah, because the doors of the mercy were open to them in their life and they turned away from them.

### The question people used to ask

In early times the question was raised how the voices of the people of the garden could reach the people of the fire at all, when the two places are so far apart, one above the skies and the other at the lowest level there is. In the present age of mass communication that question has become relative. It is now known that people can see things far away and hear voices from far away, so what was unclear in earlier times is understandable now.

The lesson drawn from that is stated carefully. If some statement of the Qur'an cannot be analysed in the light of present knowledge, nothing should be concluded against it, because with the growth of knowledge it may become an accepted fact tomorrow. What the modern discoveries show is only that in this universe of God there are arrangements by which two people far apart can see and speak to one another without difficulty. The discoveries do not mean that in the Hereafter the two groups will be connected by radio or television.

### Why the arguments never reached them

Only a person who takes an argument seriously, and means it when he asks, will feel its weight. The people who give the Hereafter no importance cannot see the point of any argument about the life to come. The reality of that life rests on evidence of the strongest kind, and such people, with their minds never properly engaged, do nothing with it but hunt for supposed defects. They raise objections of various kinds, and the result is that they themselves come to hold suspicions and doubts about it and they incline other people towards disbelief as well. Such people are, in the sight of God, guilty in the extreme. In the Hereafter they meet the scourge of God, though in this world they may have counted themselves entitled to His grace.

What follows from that is a warning about clever speech. There is no argument so strong that somebody cannot throw doubt over it with a well-turned phrase. Ordinary people cannot always tell real argument from sophistry, and so they are pulled off the truth by hearing such talk. And the people who are capable of understanding the truth and still use clever words to drive others away from it will be very far from the grace of God on the Day of Reckoning.

### The Prophet ﷺ at the well of Badr

The other half of the verse is about the punishment for that. The messenger of Allah ﷺ stood at the well of Badr and addressed the men thrown into it. He called them by name, Abū Jahl bin Hishām and ʿUtbah bin Rabīʿah and Shaybah bin Rabīʿah and the other leaders of the town, and he asked them whether they had found what their Lord promised them to be true, telling them that he had certainly found what his Lord promised him to be true, which was victory. ʿUmar asked him whether he was addressing people who had become rotten corpses. He answered, by He in Whose Hand is my soul, that they did not hear what he was saying any better than ʿUmar did, but that they could not reply. And the report is in the two Ṣaḥīḥ collections.

The verse and the scene belong together. The question the people of the garden will put to the people of the fire is the same question the Prophet ﷺ put to the men in the well, and the answer in both cases is the same.

### What the Qur'an says of the same moment elsewhere

In Sūrat aṣ-Ṣāffāt, the man in the garden looks down and sees his old companion in the middle of the fire, and says that by Allah the other nearly ruined him, and that had it not been for the grace of his Lord he would have been among those brought forth to it. Then the people of the garden say: are we then not to die any more, except for our first death, and are we not to be punished (37:55-59)?

And the Qur'an says that the disbeliever is punished for the claims he used to make in this life. This is the fire that you used to deny. Is this magic, or do you not see? Taste it, and whether you bear it patiently or impatiently, it is all the same, since you are only being repaid for what you used to do (52:14-16).

### The verdict and who it falls on

The proclamation names them wrongdoers, and the verse that follows says who they are. They held people back from the path of Allah, they wanted to make that path look crooked and winding so that nobody would follow it, and they disbelieved in the Hereafter. They denied that the meeting with Allah would ever take place, and they refused to accept it or believe in it. Because they had no fear of any reckoning or any punishment, they made light of the evil they said and did. That is why they were, and remain, the worst of people in what they say and in what they do.

### In short

- The people of the garden call to the people of the fire and ask whether the promise they were warned with turned out to be true, and the answer is yes.
- A herald proclaims between both parties that the condemnation of Allah rests on the wrongdoers, and they are the ones removed from His mercy.
- The old question about how the two groups could hear each other is answered by noting that distance is no obstacle in the arrangements of God's universe, and nothing should be concluded against a verse because present knowledge cannot yet analyse it.
- The same question was put by the Prophet ﷺ to the men thrown into the well at Badr, and they also could not reply.
- Sūrat aṣ-Ṣāffāt and the passage about the fire the disbelievers used to deny say the same thing about the state of the two groups.

45.text:
The verse completes the description the herald's words began. "those who hindered ˹others˺ from Allah's Way, strived to make it ˹appear˺ crooked, and disbelieved in the Hereafter."

### Phrase by phrase

**"those who hindered ˹others˺ from Allah's Way"** names what they did to other people. They kept people back from the path of Allah, which is His religion and the obedience He asks for. They turned others away from it.

**"strived to make it ˹appear˺ crooked"** is the second charge, and it is worse than the first. They did not merely stay away themselves. They worked at making the path look crooked and winding, so that nobody seeing it would want to walk it. Another reading gives the sense as wanting the way changed.

**"and disbelieved in the Hereafter"** is the third charge, and it explains the other two. They rejected the resurrection after death and did not prepare for it.

### Why the three charges belong together

The three are put in an order that runs from the outside in. First the harm done to others, by blocking them from the road. Then the deliberate work of making the road itself look unattractive. And behind both of those, the thing that made them possible, which is not believing that there is an account to be given.

Nothing about the punishment is settled yet at this point. The verse before gave the verdict that the condemnation of Allah is on the wrongdoers. This verse names the wrongdoers, and the naming is the evidence for the verdict. There is no wrong that is being punished here other than the three things set out, and the third of them is the root of the other two. A person who does not expect to be asked about what he did is free to block other people and to spoil the road for them, and he does it without a second thought.

### In short

- The verse names the people the verdict has just fallen on, and it names three things they did.
- They blocked others from the way of Allah, they worked to make the way look crooked, and they disbelieved in the life to come.
- The third charge is the root of the first two, since a person who expects no account has no reason to leave the road clear.
- Another reading gives the crookedness as wanting the way changed rather than simply misrepresenting it.

46.text:
A third group now appears. "There will be a barrier between Paradise and Hell. And on the heights ˹of that barrier˺ will be people who will recognize ˹the residents of˺ both by their appearance. They will call out to the residents of Paradise, “Peace be upon you!” They will have not yet entered Paradise, but eagerly hope to". The verse names the dividing wall, names the people standing on top of it, and says how they know the two crowds below.

### Phrase by phrase

**"There will be a barrier between Paradise and Hell"** is the wall that keeps the people of the fire from reaching the garden. Ibn Jarīr said that this is the wall Allah described elsewhere, where a wall will be put up between them with a gate in it, and inside it will be mercy while outside it will be torment (57:13). As-Suddī said the same in fewer words, that the screen is the wall, and that the wall is al-Aʿrāf. Mujāhid said that al-Aʿrāf is a barrier between the garden and the fire, and that it is a wall with a gate.

**"And on the heights ˹of that barrier˺ will be people"** names where they stand. The word for the heights is a plural of a word meaning the highest part of anything, and the Arabs use it for every elevated piece of land. As-Suddī explained the name in another way, that the place is called al-Aʿrāf because the people on it recognise the people below. The top portion of the wall between the garden and the fire is what the word names, and since the top of a thing is distinct and can be made out from a distance, the word fits it.

**"who will recognize ˹the residents of˺ both by their appearance"** describes what they can do from where they stand. They know the people who enter the fire by the marks on them, and they know the people who enter the garden by theirs. The signs are given plainly: the faces of the people of the fire are darkened and their eyes are blue, while the faces of the people of the garden are bright and glowing, at once handsome and radiant.

**"They will call out to the residents of Paradise, “Peace be upon you!”"** is the greeting. It is the greeting the people of the heights give to the people of the garden, and they give it in honour of them.

**"They will have not yet entered Paradise, but eagerly hope to"** describes their own position. The people on the wall have not gone in yet, and what they have in place of it is hope.

### Who the people of the heights are

Commentators differ over who these people are and why they are made to stop there, and the narrations about them vary as well. What carries weight and is accepted by the majority is that these are the people whose good deeds and bad deeds come out equal on the scale. Because of the good they did they are delivered from the fire, and because of the sins they carry they have not yet been admitted to the garden.

This is what was said by Hudhayfah, by Ibn Masʿūd and by Ibn ʿAbbās among the Companions, and by others among the Companions and the generation after them. The narrations converge in the same direction. Hudhayfah was asked about the people of al-Aʿrāf, and his answer was that they are people whose good and evil actions balance each other. What they did wrong kept them short of the garden, and what they did right was enough to keep them out of the fire, and so they are held there on the wall until Allah judges them.

Ibn Jarīr reports from Hudhayfah that the Holy Prophet ﷺ was asked about the people of al-Aʿrāf and said that they are a people whose good deeds and bad deeds are equal. They are delivered from Jahannam, and they have not yet entered the garden. They are held back at that place until the accounting of deeds and the judgement are finished. After that their case is decided, and in the end they are forgiven and brought into the garden.

There is another narration, from Jābir ibn ʿAbdullah, reported by Ibn Marduwayh, in which the Holy Prophet ﷺ was asked who the people of al-Aʿrāf are. He said that they are people who took part in the fighting without the consent of their parents, and who gave up their lives in the way of Allah. The disobedience to their parents is what kept them out of the garden, and the shahādah in the way of Allah is what kept them out of the fire.

The two narrations do not contradict each other. The second is an example of the same equality of virtue and vice, with martyrdom in the way of Allah on one side of the scale and disobedience to parents on the other, and the two weighing the same.

### What the hope on their faces means

Maʿmar said that al-Ḥasan al-Baṣrī recited this passage of the verse about them not having entered yet although they hope to, and then said: by Allah, Allah did not plant this hope in their hearts except for an honour He intends to give them. Qatādah said that those who hope are the ones among you whom Allah informed of their places on the Day of Resurrection. And al-Ḥākim reported that Hudhayfah ibn al-Yamān said that while they are standing in that state, God appears to them and says: rise up and enter the garden, for I have forgiven you.

### Three groups, and the wall that separates them

The verses of Sūrat al-Ḥadīd set out what the wall is for. They tell of three groups of people on the Day of Resurrection. The first are the declared disbelievers and those who associated partners with Allah, who never reach the bridge of Ṣirāṭ at all, because they are thrown into the fire through its doors before that stage is reached.

The second are the believers, who have the light of their faith with them as they walk. The third are the hypocrites, who followed the believers about in this world and who therefore start out behind them on the same path. When they begin walking on the bridge, a heavy darkness comes over them all. The believers keep moving ahead on the strength of their light, and the hypocrites call out to them to wait, so that they can take some of that light. Then a caller calls out for the sake of Allah: turn back, and find your light where you came from. The meaning is that the light they want is the light of faith and of good deeds, and that it could only be got at the place they have left behind. Whoever did not get that light there, through faith and through deeds, will not have the benefit of it here.

And in that state a wall is set up between the hypocrites and the believers. The wall has a gate. Beyond the gate there is nothing but punishment, and inside it are the believers with the mercy of Allah filling the air and the garden in view. The verses put it as follows. On the Day when the hypocrites, men and women alike, will turn to those who believed and ask them to hold back and spare a share of their light, the answer they get is that they should go back where they came from and look for light there. And then a wall will be put between them with a gate in it, and inside the gate will be mercy, and outside it, facing them, the punishment (57:13).

The word used for the wall in that verse is the word for a wall built round a great city. Such a wall is usually wide and fortified, with guards posted in it who keep watch against enemies. And the word used in this verse for the barrier is a different one, meaning a screen. Ibn Jarīr and other authorities hold that the screen in this verse is the same wall that the other verse calls by the city-wall word, and that the top of it is al-Aʿrāf.

### Why these meeting points exist

When the people of the garden reach the garden where they belong and the people of the fire reach the fire where they belong, the two places are far apart in every respect. Even so, many verses of the Qur'an confirm that between the two there will be points from which one side can see the other and hold a conversation with it.

Sūrat aṣ-Ṣāffāt tells of two men who knew each other in this life, one a believer and one a disbeliever. In the Hereafter the believer goes to the garden and the disbeliever to the fire, and they notice each other and speak (37:55). When the friend in the garden looks for the friend in the fire, he finds him lying in the middle of it, and he curses him, remarking that he had wanted him ruined along with himself, and that had it not been for the grace of Allah he would have been lying there too. Then he reminds him of what he used to say in the world, that there was no life after death, no accounting, no reward and no punishment. He can now see for himself what the reality is.

Conversations of that kind between the people of the garden and the people of the fire appear not only in those verses but continue through almost a whole section of the Qur'an.

And the meeting points are themselves a punishment of a kind for the people of the fire. They find themselves reproached from every side. They see the blessings being enjoyed by the people of the garden, and they burn with rage at having missed them, and they are already burning in the fire. For the people of the garden the same view is a comfort of another kind. Having seen the plight of the people in the fire, they are more grateful for what they have been given. Then they remember the people who used to mock them for believing, and who could do nothing against them, and when they see those people disgraced and punished in the end, they have the last laugh at their undoing.

Sūrat al-Muṭaffifīn says the same: on that Day those who believed will be laughing at the disbelievers, seated on raised couches watching, and the disbelievers will have been repaid for what they used to do (83:34-36). And against the record of the people of the fire, the admonition also comes from the angels, who tell them that this is the fire they used to deny, and ask whether this is magic or whether they simply do not see (52:14-15).

### The greeting itself

The greeting the people of the heights give is one we already use in this world. When people meet, the greeting is offered as a gift and as a mark of respect and goodwill for the one greeted. It is a sunnah practice, a way the Holy Prophet ﷺ lived by and recommended to his community. The same words are said to the dead when their graves are visited. The same words will serve as the greeting on the plain where all are gathered, and in the garden itself.

Looking closely at the Qur'an and the narrations, there is a distinction worth noting. The full greeting with the definite article at the front is what is prescribed while we are alive in this world. Once a person has left this world, what is prescribed is the form of the words without that article at the beginning. The greeting given to the people of the garden in one verse runs in that form, peace be upon you for what you patiently endured, and how excellent is the final home (13:24). And when the angels receive the people of the garden it appears in the same form, peace be upon you, you have done well, so enter it to live there for ever (39:73). And here, on the heights, the people on the wall greet the people of the garden with the same words.

### The inner reading

What sort of people are these, that the Exalted Lord should give them the name of men? A wind of solicitude and a breeze of kind favour passed over them suddenly from the side of nearness. Everyone knows what happens when the north wind blows across a rose, and the rose leaves its scent behind it in the garden. When the wind of His care passes over these people, it wakes their hearts with the light that comes from recognising Him. It makes their spirits sweet with the perfume of union with Him, and it brightens what is hidden in them with the polish of His care. It lets them enjoy the company of aspiration and the beauty of conduct, so that they lift their aims altogether away from creatures and busy themselves with love for the Real.

The yearning for Him has left the one who yearns bewildered in His street. Cut off from creatures, he is content with rags. His eyes are like a ring of pearls from the burning in his heart, and his sighs like a string of coral from the fire in it.

So in this world the Exalted Lord lets them look down on the inner lives and the states of the servants, and in the world to come He will let them look down on the stations and degrees of the faithful. He raises their standing above that of all creatures, so that they see everyone while nobody sees them, and know everyone while nobody knows them. Hence the words of the verse about recognising each one by his marks. Each person carries a mark, and the mark these people carry is that they carry none. Each person stays tied to some quality of his own, and the quality belonging to these people is that they have none.

What holds the people of the fire away from the Real is the chain of opposition. What contents the people of the garden is what has been apportioned to them there. But He keeps these people away from both, and gives them an overview of all. And one of the masters of the path prayed: O God, how lovely are the days Your friends spend with You, how beautiful their practice as they hope to see You, how sweet their conversation on the road as they search for You, how magnificent their time when they are at work in Your cause.

### In short

- A barrier stands between the garden and the fire, and the heights are the top of it, from which both crowds can be seen.
- The people standing there recognise both groups by their marks, the darkened faces of one and the glowing faces of the other.
- The majority reading is that they are the people whose good and bad deeds weigh equally, delivered from the fire and not yet admitted to the garden, and the narrations from Hudhayfah, Ibn Masʿūd, Ibn ʿAbbās and the Prophet ﷺ converge on that.
- A second narration gives them as those who fought without their parents' consent, so that the disobedience and the martyrdom balance each other, and the two accounts do not contradict.
- The verses of Sūrat al-Ḥadīd show what the wall does, and the greeting the people on the heights give is the form of greeting proper to the next life rather than to this one.

47.text:
The other direction. "When their eyes will turn towards the residents of Hell, they will pray, “Our Lord! Do not join us with the wrongdoing people.”"

### Phrase by phrase

**"When their eyes will turn towards the residents of Hell"** describes the look in the other direction from the heights. What they see is the severe punishment that those people are in.

**"they will pray"** marks the turn in the verse. The same people who greeted the people of the garden with a blessing now speak about themselves.

**"“Our Lord! Do not join us with the wrongdoing people.”"** is the prayer, and it is a request to be kept out of their company. What the wrongdoing is, another reading spells out: they disbelieved and they worshipped others besides Allah.

### What the two looks do

The verse completes the picture that the one before it began, and the two verses, 46 and 47, describe the same group from the two directions. From the top of the wall the people of the heights can look both ways, and the verse gives the two looks in order. And they are people of the early generations as much as of any later time, since the sects and parties of this world are not what carries weight there. First they look at the garden, and what comes out of them is a greeting offered in honour of the people there. Then they look at the fire, and what comes out of them is a prayer about themselves.

The prayer is worth noticing for what it does not say. They do not ask to be admitted to the garden. They ask not to be placed among the wrongdoers. The request is the smallest one a person can put, and it is put by people who have already been told that their good and their bad deeds came out equal, and who have hope and nothing else to stand on. Their own situation is the reason for the prayer. The report from Ibn ʿAbbās has it that when the people of al-Aʿrāf turn their gaze to the people of the fire and make them out, this is the supplication they make.

### In short

- The verse gives the second of the two looks from the heights, and this one is directed at the fire.
- What the people there say is a prayer about themselves, and it asks to be kept out of the company of the wrongdoing.
- The wrongdoing named is disbelief and the worship of others besides Allah.
- They do not ask for the garden. They ask only not to be placed among the wrongdoers, which is the smallest request a person can make.

48.text:
The people on the wall now look the other way and speak. "Those on the heights will call out to some ˹tyrants in the Fire˺, who they will recognize by their appearance, saying, “Your large numbers and arrogance are of no use ˹today˺"". The verse is an admonition delivered from above, and it is delivered to the men who led the crowds below.

### Phrase by phrase

**"Those on the heights will call out"** means the people of al-Aʿrāf, who are still standing where they were in the verse before this one.

**"to some ˹tyrants in the Fire˺"** picks out particular men. They are among the disbelievers, and the people on the wall know them before they go into the fire. The word for them is the word for the chiefs and the great ones.

**"who they will recognize by their appearance"** repeats what the previous verse said about how the two groups are known. The people of the fire are known by the mark on them, which is the darkening of the face and the blueness of the eye.

**"saying, “Your large numbers and arrogance are of no use ˹today˺"** is the admonition itself. Their large numbers did not save them, and their arrogance did not save them. What the words mean is that the great numbers and the wealth did nothing for them at all against the torment of Allah. Instead of being spared, they are the ones dwelling in it.

### They are called by name

One reading of the verse fills in the names, and the names belong to the men who had been the leaders of the town. In that reading they are called out one by one, Walīd ibn al-Mughīrah first, then Abū Jahl ibn Hishām, then Umayyah ibn Khalaf, then Ubayy ibn Khalaf al-Jumahī, then Aswad ibn ʿAbd, of the clan of al-Muṭṭalib, and after them the rest of the leaders. Then the question is put to them, about the multitude of their wealth and their servants, and about the thing they took such pride in, which was what made them scorn belief in Muhammad ﷺ and in the Qur'an.

This is the shape of the admonition. It is not addressed to the crowd. It is addressed to the men the crowd followed, and the question is what all their following came to. The wealth and the power they had leant on, and the pride they had taken in both, went to waste in the one hour when they needed them, and none of that strength worked for them at their hour of need.

### Who the people of the heights are, on another reading

One view, reported from al-Qurṭubī, is that the people of the heights in this verse are the shuhadāʾ, the witnesses. What is meant is those special servants of God who were witnesses, in the service of His religion, to what the nations of the world did. Some of the people they called accepted the call and some rejected it.

People of that kind are mentioned in the Qur'an under many names: warner, bearer of glad tidings, the one who calls. The group began with the prophets and was afterwards made up of those special servants of God who followed the prophets' example and carried the call to the people of their own times. The final judgement on human beings, which will take place in the Hereafter, is based on the task the witnesses performed for the people of the world. That task is what divides the world into two groups, one accepting the divine message and the other rejecting it, and on the Day of Judgement the two groups are separated and judged by their deeds and sent to two different ends.

The judgement is God's judgement entirely, and what these servants do is announce it. That is a great honour for them. On that Day high platforms will be raised for these people to stand on, from which they can see everyone and pronounce God's judgement to the people. Those who bore witness and those who called people to the truth worked hard in the world to carry the message of God to people, and they gave their whole lives to the mission as though it were their own personal work. So the honour done to them on that Day is that they are the ones asked to announce how the call they gave turned out. They ranked high in the world by their mission, and they will be called high-ranked on that Day by the result of what they did.

The task of carrying the message, which has been laid on the Muslims, is not an optional subject that a person may take up or drop when he finds an excuse. It is the kind of duty that must be discharged whatever it costs. No excuse will be heard from the followers of the Prophet ﷺ and found acceptable by God. The other acts of worship and good deeds will not save the believers either, if the duty of carrying the message to all people has been ignored. Men and women by the thousand die every day with nobody having brought them the message of God, and never having had the chance to accept it, they have lost their opportunity to better their state in the life to come. In that situation it is the serious duty of the believers to stop making excuses and take up the mission of proclaiming the divine truth.

### In short

- The people of the heights speak to the chiefs among the people of the fire, and what they know them by is the mark on them. The witnesses, as the word shahādah is used of those who carry the call, are the ones standing there.
- What they say is that the great numbers and the arrogance did nothing for them, since neither saved them from the torment.
- One reading of the verse names the leaders by name, and the question is put to them about the wealth and the pride that made them scorn belief.
- A further view is that the people of the heights are the witnesses, the ones who carried the call to the nations, and on that Day they announce the judgement their call divided people towards.

49.text:
The verse turns the admonition into a question, and then into an announcement. "Are these ˹humble believers˺ the ones you swore would never be shown Allah's mercy?” ˹Finally, those on the heights will be told:˺ “Enter Paradise! There will be no fear for you, nor will you grieve.”"

### Phrase by phrase

**"Are these ˹humble believers˺ the ones you swore would never be shown Allah's mercy?"** is the question put to the people of the fire. What the people of the heights are doing is looking at the dwellers of the garden as they say it. The ones being pointed at are the weak and the lowly among the believers, and the names given in one reading are Salmān al-Fārisī, Ṣuhayb ar-Rūmī, ʿAmmār ibn Yāsir and every other humble and weak believer of the same kind.

**"you swore would never be shown Allah's mercy"** is what the great ones of the world had said about them. They swore in this life that Allah would not show these people mercy and would not bring them into the garden. And the point of the question is that they have gone in, in spite of everything that was said about them.

**"Enter Paradise!"** is then said to the people of the heights themselves. One variant reading has the words as a passive, that they have been admitted, and another has them as a past tense, that they entered. The negation that follows, about no fear and no grief, is a state they are in as they enter, so the sense is that they go in with those words being said over them.

**"There will be no fear for you, nor will you grieve."** means no fear of anything that awaits, and no sorrow over anything that has passed.

### When the announcement comes

Ibn ʿAbbās explained the order of the scene. When the questions and the answers between the people of al-Aʿrāf and the people of the garden and the people of the fire are all finished, the Lord of all the worlds addresses the people of the fire about the people of al-Aʿrāf. He tells them about those people, whom they had sworn would never be forgiven their sins and would never be shown mercy.

Then comes the declaration of mercy, immediately after. The people of al-Aʿrāf are told to go and enter the garden. What they are told about the two fears is exact: there is nothing to fear from what has already happened, and nothing to be anxious about in what is to come. Their past is settled and their future is safe.

### In short

- The question put to the great ones is about the humble believers they had sworn would never see mercy.
- The people being pointed at are the weak and lowly, named in one reading as Salmān al-Fārisī, Ṣuhayb ar-Rūmī and ʿAmmār ibn Yāsir.
- The announcement to the people of the heights themselves is that they should enter the garden, with no fear about the past and no grief about the future.
- The order is that the exchanges finish first, then the Lord speaks to the people of the fire about the people of al-Aʿrāf, and then the declaration of mercy is made to them.

50.text:
The people below now begin to speak, and what they want is small. "The residents of the Fire will then cry out to the residents of Paradise, “Aid us with some water or any provision Allah has granted you.” They will reply, “Allah has forbidden both to the disbelievers"". The verse sets the two groups against each other at the one point where the difference shows most plainly.

### Phrase by phrase

**"The residents of the Fire will then cry out to the residents of Paradise"** begins the asking. The word for crying out is the word for calling at the top of the voice, which is what people do when they have nothing else left.

**"“Aid us with some water or any provision Allah has granted you.”"** is the request. What they ask for is water and food from what the people of the garden have been given. The provisions named are the fruits of the garden.

**"They will reply, “Allah has forbidden both to the disbelievers""** is the answer, and it is final. Both the water and the food of the garden have been made forbidden to the disbelievers.

### How the answer is given

As-Suddī identified the provision as the food of the garden. ʿAbdur-Raḥmān ibn Zayd ibn Aslam said that what is forbidden is the food and the drink of the garden, both of them.

Saʿīd ibn Jubayr described the moment in the plainest terms. One of the people of the fire will call to his own father or to his brother and say that he has been burned, and ask him to pour a little water over him. The believers are asked for an answer, and the answer they give is that Allah has forbidden both to the disbelievers.

That is the whole of what the verse does. It puts a father and a son or two brothers on opposite sides of a wall, with the one on the near side unable to help the one on the far side, and it makes the words of the refusal a statement about what was already decided. The believers are not the ones refusing. The matter was settled long before, and the verse says so plainly, because of their disbelief.

The point of the scene is the disgrace of the people of the fire. They ask the people of the garden for some of their drink and some of their food, and they are given none of it, and the reason given is not a wish of the people of the garden but a decree of Allah.

### In short

- The people of the fire beg for water and for food from the people of the garden, and they are refused.
- The prohibition covers both the water and the food of the garden, and the reason given is the disbelief of the ones asking.
- Saʿīd ibn Jubayr described a man calling to his father or his brother, saying he has been burned, and the answer that comes back.
- The refusal is not the wish of the people of the garden but a decree already settled.

51.text:
The verse says who these people are. "those who took this faith ˹of Islam˺ as mere amusement and play and were deluded by ˹their˺ worldly life.” ˹Allah will say,˺ “Today We will ignore them just as they ignored the coming of this Day of theirs and for rejecting Our revelations.”"

### Phrase by phrase

**"those who took this faith ˹of Islam˺ as mere amusement and play"** names what they did with religion itself. The adjectives used mean falsehood, merriment, and also a joke and mockery. Religion was not something they took seriously or lived by. It was something they treated as a pastime.

**"and were deluded by ˹their˺ worldly life"** is the second charge. What deceived them was the comfort and luxury of this world, and it kept them from working for the Hereafter as they had been commanded.

**"Today We will ignore them"** is the recompense. The word does not mean that Allah forgets, since nothing escapes His perfect watch and He never forgets anything. The Qur'an says as much elsewhere, that the record is with my Lord, who neither errs nor forgets (20:52). What the word means is that He treats them as if He had forgotten them, and leaves them where they are.

**"just as they ignored the coming of this Day of theirs"** gives the measure of it. The recompense matches the offence exactly. They forgot Allah, so He forgets them (9:67). Their verses came to them and they disregarded them, and so on that Day they are neglected (20:126). And it will be said to them that on this Day He forgets them as they forgot the meeting of this Day of theirs (45:34).

**"and for rejecting Our revelations"** names the second offence that the same response answers. They used to deny the Scripture and the messenger.

### What the forgetting means

The explanations given for the verse come to the same point from different sides. Al-ʿAwfī reported from Ibn ʿAbbās that Allah will put out of mind the good there was about them, and will not put their evil out of mind. ʿAlī bin Abī Ṭalḥah reported from him that the meaning is that they are forsaken as they forsook the meeting of this Day of theirs. Mujāhid said that they are left in the fire. As-Suddī said that they are left outside any mercy, just as they left aside any action on behalf of the meeting of that Day.

And the two sahih collections record what Allah will say to a servant on the Day of Resurrection. He will ask him whether He had not given him a wife, honoured him, made horses and camels serve him, and allowed him to become a leader and a master, and the servant will agree that He had. Then He will ask whether the servant thought he would meet Him, and the servant will say no. And Allah will say that on this Day He forgets him just as he forgot Him.

### The two foods

There is a way of seeing the whole passage that puts this verse beside the one before it. The world offers a spread with two kinds of food on it, one worldly and one belonging to the life to come.

One kind of person takes his nourishment from seeing himself hold the first place. He is happy when he is surrounded by worldly glories, and he counts himself a success when he acquires and owns the goods of the world. This man is entirely forgetful of God and of the Hereafter. If something about God is brought to his attention, he counts it unimportant and passes over it. He deals with it as though it were nothing serious, a trivial entertainment. And there is no share for such a person in the good things of the Hereafter. He has grown in himself a soul that feeds only on worldly material, and the things of the next life cannot nourish a soul like that.

The other kind of person has been lost in things unseen. His soul relishes the remembrance of the Hereafter, and his bread and his drink are living in God and breathing the air of God. For him the Hereafter is the place where he finds every good thing he wanted. And just as he found God in the unseen world, so he finds God in the seen world of the Hereafter.

Why does a person forget God at all in a world God made? The reason is that God makes Himself felt in the world through signs that a person grasps only by reflecting. People lean towards outward things and ignore the signs that point to God, and doing that is nothing other than giving up the Hereafter for the sake of this world. And whoever takes no account of the Hereafter in this life is kept out of it in the next.

There is one more layer in it. When people show open disregard for something God has presented to them as the truth, they are in effect treating God Himself as too unimportant to be given serious thought. The divine power behind the truth is invisible, and they may be deceived by that. But they risk exactly the same treatment being handed back to them on the Day of Reckoning, being passed over as they passed over God, imagining all the while that no harm would come of it.

### In short

- The verse names what the people were: they turned religion into a pastime, and the comfort of this life deluded them.
- "Today We will ignore them" does not mean that Allah forgets, since He neither errs nor forgets (20:52). It means He treats them as though He had.
- The response matches the offence, as the other verses put it: they forgot Allah, so He forgets them (9:67), and they are neglected as they neglected His signs (20:126 and 45:34).
- Ibn ʿAbbās said the good about them is put out of mind and the evil is not, and the other readings say they are left in the fire and left outside mercy.
- The two kinds of food are the world's and the Hereafter's, and a soul fed only on the first cannot be nourished by the second.

52.text:
The passage turns back to what was given in this life. "We have certainly brought them a Book which We explained with knowledge—a guide and mercy for those who believe". After the loss the idolaters end up with is set out, the verse states that they were left no excuse. The Book came to them, and it is set out in detail, so that the warning had reached them before the punishment.

### Phrase by phrase

**"We have certainly brought them a Book"** identifies what was sent: the Qur'an, sent with Muhammad ﷺ to the people of Makkah.

**"which We explained with knowledge"** says what the Book is like. It is set out in detail, and the detail comes with perfect knowledge of what has been explained in it. Another verse describes the same Book as one whose verses are perfected and then explained in detail (11:1). And the knowledge is Allah's own, as another verse says of it that He has sent it down with His knowledge (4:166).

**"a guide and mercy for those who believe"** names what the Book does for the people who accept it. It guides them out of error and it is a mercy that saves them from the torment. One reading makes both words describe the Book itself, so that the Book is the guidance and the Book is the mercy.

### Why the Book is mentioned here

The connection with the verses before and after is exact. Having set out what the idolaters lose in the Hereafter, the Qur'an now says that the messengers and the books were sent in this life, so that the excuse was taken away from them. And the principle is stated elsewhere: no one is punished until a messenger has been sent (17:15). So the mention of the Book here is not a change of subject. It is the reason the punishment that has just been described is just.

What the Book is, and what it does for the people who take it, are set out in the same sentence. It is explained in detail, which is the opposite of being vague. It is guidance, which is what a person needs. It is mercy, which is what a person hopes for. And it works for those who believe, since the guidance and the mercy are received by the people who accept them.

One reading of the verse draws out what the mercy consists of. The Book points the believers towards the right road and towards the truth, and the mercy in it lies in what it brings them to, of good in this world and good in the next.

### In short

- The Book is the Qur'an, sent to the people of Makkah, and it is set out in detail with perfect knowledge.
- The same Book is described elsewhere as having verses perfected and then explained in detail, and as having been sent down with His knowledge.
- It is a guide out of error and a mercy that saves from the torment, and both are for the people who believe.
- It is mentioned here because the sending of the Book is what removes the excuse, and no one is punished before a messenger has come (17:15).

53.text:
The passage closes on the question. "Do they only await the fulfilment ˹of its warning˺? The Day it will be fulfilled, those who ignored it before will say, “The messengers of our Lord certainly came with the truth. Are there any intercessors who can plead on our behalf? Or can we be sent back so we may do ˹good,˺ unlike what we used to do?” They will have certainly ruined themselves, and whatever ˹gods˺ they fabricated will fail them". The verse follows them to the moment they finally believe, and it shows what that belief is worth by then.

### Phrase by phrase

**"Do they only await the fulfilment ˹of its warning˺?"** asks what the people of Makkah are waiting for, now that they have refused to believe. What is meant is the outcome of what Allah has promised them in the Book, and one view is that the promise in question is the torment and the punishment and the fire, while another is that it takes in the garden as well, which is how Mujāhid and several others read it.

**"The Day it will be fulfilled"** is the Day of Resurrection, which is how Ibn ʿAbbās identified it.

**"those who ignored it before will say"** describes the people who passed over the Book in this life and did not act on what it required of them.

**"“The messengers of our Lord certainly came with the truth."** is the first thing they say. What the messengers brought was the truth about the resurrection, about the garden and about the fire. Another reading adds what follows in their own minds, that they denied all of it at the time.

**"Are there any intercessors who can plead on our behalf?"** is the first request. They are asking for someone to intercede for them, so that the torment might be kept away.

**"Or can we be sent back so we may do ˹good,˺ unlike what we used to do?”"** is the second request, and it is the larger one. They want to be returned to the life of this world so that they can act differently from the way they acted, believing and doing good instead of the idolatry they practised. And what follows in the same passage of the Qur'an answers the request before it is fully made. If you could see them when they are held over the fire, they will say that they wish they were sent back, that they would not deny the signs of their Lord and would be among the believers. But no, what they had been concealing has become clear to them, and if they were sent back they would go straight back to what they had been forbidden, since they are liars (6:27-28).

**"They will have certainly ruined themselves"** is the verdict. They have destroyed themselves by entering the fire to stay there.

**"and whatever ˹gods˺ they fabricated will fail them"** is the last line. What they used to worship instead of Allah has abandoned them. Those things will not intercede for them, will not help them and will not save them from what is coming.

### Why the warning did not wake them

The Qur'an warns human beings about the life to come and tells them about the reckoning, and still people are not awakened by it. The reason is what those intimations are in themselves. They are not simply pieces of news. They are the inevitable realities of the universe, and they have not yet appeared as events. They are still hidden behind the veil of the future. So a person, paying no attention, takes the whole thing for meaningless talk and counts it unimportant.

But these messages come on behalf of God, who knows all things. Anyone whose nature has not been spoiled, and whose eyes are not covered by veils of his own making, will find that the tone of the Qur'an matches the voice of his own heart. He will find that this is the very thing his nature was searching for, and the Qur'an becomes for him a treasure of life and of faith.

The position of those who do not take the warnings seriously is completely different. They linger in their slumber until the event they were warned about breaks on them. At that point a person suddenly understands that he is completely helpless. The problems he had thought important, and the ones he had entangled himself in, turn out to have had no basis. The things he had relied on have ceased to be with him. The rosy hopes he had lived on all prove false.

Belief in the Hereafter looks like an abstract idea, and that is the reason a person never gets serious about it. Then the life after death arrives, and the Hereafter with all its terror is thrust upon him. At that point everyone is compelled to accept what he had refused to accept before. And when he leaves the world behind and turns to the oneness of God at last, it is too late for the admission to count. He understands then that what had been told to him in the language of argument was plain fact, and that not being serious about it is what stopped him from grasping its meaning. When everything he had leant on leaves him in the lurch, he wants to be sent back to the earth to live his life properly. And no one is given that chance twice.

### In short

- The verse asks what the people of Makkah are waiting for, and the answer is the fulfilment of what the Book promised and warned about, on the Day of Resurrection.
- On that Day those who ignored the Book admit that the messengers came with the truth, and then ask for intercessors and for a return to the world.
- The request for a return is answered before it is made, since the Qur'an says that if they were sent back they would go straight back to what was forbidden them (6:27-28).
- They ruin themselves by entering the fire to stay, and everything they set up beside Allah abandons them and cannot help.
- The warning does not wake people because it speaks of realities that have not yet appeared as events, and no one is given the chance to live his life over again.

54.text:
The verse lays the ground for everything the chapter says after it. "Indeed your Lord is Allah Who created the heavens and the earth in six Days, then established Himself on the Throne." Then the second half. "He makes the day and night overlap in rapid succession. He created the sun, the moon, and the stars, all subjected by His command." And the close. "The creation and the command belong to Him ˹alone˺. Blessed is Allah, Lord of all worlds". This verse 54 rests its argument on things a person can watch happening, and from them it draws a conclusion about the One who made them.

### Phrase by phrase

**"Indeed your Lord is Allah"** opens with the name of nurturing care, and then gives the name of the One who is worshipped. The heavens and the earth and the planets and the stars all perform their functions inside a system that is firmly established, and the maker of such a system must hold a power than which nothing more perfect can be conceived. That is where the verse invites every reasonable person to stop and think. Here is the Being who brought this universe out of nothing and keeps it running on the wisest of arrangements. Why should it be difficult for Him to undo the whole of it and bring it back on the Day of Qiyamah? The best course for a human being is to give up denying the rising and turn to this same Lord as master and nurturer, asking of Him what is needed and worshipping Him alone. He should come out of the swamp of worshipping his own kind, and he should recognise the truth.

**"Who created the heavens and the earth in six Days"** states a fact the rest of the Book repeats in several places, and the verse does not leave the number unexplained. The days are taken up below, together with the question of what kind of days they were.

**"then established Himself on the Throne"** is the clause that has drawn the most discussion, and what the early generations said about it is set out further down as well.

**"He makes the day and night overlap in rapid succession"** describes something the reader sees twice every day. What the eye watches is the light driving the dark out of the sky and then the dark coming back over the light. Neither of the two lags behind its partner. One has barely gone before the other is in place. So the alternation carries the whole world from light into darkness and back again, and it answers to the subduing power of its Lord so smoothly that not the least delay enters into a change of that size.

**"He created the sun, the moon, and the stars, all subjected by His command"** means that every one of them stands under His command, His will and His dominion. They move in obedience to Him and by His leave. In the Arabic of this sentence the three names may be read in one case as a continuation of the mention of the heavens. In another case they are the subject of a sentence whose predicate follows. The sense in either reading is that they run subject to His command and His power.

**"The creation and the command belong to Him ˹alone˺"** is put in the form of a general rule. The word for creation means bringing things into being, and the word for command means ordering and deciding. Being the creator and being the master belong to Him exclusively. No one besides Him can create the smallest thing, and no one has the right to subject another person to his command, except where Allah Himself gives someone a particular task, and even then the command at work is really His. So the line says that bringing all these things into being was the work of none but Him, and that putting them into service was a burden no one else could carry either. One line of teaching reads the two words as two domains, and that reading also belongs to this verse.

**"Blessed is Allah, Lord of all worlds"** closes the verse with a word built on blessing, which carries the senses of increase, growth, remaining and sustaining. In this place it means that He is high and supreme, or high and sustaining, since He is both. The reading that He is the Possessor of grace, and the reading that He is magnified and far exalted above every fault, both belong here. He is the master and disposer of all the worlds, the Lord of everything and the keeper of every being.

### Why six days, when one word would do

A question arises at once from the first line. The power of Allah is great enough to create the whole universe in a single moment, and the Book says so in more than one place. In Surah Al-Qamar the command is described as a single word, like the twinkling of an eye (54:50). In Surah Ya Sin the word is that when He intends a thing He says to it, "Be", and it comes to be (36:82). So why were six days spent on the work?

One answer given by Saʿīd ibn Jubayr is that Allah is certainly able to create everything in an instant, but divine wisdom asked for a measured span instead. Six days were chosen so that men and women might learn from the pattern what graduality means, and how a great work is perfected by being carried out step by step. A hadith supports the same point, that working with deliberation and dignity and at a steady pace comes from Allah, and that hurrying comes from Shaytan. That report is carried in the collection of traditions known as the Shuʿab al-Iman of Al-Baihaqi, and it stands behind a general lesson. Rushing into things is not good for a human being, because a person driven by haste cannot give due thought to all sides of the question in front of him. What is done in haste spoils the thing done and ends in regret. Whatever is done after proper thinking and with room to work brings barakah, the increase that Allah puts into an effort so that it works better and goes further than its means suggest.

A second question follows. Day and night are known by the movement of the sun, so before the earth and the heavens existed, and with no sun and no moon in place, on what basis were six days counted? Some say the six days were a stretch of time equal to six days and nights as the world counts them now. A clearer approach is that day and night in our sense are terms that belong to this world. Before the universe existed Allah had other signs by which a day and a night could be marked, much as the day and night of Paradise will not depend on the movement of the sun. And it does not follow that the six days of the creation were equal to six of ours. They may have been longer, since the Book speaks of a day with the Lord that is like a thousand years.

Imam Ahmad and Mujahid said the six days here mean the six days of the Hereafter, and the same appears in a narration of ʿAbdullah ibn ʿAbbas reported by Ad-Dahhak. Against the thought that such spans are hard to imagine, one authority has a remark about the speed of the outermost firmament. In the time it takes a running man to bring his raised foot back down to the ground, that firmament covers three thousand miles. That observation is recorded in Al-Bahr Al-Muhit.

### The days themselves, and the day of rest

The six days on which the creation was made began, according to the sound reports, on Friday and ended on Friday. On Yawm as-Sabt, the day of the Sabbath, which is Saturday, no work of creation was done. Some say the word sabt means to discontinue, and the day took its name because the work of creation had come to an end by then.

The order of the work is given in a hadith of Abu Hurayrah. He reported that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ told him that Allah created the dust on the Saturday, the mountains on the Sunday, the trees on the Monday, the unpleasant things on the Tuesday, the light on the Wednesday, and spread the creatures through the earth on the Thursday. Adam came after that, in the afternoon of the Friday. He was the last of the creation, made in the final hour of that day, between the afternoon and the night.

In another accounting the six days are given as Sunday, Monday, Tuesday, Wednesday, Thursday and Friday. On the Friday the whole creation was assembled, and on that day Adam was created. The question whether these days were the same as the days we count, or whether each of them is a thousand years, is one on which there is a difference of opinion. The longer reading is reported from Mujahid, from Imam Ahmad bin Hanbal, and from Ibn ʿAbbas as Ad-Dahhak's narration from him gives it. Saturday is left outside the count of creation because it is the seventh day of the week.

### The four days of the earth and the two days of the heavens

The details of the six days are set out in Surah Ha Mim As-Sajdah, that is Surah Fussilat. The earth was created in two days, and then the measures of its sustenance were determined in four days, and then the seven heavens were completed in two days. The first two days, in which the earth was made, are Sunday and Monday. The four days in which the mountains, the rivers, the tributaries, the trees, the vegetation and the things human beings and animals eat were created run from the same starting point and are Tuesday and Wednesday. Then the two days in which the seven heavens were finished are Thursday and Friday. By Friday the total comes to six days, and the count agrees with what the earlier reports give. The wording runs: the earth in two days, and its sustenance measured in four days (41:9 and 10), and then the seven heavens completed in two days (41:12).

### What is said about the rising over the Throne

The clause about establishing Himself on the Throne has drawn many opinions. The safest creed to hold is the one that is clear and correct and fairly free of doubt, and it is the creed of the most righteous elders, the Companions and those who followed them, and later of many of the thinkers of the inner life as well. Their creed is that human reason cannot comprehend the reality of the Being of Allah and of His attributes, and that pursuing the exact reality of these things is an exercise in futility and is even harmful. A person should hold, as a general principle, that the meaning Allah intended is the one correct and true meaning, whatever it is, and he should not try to fix a meaning on his own.

The word Al-Istawa, which is translated as established, carries in the language the sense of taking position on something, or settling on it, or being established, and the word arsh means throne. The arsh, in the classical usage, is the elevated seat on which a king sits. What that throne is, and how it is shaped, and what the establishing on it means, are matters beyond the reach of human reasoning.

Someone asked Imam Malik about the meaning of the phrase. He paused for a while and then said that everyone knows the meaning of the word for establishing. Its particular nature and reality are such that human reason cannot grasp them. Having faith in it is obligatory, and asking about its nature and reality is an innovation in the established religion. The reason he gave that last part is that the noble Companions never put such questions to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ.

The ancient teachers took the same line about all the verses that speak of the Being and the attributes. The names in that list are Sufyan Al-Thawriy, the Imam Al-Awza'i, Layth ibn Saʿd, Sufyan ibn ʿUyaynah and ʿAbdullah ibn Mubarak. Their word was that these verses are to be taken as they have come and exactly as they stand, with nothing added by way of explanation or interpretation. That is the way of guidance here, and it is the way the early generations took. Among them are Malik, Al-Awza'i, Ath-Thawri, Al-Layth bin Saʿd, Ash-Shafiʿi, Ahmad and Ishaq bin Rahwayh, and the rest of the scholars of the community in the past and in later times. They accept the plain statement of the establishing without asking how its reality is, without equating it with anything in the creation, and without altering or denying it.

One of that company, Nuʿaym bin Hammad Al-Khuzaʿi, the teacher of Al-Bukhari, put the two errors plainly. Whoever likens Allah to His creation has committed kufr, and whoever denies what Allah has described Himself with has committed kufr. There is no resemblance to the creation in anything Allah and His Messenger ﷺ have described Him by. Anyone who affirms for Allah the attributes that the plain verses and the sound hadiths mention, in the manner that suits His majesty, and who at the same time rejects from Him every shortcoming, has taken the path of guidance. The Book gives the same measure in another place: nothing is like Him, and He is the All-Hearing, the All-Seeing (42:11), so any meaning that lets someone equate the Creator with what He made has to be put away from Him.

It can be said, in short, that the meaning of the phrase is known, its reality is unknown, faith in it is wajib, and asking about its how and its why is what the elders refused to do.

### The night, the day, the sun, the moon and the stars

The verse puts the day and the night beside the sun, the moon and the stars, and they are all signs of the same order. Of the night it is said elsewhere that it is a sign. The day is withdrawn from it, and the people are left in darkness. The sun runs to a term fixed for it, which is the decree of the All-Mighty, the All-Knowing. The moon is measured in mansions until it comes back like an old curved stalk. The sun cannot overtake the moon, and the night cannot outstrip the day. All of them float, each in its own orbit (36:37-40). The line that the night does not outstrip the day (36:40) means that the night follows the day in its order, never coming before or after its proper time. Another verse gives the same praise to the One who set big stars in the heaven (25:61), and the praise in this verse too rests on the same works.

A person looking at all this is invited to think about the machines he sees made by hands. Engineers make machines of every kind. With some of them the problems begin from the first day. Others run well enough at the start, but a machine remains a machine, however strong its material and however careful its design. Its parts wear, or need adjusting, or need repairs and servicing, and while they are being fixed the machine stands idle, perhaps for weeks. Now look at the machines made by God. The efficiency and the perfection they had on their first day are still in them. They work without stopping, their movement is as exact as it ever was, not a second fast and not a second slow, and there is no wear in their parts and no workshop they need to visit. The reason is in the verse itself. They are subject to His command, and so they need no fuel to move them and no engine to drive them. They work under the divine command alone, and a defect appearing in them is impossible. When the Absolute Master decides to remove them at a time He has appointed, the whole system will come apart, and that day is the day of Qiyamah.

### Creation and command as two words

The two words at the heart of the verse, creation and command, have been read as two domains in one line of teaching. Creation relates to matter, and command relates to the refined and the abstract. The Book points in that direction where it has the Lord say of the soul that it is a command from Him (17:85), since the ruh is named there as a command of the Lord. On this reading, everything between the heavens and the earth is matter, and its bringing into being is called creation, while what lies beyond these things, free of matter, has its bringing into being called command. On the plainer reading, the verse means that the making of the creatures and the ruling of them are both His, and that no one else shares either.

### The blessing in the last line

The last word of praise is built on barakah, and barakah carries the senses of increase, of growth, of becoming more, of remaining and of sustaining, among many other shades. In this place it means that He is high and supreme, and it can also be taken as high and sustaining, since He is both. The sense of height is confirmed by a hadith in which the servant says to his Lord that He is blessed and high, O Master of Glory and Honour. In that same line of praise the word for being blessed is explained by the word for being high.

The praise at the end of this verse is like the praise given to the One who set big stars in the heaven (25:61), and it belongs to Him as the Lord of all the worlds. One of the Companions, Abu Ad-Darda, is reported to have used a supplication that has also been attributed to the Prophet ﷺ. In it the servant says that all the kingdom is Allah's, that all praise is His, and that the ownership of all affairs is His. He then asks Him for every kind of good and seeks refuge with Him from every kind of evil.

### A reading of the two names

One strand of teaching gives the two names in the opening of the verse a work of their own. The Lord is the one whose name is light and whose message is light, and who is joined to love. He nurtures the people of this world and keeps every creature safe. He requites what people do, and His loving is kind. Nothing unworthy comes near Him, for He is pure and without peer, and He is the judge of how and why. He is clear to Himself in rightness, clear to Himself in being, and clear to the heart in friendship. He is one, and one is enough. He looks after what each has, He is able to keep hearts on the straight way, He is Lord over everything, the keeper of every being, and the nurturer of whatever is able to rise higher.

First He said Lord, which is the portion of ordinary people, and then He said God, which is the portion of those who recognise Him and of the sincerely truthful. The name Lord puts the hearts of good men at ease, while the name God carries away the spirits of those who recognise Him. The name Lord pours blessings on those who ask, and the name God throws love into the hearts of the friends. The name Lord pours the blessings of vision on the faithful, and the name God lights the lamp of love in the hearts of those who know Him.

In that line of teaching, love and vision are two gifts, and a story is told of them. They met, and love said to vision that it is like light, because it brightens the world, and vision answered that love is like fire, because it burns the world. Then vision said that when it discloses itself it pulls suffering out of the heart, and love replied that when it settles in the heart it plunders it. Vision called itself a gift for those who are tested, and love said that it throws tumult into the world.
