Vision, on this reading, is the share of those who come to know Him through what He has made. They reach Him by way of the engendered, the determined and the newly arrived, which are the earth and the heavens, the sun, the moon and the stars held in subjection. Love is the share of those who come to know Him through Him, arriving at the made things from His side rather than climbing up to Him from them. And on that same reading, three kinds of people have missed the higher road. They are the one who knows Him only by the things He made, the one who loves Him for the sake of His blessings, and the one who searches for Him by his own effort. To know Him by the made things is to worship Him in fear and want.

### What the verse asks of a person

The creation could have been left haphazard, with things made and then abandoned in confusion. It was not left that way. All things were linked in a system that is perfectly ordered and wisely regulated, and each of them was set working in the way that serves the interest of the whole. Man is a small part of this world, and his role in an environment so well formed should be the same as the role of everything else. He should devote himself to the plan of his Creator, in the way the whole universe has given itself over to that plan in obedience. Every other thing in the universe takes part in the plan of God with the utmost ihsan, doing what it was made for and doing it well. Man is asked to do the same, and not to step past the limits of justice and of truth that God has prescribed for him. Man has something more than the rest of creation, which is speech and consciousness, and so his surrender has to be expressed at that level too. The recognition of God should sit so deep in him that it keeps coming out in words, and he should call on God as a servant calls on his Creator and Lord. His awareness of God's godhead should be such that nothing but God is left at the centre of his hopes or his fears. He should fear God alone and fasten his hopes on Him alone, and to bring one's fears and one's hopes to God alone is the last stage of obedience to Him.

### In short

- The verse builds its argument on the created order, and it invites the reader to see the power of the One who made it, so that the raising of the dead is no difficulty for Him.
- The creation took six days although a single word would have been enough, and the wisdom in the measured pace is that human beings should learn to work deliberately rather than in haste.
- The days and their order are given in the reports, with the work of creation finished on the sixth day and no creative work done on the day of the Sabbath.
- The establishing on the throne is affirmed as the early generations affirmed it, without asking how its reality is, without likening Him to anything, without denying it and without turning it into something else.
- The day and the night, the sun, the moon and the stars run subject to His command with a precision no made machine can keep, and the whole of them will end when He decides.
- Creation and command belong to Him alone, and the last word of the verse is praise of the Lord of all the worlds.

55.text:
The verses before this one showed the perfect power of the Lord and the great blessings that come from it. From that the next step follows by itself. If He holds that power, sends those blessings and is the Lord of all the worlds, then He is the One to be called on in every condition, in want and in distress. To pass Him by and turn somewhere else is ignorance and loss. "Call upon your Lord humbly and secretly. Surely He does not like the transgressors". With the command come the rules of conduct that belong to it, and when those rules are kept, the hope that the prayer is answered grows.

### Phrase by phrase

**"Call upon your Lord"** rests on a word that means asking someone to remove a need, and the same word is also used for remembering in the plain sense. Both meanings can be taken here. On the first, the verse says to ask Allah alone for what you need. On the second, it says to keep your remembrance and your worship for Him alone. Both explanations have been reported from the early authorities.

The act itself is given a high rank. Muṣṭafā said that supplication is worship. Allah commands His servants to call on Him, since that is what secures their welfare in this life and in the next. In one place the Book says, "and remember your Lord within yourself" (7:205). The Two Sahihs carry a report from Abu Musa al-Ash'ari, who said that the people raised their voices in supplication, and that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ told them: O people, take it easy on yourselves, for you are not calling on one who is deaf or absent. The One you are calling is All-Hearing and Near. If it is taken as calling out, then it is the same as praise. If it is taken as asking, then it is the proper business of a servant. Either way it is worship and a means of deliverance.

**"humbly"** translates a word that carries the sense of knowing one's own inability, of humility, and of submission with a refined lowliness of spirit. The one who prays is to stand before his Lord as weak, helpless and unable to hold his own, modest and low, with the pride and the self-view put away, and then ask. Supplication belongs to the soul. It requires that its words match the weakness of the one who speaks them, that the manner of it mirrors that modesty, and that the humility show in the very way he comes to the act.

That is why a great deal of what passes for supplication today cannot really be called by that name. It is recitation rather than asking. People do not know what they are saying, and the words roll on as a routine. An imam reads out words in Arabic that he has memorised at the end of the prayer, and often he does not know what they mean, while the people behind him repeat Amen after each line with no idea of what has been said. What comes out of all of it is the sound of some words, while supplication has a reality of its own that is not there. That Allah in His mercy may accept even such lifeless words and give them the effect of an answered prayer is another matter. But it has to be understood that supplication is not read out. It is asked. And so it should be asked in the way that asking deserves.

There is a further point. If a person does know the meaning of the words he uses, and understands what he is saying, but comes without the right approach and manner, the whole thing is reduced to a claim that no created servant is entitled to make.

**"and secretly"** gives the second rule. The asking is to be done privately and in a lowered voice, which is better in merit and more likely to be answered. Three drawbacks attach to a raised voice. It is hard to keep modesty and humility while doing it. It opens the door to showing off and to wanting to be noticed. And the manner of it suggests that the one praying hardly knows that Allah is All-Hearing and All-Knowing, who hears what is said quietly and knows what is hidden inside. When the voices of the Companions rose loud in supplication on the day of Khaybar, the Messenger of Allah ﷺ told them that they were not calling on one who is deaf or absent. The One they were calling is Hearing and Near. Allah Himself has described the supplication of one of the righteous in the words "when he called his Lord with a call kept quiet" (19:3). The state that He likes is the one in which the asking is kept lowered and subdued.

**"Surely He does not like the transgressors"** names the fault that spoils all of this. The word comes from going past a limit, and the sense is that Allah does not love those who cross the lines. Crossing the line in supplication takes several forms. The first is when the prayer is dressed up with rhyming and ornamental devices that damage the humility and submission which are its real substance. The second is when unnecessary restrictions are laid on what is asked. Abdullah ibn Mughaffal heard his son praying for the white palace on the right side of Paradise, and stopped him, saying that fixing such conditions is crossing the limit that the Book and the hadith have forbidden. The third is when a person prays for harm to Muslims in general, or asks for something that will hurt them. And it is also a form of the same fault that a prayer be made in a raised voice where there is no need for it.

Ibn Abbas said of this line that it covers supplication and everything else as well. Abu Mijlaz said that an example of it is a person asking to reach the rank of the prophets. Imam Ahmad reported that Abu Ni'amah said that Abdullah bin Mughaffal heard his son making a supplication in which he asked for the white castle on the right side of Paradise if he entered it. He told his son to ask Allah for Paradise and to seek refuge with Him from the fire, and then said that he had heard the Messenger of Allah ﷺ say that there would come people who go past the limit in supplication and in purification. Ibn Majah and Abu Dawud recorded that report.

### Keeping the voice where it belongs

One of the early teachers said that a prayer made quietly stands seventy degrees above one made loudly. The habit of the righteous elders was to exert themselves to the full in remembrance and prayer, so that these kept them busy most of the time, and yet nobody heard their voices. Their supplications stayed between them and their Lord. Many of them had the whole Qur'an by heart and recited it while nobody knew. Others were deep in religious study and never told anyone about it. Others would come home after long sessions of prayer and no one would know anything of it. He said that he had seen such people who never performed a private act of worship out in the open where others could see, and whose voices in supplication stayed very low.

Ibn Jurayj said that raising the voice in supplication and making a noise of it is makruh. In his book on the rulings of the Qur'an, Imam Abu Bakr al-Jassas said that this verse shows a lowered voice to be more deserving than a raised one, and that the same has been reported from Hasan al-Basri and from Ibn Abbas. The same verse shows that the Amin said at the end of the al-Fatihah should also be said quietly, since that Amin is itself a supplication.

The same teaching bears on the imams of the mosques, who in our time seem to have forgotten what the Book and the Sunnah and the elders said on this subject. What follows the prayer as a collective supplication has become an artificial performance. Words are read out loud, which is against the etiquette of supplication, and which disturbs the prayer of those who joined the congregation late and are still finishing what they missed. Custom has such a hold on people that they do not notice the harm. There is no objection where a group has to make one supplication together and a single person says the words in a reasonably audible voice while the rest say Amen, provided that it disturbs nobody and does not turn into a habit that ordinary people take as the standard way of praying.

In the second sense of the verse, where the command is taken as remembrance and worship, the position of the early scholars is that quiet remembrance is better than loud. Those who advise loud remembrance for beginners in the Chishtiah order do it with an eye on the condition of the seeker, as a treatment, so that the voicing of it drives away sluggishness and the heart learns to settle into the remembrance of Allah. Even with them, raising the voice in remembrance is not desirable in itself. It is permitted, and its justification is established from the hadith, so long as no showing off or desire to be seen enters into it.

The weight of the matter is settled in a report that Imam Ahmad ibn Hanbal, Ibn Hibban and Al-Baihaqi all carry from Saʿd ibn Abi Waqqas, that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said that the best remembrance is the hidden one and the best provision is what suffices.

There are times and places, however, where a voice is wanted. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ taught those by his words and by his practice. The Adhan and the Iqamah are given aloud, the recitation in the prayers that are said aloud is raised, and so are the takbirs of the Salah, the takbirs of the days of sacrifice, and the Talbiyah of the Hajj. On that basis the jurists concluded that where the Prophet ﷺ taught by word or by deed that the voice should be raised, it is raised, and that in every other place quiet remembrance is better and more useful. The same measure holds for every act of worship. Take Salah, Sawm, Hajj and Zakah, and all dealings and transactions. When the limits set by the sacred law are crossed in them, they do not remain acts of worship, and they become sin instead.

### What the verse asks of the one who calls

The words humble and secret have been explained in more than one way. Ibn Jarir said that the first means obeying Him in humility and lowliness, and that the second means humbleness in the heart together with certainty of His oneness and His lordship, and that a person should not pray loudly in order to be seen. Others read the two words as openly and in secret, and others again as humble and out of fear. The transgressors, on that reading, are those who call for what is not allowed for them against the righteous. Another reading of the same line says that the transgressors here are the braggarts and the loud-mouthed.

One short commentary puts the whole command in a few words. Believers are to call on their Lord with complete humility, silently and in private, sincere in their prayer, not showing off and not worshipping others along with Him in their prayers. Those who pass beyond the limits in their prayers are not loved by Him. One of the worst ways of doing that is calling on others alongside Him, which is what the idolaters do.

There is a wider frame around all of this. The greatest thing a human being can reach is the mercy of God, and that grace falls to the lot of those who are attached to God so completely that every emotion they have is turned towards Him. They call out to Him only, they are humble before Him alone, they hope to receive from Him, and they fear Him alone lest what they have be taken away. Those who live like that are seeking nearness to God, and God gives them a place near to Him.

### What the earliest teachers said of the call

The inner preconditions of supplication are given a full treatment in one strand of teaching. The servant is told to plead, to weep, and to throw himself down in lowliness at the Exalted Threshold, and it is to that state that the words "in pleading and secret" point. Yaḥyā Muʿādh said that worship is a storehouse, that supplication is the key to it, and that the teeth of the key are lawful morsels, which is to say that a prayer fed on unlawful food does not turn the lock.

A report tells of Adam, who mourned and pleaded over his slip for a hundred years. Finally Gabriel asked how long the pleading and the weeping were to go on, and whether there was any way for the apology to be accepted and the wound to be healed. The answer came that Adam was to be left alone, for if that pleading and weeping had not been foreseen from him, the slip would not have been decreed for him in the first place. It was decreed because it was known that helplessness would bring him to supplication and pleading, and because the lament of a servant and his weeping for his Lord are loved. The sobs of the sinner are dearer than the murmur of the one who glorifies.

The same teaching is in another verse of the Book, where the Lord says, "supplicate Me and I will respond to you" (40:60). The sense is that a person should call on Him so that He answers, know Him so that He forgives, and ask of Him so that He gives. And in another place the Book praises the One "who responds to the distressed when he calls on Him" (27:62). The distressed person is the one whose capacity to bear the trial has run out. Who else would answer his call, or hear his supplication, or come to the aid of his helplessness? He has no handhold left, and he looks at his own days as so many days given to the wind, his hands empty of every means of approach and of every act of obedience. The supplication of such a person is like an arrow that flies straight to its target.

### In short

- Supplication is worship, and the word carries both the sense of asking for a need and the sense of remembering, so the verse commands both kinds of turning to Him.
- The prayer is to be made with the humility of a person who knows his own helplessness, and in a lowered voice, since the loud voice is hard to keep modest, invites showing off, and forgets that Allah hears everything.
- The line about the transgressors covers every kind of excess in prayer, from ornamental wording and invented restrictions to asking for what is forbidden or praying for harm.
- Quiet remembrance is the better way, and it is the way the righteous elders kept, while a raised voice belongs to the few places where the Prophet ﷺ himself taught that it should be raised.
- Even the Amen at the end of the al-Fatihah is a supplication, and so it too is said in a low voice.
- The ones who reach the mercy of God are those whose hopes and fears have been gathered onto Him alone.

56.text:
From the manner of calling, the passage turns to the state of the world in which the calling is done. "Do not spread corruption in the land after it has been set in order. And call upon Him with hope and fear. Indeed, Allah's mercy is always close to the good-doers". The three parts of the verse hold together. The earth was put right, the one who lives on it is not to spoil it, and the call that goes up from it is to carry both fear and hope.

### Phrase by phrase

**"Do not spread corruption in the land after it has been set in order"** is built on two words set against each other. The first word means the state of being good, correct and properly arranged, and the second means the state of evil, corruption, mischief and disorder. Imam Raghib al-Isfahan said in his study of the words of the Qur'an that this second word describes a thing going past the limits of moderation, whether the crossing is small or enormous. The amount of corruption in any case is measured by how far those limits were crossed. Since the word for corruption means making things bad while its opposite means correcting, reforming and putting into order, the verse as it stands means that they should not make things bad on the earth after Allah had made them good and proper. The same command is given elsewhere in the Book: "and do not do mischief on the earth after it has been set in order" (5:56).

**"And call upon Him with hope and fear"** gives the inner state of the one who prays. The fear is of the severe punishment He holds, and the hope is in the tremendous reward He holds.

**"Indeed, Allah's mercy is always close to the good-doers"** closes the verse with a promise. His mercy is for those who do good, which is to say those who obey His commands and keep away from what He has forbidden. The Book says in another place, "and My mercy encompasses all things, and I will ordain it for those who are mindful of Me" (7:156). Matar Al-Warraq said that a person should earn the promise of Allah by obeying Him, since He has decreed that His mercy is near to those who do good. Ibn Abi Hatim collected that saying.

### The three ways a thing is set right

The same authority set out three ways in which Allah puts a thing right. He may begin by creating it right and proper, as when the Book says that He will improve the condition of a people (47:2). He may take out a corruption that has entered into something, as when the Book says that He may make deeds good and right (33:71). Or a command may be given to put something in order. This verse carries a command to abstain from corruption on the earth after it has been set in order, and the ordering of the earth spoken of here can be taken in two senses.

In the first sense the ordering is outward. The earth was made arable and able to grow trees, rain was made to come from the clouds, and flowers and fruits come from plants and trees as gifts. The earth was made the means by which human beings and animals are kept alive.

In the second sense the ordering is inward and spiritual. Allah set things right on the earth by sending His messengers and His Books, with instructions, and by clearing it of error, of shirk and of kufr. The verse may well mean the outward ordering and the inward ordering together. On that reading it says that God has put the earth in order, physically and spiritually, and that people are not to create disorder in it or engineer evil there through their sins and their disobedience.

### The order that is inward and the order that is outward

The outward ordering can be seen in the way the earth itself was made. It was given a middle state, neither liquid like water, on which it would be hard to settle, nor hard like rock or iron, which could not be dug. It can be worked, broken up and smoothed, so that it lends itself to farming and to growing plants and trees, flowers and fruits. It can be dug for wells, cut for moats and canals, and built upon with strong foundations. Inside the earth and on it, things and conditions were created that help people live there and that bring vegetation, trees, flowers and fruits out of it. From outside it, wind, light, heat and cold were created, and water was made to rain down from the clouds so that trees could grow. The stars and the planets were brought into service, casting warm and cold rays on the earth, and those rays fill flowers and fruits with colour and juice. Human beings were given intelligence, and with it they dig raw materials out of the earth, iron, copper, wood and many other metals and rocks, and work them into a whole new world of industry and craft. That is the outward ordering of the earth, and it was brought about by the perfect power of Allah.

The inward ordering of life rests on three things, on the remembrance of Allah, on a person's tie with his Lord, and on obedience to Him. To begin with, a basic substance and an urge to remember Him and to obey Him have been put into every human heart, as the Book says of the soul that He inspired it with its wrong and its right (91:8). Beyond that, there is no particle anywhere around a human being in which Allah has not placed wonders of His power and His creativity, and a person of ordinary understanding is moved by them to say, "blessed be Allah, the best of creators" (23:14). And beyond those signs, He sent the messengers and revealed the Books, and through them the essential link between the Creator and the created was established. The command that follows is that the earth, having been put in order outwardly and inwardly, should not be allowed to go bad through human misdeeds.

### How the two kinds of disorder feed each other

Disorder has two aspects as well, the outward and the inward, and the verse forbids both. The recurring insistence of the Book and of the Prophet ﷺ is on the inward order, since that is the central duty, and the aim of that insistence is to stop any inward disorder from rising. But the link between the two runs in both directions in the world we live in, and disorder in one becomes a source of disorder in the other. So when the sacred law closed the doors of inward disorder, it also closed the doors of outward disorder. Theft, robbery, murder and every kind of immodesty and indecency create disorder of both kinds, and firm restrictions were laid down and penalties prescribed against such acts in particular. The ordinary sins and offences were forbidden too, because every sin sooner or later becomes a source of outward disorder, and at another time a source of inward disorder. Looked at closely, every outward disorder turns into an inward one, and every inward disorder ends by producing an outward one.

That outward disorder leads to inward disorder is plain enough, since it is a violation of the command to obey what has been laid down, and disobedience to Allah is another name for inward disorder. How inward disorder turns into outward disorder takes a little reflection to see. The whole world and everything in it was created by the Master of creation, and all of it stands subject to His command. As long as human beings obey Allah, everything stands harnessed into their service as is proper. But once they begin to disobey Him, everything around them begins to disobey them, working from behind a curtain that their eyes cannot see through. The proof of that hostility shows up when a person studies the effects and outcomes of things.

On the surface, people go on using these things as usual. Water goes down the throat and does not refuse to quench the thirst. Food does not stop removing hunger. Clothing and housing do not fail to defend against heat and cold. But if the final outcome is considered, it turns out that none of these things is doing its assigned job, because the real function and use of them is to give peace and comfort, to take away anxiety and to cure sickness. Look at the condition of the world now. Comforts and the means of curing disease have multiplied far beyond anything once imagined, and at the same time most human beings are caught in extreme distress and illness. Diseases that were never known and disasters that follow one after another have become ordinary. Nobody, not even the greatest among people, is content and at peace in his station. The more the output of these comforts and skills rises, the more the diseases, anxieties, disasters and hardships rise alongside them, very like the saying, "the more they treat you, the more sick they make you".

If a person caught up in the modern world could lift his head a little above his fascination with machines and gadgets, and above his enchantment with what energy can do and with the material gains that come with it, he would see something. The whole effort to invent and to build, and to raise a society on top of those inventions, has failed to deliver the peace and comfort that was its real purpose. Nothing explains that failure except the inward disorder described above, the disorder in which people have turned away from their Lord, their Creator and Master. What He made has turned away from them on the inward front, and it refuses to give them real rest, however fast they run. The famous Maulana Rum put his finger on this when he observed that dust, water, air and fire, four elements that look senseless and inert, in truth carry a measure of intelligence and so serve the command of their Master. The same Maulana Rumi says that the cloud holds back its rain when people stop paying Zakah, and that an epidemic follows from Zina and spreads in every direction. That is not poetic imagining. It is a reality supported by the Book and the hadith. What shows itself here, in illness, epidemics, storms, hurricanes and floods, is only a small sample of the punishment that is still to come.

So the command not to spread corruption includes the crimes and sins that bring outward disorder into the world, and it also includes sin, disobedience and heedlessness towards Allah. And so this same verse goes straight on to say that He should be called upon in fear and hope. The calling is to be done in a way that keeps a person afraid that his prayer may go unanswered, and at the same time full of hope tied to the mercy of his Lord.

### The two wings of fear and hope

The two together are the wings on which the human soul flies, and the journey they carry it on is the journey with the truth. By them it rises and reaches the ranks prepared for it. The text shows that the two should be kept in balance. Some scholars said that fear should dominate through life while a person is healthy, so that no shortcoming creeps into his obedience. When death comes, they said, hope should dominate, since the strength to do what should have been done is gone and there is nothing left but to hope for the mercy of Allah. That observation stands in Al-Bahr Al-Muhit. Others among the researchers said that the purpose of the two is to keep a person on the straight path of the religion and constant in obedience. Since temperaments differ, some hold to that constancy through fear while others hold to it through love and hope, and each should take the way that helps him.

So the first verse carries two rules of the etiquette of supplication that belong to the outward person, that the supplication be made with humility and submission and that it be kept quiet, and this verse carries two rules that belong to the heart. The one praying should feel the danger that his prayer may not be answered, and he should hope at the same time that it will be. To grow careless about one's errors and sins is contrary to iman, and to lose hope in the boundless mercy of Allah is kufr. Both are extremes that are not allowed. The hope of being answered can only be held in the space between fear and hope.

The hint at the end of the verse is that of the two, hope carries more weight. The one who prays is addressing the Lord of all the worlds, whose mercy cannot be measured and whose generosity has no limit and no reluctance. He can answer the prayer of the worst of offenders. If a prayer stands in danger of going unanswered, that can only be because of the person's own misdeeds or because of a curse of sins hanging over him. Good deeds are needed for a person to come near the mercy of Allah. The Prophet ﷺ said that there are people who travel long distances, who look like the poor, who raise their hands to Allah, and yet their food is haram and their drink is haram and their clothing is haram. How is the prayer of such a person to be answered? That report comes from Abi Hurairah and is carried by Muslim and Tirmidhi. In another hadith the Prophet ﷺ said that the prayer of a servant keeps finding acceptance so long as he does not pray for a sin or for the cutting of a relationship, and so long as he does not make haste. The Companions asked what making haste meant, and he said that it is when a person thinks that he has been praying for so long and has not been answered, until he loses hope and gives up. And in a further report he said that when a person prays to Allah, he should do it in a state in which he has no doubt that it will be answered. The meaning is that he should keep his eye on the widest mercy of Allah and let his heart believe that the prayer will be answered, and that this does not contradict the fear that his sins may stand in the way of acceptance.

### The beautiful doing that brings mercy near

The last words of the verse speak of mercy coming close to those who do good. Muṣṭafā defined the beautiful doing when he said that it is to worship God as though you see Him, for if you do not see Him, He surely sees you. That report points to the meeting of the heart with the Real, to the secret core coming together with the Unseen, and to the spirit contemplating God. The verse urges the servant to purify himself in his deeds, to cut back his wishes, and to be loyal to what he accepted on the day of the compact and the covenant of Yes indeed (7:172). Since a person knows that He sees him, he should keep his heart on Him and pull it away from everything else. He should be a purifier of himself in his deeds and truthful in his states. In that line of teaching the Pir of the Tariqah said that an eye which has seen Him will not busy itself glancing at anything else. A spirit that has found companionship with Him will not long be content with water and dust. One accustomed to the presence of contemplation will not put up with the humiliation of the veil, and the ruler of his own city will not spend his life in exile. The words "as though you see Him" point to the Real being seen, and the words "for He sees you" are the seeing of the Real. And it was said in the same line that when the awe of seeing the Real is present, the blame of those who deny it does not matter. A person should strive in a service worthy of the One he worships rather than settle for the portion of water and dust, since awe at the sight of the Real is a flood, while the approval of people is only debris.

### In short

- The earth was set right outwardly and inwardly, and the command forbids spoiling that order through corruption, sin and disobedience.
- Corruption is any crossing of the limits of moderation, and setting right is the work of putting things back into order.
- Keep the call to Him balanced between fear of the punishment and hope in the reward, and the mercy He promises is near to those who do good.
- Outward disorder and inward disorder feed each other, and all the comfort and technology in the world cannot give real peace while people are disobeying their Lord.
- To lose hope in the mercy of Allah is as wrong as to grow careless about one's sins, and the prayer of a person whose food, drink and clothing are haram does not rise.
- Doing good in the sense the Prophet ﷺ gave it, worshipping as though seeing Him, is what brings a person close to that mercy.

57.text:
After Allah had stated that He created the heavens and the earth, that He owns and disposes of all affairs, and that He has made things subservient, He laid down that He be called upon in supplication, since He is able to do all things. The chapter has been speaking of the Lord's power in the heavens and the earth. It now turns to a mercy that falls from above and works below. "He is the One Who sends the winds ushering in His mercy." Then the next stage. "When they bear heavy clouds, We drive them to a lifeless land and then cause rain to fall, producing every type of fruit." And the argument is drawn. "Similarly, We will bring the dead to life, so perhaps you will be mindful". The rain is put forward as proof of the rising, and nothing in it is hard to watch.

### Phrase by phrase

**"He is the One Who sends the winds ushering in His mercy"** announces good news before a blessing. The winds are sent ahead of the rain, and the Book says in another place that among His signs is that He sends the winds with glad tidings (30:46). The mercy spoken of here is the rain itself, and the sending of it belongs to Allah alone.

The practice of the Lord in this matter is a standing one. Cool winds come before the rains arrive. They are a blessing in themselves, since they brace and refresh the creation, and they also tell people that rain is on its way well before it comes. Human beings are a delicate kind of creation, and rain can stop them from doing what they need to do. If they know in advance, they can arrange their affairs and find cover for themselves and for what belongs to them. So the winds carry two blessings at once.

**"When they bear heavy clouds"** describes the next stage. The clouds are heavy because they are loaded with water. They travel as if riding on the shoulders of the wind, and the water that weighs thousands of tons is carried high on those wings without a machine and without anyone labouring over it. When the Lord wills, vapour rises from the waters, turns into cloud, and what results is a vessel of the sky carrying hundreds of thousands of gallons in its hold, moving on the cushion of the winds towards the higher air.

**"We drive them to a lifeless land"** explains where the rain is taken. The word for driving carries the sense of herding something towards a chosen destination, and the word for the land means a town or a settled place, while the lifelessness means that the place has died. So the verse says that the clouds are herded to a dead town, which is a settlement left desolate by the lack of water. That a settled place is named, rather than open wilderness, fits the purpose of the rain, since the rain is sent to feed a thirsty land and to bring out what human beings need, and the place for that is where people live.

Two things are settled by this point. The first is that rain comes through the clouds, so that wherever the Book speaks of rain coming down from the sky, the sky there means the clouds. Whether the clouds form directly in the upper air, rather than rising from the waters as the monsoons do, is not impossible either. The second is that the direction a cloud takes, and the particular stretch of land it goes over, are matters of the divine command. He gives the order for rain when He wills, where He wills and in the measure He wills, and the clouds carry out that order.

Anyone can observe the proof of it. A town may lie under heavy clouds and be in great need of rain, and still not receive a drop. The clouds move on to a town for which the share of water has been determined, and it rains there and nowhere else. Nobody has the power or the boldness to pull water out of those clouds at any other place. The weather scientists have worked out rules about the movement of the monsoon from the waters of the sea, and there are offices in many countries that publish forecasts. Experience shows that the news from those offices is often the opposite of what happens. When the divine command goes another way, their rules do not hold, and the winds and the laden clouds turn somewhere else, and the experts can do nothing about it. None of that denies the rules the meteorologists propose, since the practice of the Lord in the affairs of this world is that His command shows itself from behind the curtain of physical causes. People pick those causes up and build rules on them, while the reality lies elsewhere.

**"and then cause rain to fall, producing every type of fruit"** is the third stage. Water comes down on the dead land, and by that water the land brings out fruits of every kind.

**"Similarly, We will bring the dead to life, so perhaps you will be mindful"** draws the conclusion. The way dead land was given new life, and trees, flowers and fruit were brought out of it, is the way the dead will be raised on the day of Qiyamah after they have died. The examples are set out so that people may reflect on them. In one comparison, the dead land is given as a sign, which is the same sign that appears elsewhere in the Book where the dead earth is given life, and the raising of the dead is mentioned in the same breath (36:33).

The Book says of the rain in another place that it is sent down after people have given up hope, and that the Lord spreads His mercy, and that He is Al-Wali, the Guardian, and Al-Hamid, the Praiseworthy (42:28). And it invites the reader to look at the results of the mercy of Allah, how He revives the earth after its death, and it says that the One who does that will surely raise the dead, and that He is able to do all things (30:50).

### What the clouds are, and how they are loaded

The clouds that carry rain are heavy, and their heaviness is the water inside them. That is why they hang low near the earth and their colour is dark. The land they are driven to is dry and has no vegetation of any kind. Rain falls on it, and the surface that had died comes back to life, and every kind of fruit is produced from it.

On the day of the raising, the Lord will send rain down from the sky, and it will pour on the earth for forty days. The bodies will then be brought up out of their graves in the same way that seeds come up out of the ground when the rain reaches them. This likeness between the greening of the earth and the raising of the dead is one the Book uses often when it sets out what will happen on that day.

The reports give more of the order of that day. In a narration from Abu Hurairah, the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said that the Sur, the horn, will be blown twice on the day of Qiyamah. At the first blowing the whole world perishes and nothing that lives remains. At the second, a new world comes into being and the dead become alive. The same report mentions an interval of forty years between the two blowings, with rain falling throughout those years. In that span, the parts of every dead human being and animal are gathered back into them, so that each has a complete skeleton. Then, when the second blowing comes, the ruh enters those bodies and they rise alive. A large part of this narration is found in Al-Bukhari and Muslim, and some portions of it are taken from the book on the raising of the dead by Ibn Abi Dawud.

### The rain that falls on the heart

There is a reading of this passage that turns the rain inward. When the hearts catch the breeze of nearness, they are carried away into the dominion of majesty and stripped of everything they had traced out and grown used to. Once that breeze of the Beginningless comes from the side of nearness, and the wind of generosity blows out of solitariness, servanthood turns into freedom and every suffering turns into happiness. Fear carries the fearful one to safety. Want carries the hopeful one to the shore of the gift. Regret takes the disobedient person to the shore of repentance. And tawhid takes the one who declares the oneness of God to the shore of solitariness.

Rain comes from the sky, and the dead earth comes alive, and plants and flowers and blossoms appear. In the same way, the rain of mercy comes out of the storehouse of power, and withered hearts come alive. One heart received the seed of regret, and when the water of success reached it, its owner turned away from the world. Another received the seed of concern, and the water of kind favour produced a repenter. A third received the seed of awe, and the water of reverence produced a knower of God. In that line of teaching the Pir of the Tariqah spoke of the water of solicitude reaching a stone, so that the stone itself became pregnant, and fruit grew from the stone and gained flavour and became food. He spoke of the remembrance of the Lord bringing the heart to life, throwing down the seed of love, making the tree of happiness grow, and the tree giving the fruit of freedom. And he said that a seed comes up as a goodly tree (14:24) and gives nothing but the jasmine of the Covenant when the clay has become receptive, the soil sweet and the earth soft.

That reading is carried by the same material that the earlier verses used. Before this passage the Lord had shown His particular blessings in the upper domain, and the blessings in this passage belong to the lower one, which is to say the rain and the trees and the farmland and its produce. On that arrangement the needs of the creation are in the hand of no power but the sacred Being, and so the turning to Him is the key to success, and no one else should be asked for anything. That is the observation recorded in Al-Bahr Al-Muhit.

### The land that drinks and the land that does not

Something particular is marked out in the second of the two verses. The blessing of rain is common to every part of the earth, falling on rivers and mountains, on good land and on bad alike. What grows from the earth, however, grows only from land that has the quality to make it grow. Rocky and sandy ground takes nothing from the rain.

The same figure explains how guidance works. The message of the Book, the prophets who brought it, and the teaching and training carried on by their successors, the scholars and the teachers of the community, are like the rain, and they are open to every human being. But just as not every land takes benefit from the rain, so not every person takes benefit from that spiritual rain. It is taken by those who have the capacity to absorb it. Hearts that are like rocky, sandy ground, without that capacity, hold to their error even with clear guidance, clear signs and scriptures in front of them.

This is why the verse ends with the words about the verses being varied for a people who give thanks. The statement was made for everyone, and in the end it profited those who had the capacity for it and saw what it was worth.

### In short

- The winds are sent ahead of the rain as good news, and they are a blessing in themselves, since they refresh the creation and warn people that rain is coming.
- The clouds are heavy because they carry water, and they are herded by the divine command to a dead and settled land, where the rain revives the ground and brings out fruit of every kind.
- Which land receives the rain and which stays dry is settled by the command of Allah, and the forecasts of the experts fail whenever that command goes another way.
- The revival of dead land is the likeness of the raising of the dead, with the rain of that day falling on the earth and the bodies coming up out of their graves as seeds come up.
- The reports of the two blowings of the Sur and the entry of the ruh into the gathered bodies belong to the same subject, and they are carried by the sound collections.
- The rain is also read as the mercy that falls on hearts, which come alive or stay dry according to what they can receive.

58.text:
The lesson is now put in one line about two kinds of ground. "The fertile land produces abundantly by the Will of its Lord, whereas the infertile land hardly produces anything. This is how We vary ˹Our˺ lessons to those who are thankful". The rain has fallen on both, and the difference is in what the ground does with it.

### Phrase by phrase

**"The fertile land produces abundantly by the Will of its Lord"** describes ground with something good in it. Its vegetation comes out quickly and well, and its flowers and fruits and its many other benefits are brought out by the permission of its Lord. The Book uses the same image elsewhere of a good upbringing, where it says of Maryam, the mother of ʿIsa, that her Lord made her grow in a good manner (3:37).

**"whereas the infertile land hardly produces anything"** describes the other kind. The word carries the sense of what is useless and scanty at the same time. This is hard, barren or saline ground that has no ability to grow plants. Very little comes up on it, and what does come up is small in quantity and worthless in quality. Mujahid and others, among them As-Sibakh, said the same.

**"This is how We vary ˹Our˺ lessons to those who are thankful"** closes the verse. The verses are turned this way and that, and put in different forms, for people who are grateful, since gratitude is what opens a person to what is being said.

### The two lands and the two hearts

The comparison that runs through the material is between the two kinds of ground and the two kinds of hearers. Good land is ground that is not a swamp, and its plants come out by the will of its Lord without toil and without effort. That is the sincere believer, who does what Allah commands him to do willingly and with a good disposition of his soul. The other ground is bad and swampy, and nothing but what is useless comes out of it, and it comes out only with labour and great effort. That is the hypocrite, who does not do what Allah commands except when he is compelled, and without any good disposition in his soul.

Another reading of the same comparison says that the good land is the one with rich soil, whose plants come up wholesome by the permission of its Lord, and that this is the likeness of the believer who hears an admonition, takes it in and benefits from it. The bad soil brings its vegetation out miserably and laboriously, and that is the likeness of the disbeliever. Even so the Book sets out what it has to say, and makes the signs plain for a people who give thanks to God and so believe.

A third reading of the same lines says that good land brings its vegetation out in abundance by the permission of Allah, and that the believer is like it, understanding the teaching he is given, benefiting from it and acting on it with righteousness. The rotting, salty land produces only a little, and there is little good in what it produces. The disbeliever is like that land, since he does not benefit from the true teaching that reaches him, and he does not perform the good acts that would help him. By varying the examples in these ways, Allah reveals His signs and His proofs, confirming the truth to a people who are thankful for His blessings, who do not deny them, and who follow their Lord.

One of the early teachers said of the goodly land that its goodliness comes about through the continuity of security, through the justice of the ruler, and through the obedience of those who obey. And Abū ʿUthmān said that the good land is the heart of the person of faith, on whose limbs the lights of obedient acts become visible, while the vile land that yields so little is the heart of the disbeliever, on whose limbs nothing but acts of opposition appears.

The Prophet ﷺ gave the whole matter in a parable of his own. Al-Bukhari recorded from Abu Musa that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said that the guidance and knowledge with which Allah sent him are like a heavy rain falling on a stretch of land. One part of that land was good soil, which took in the water and brought out vegetation and grass in abundance. Another part was hard ground, which held the water, and Allah made it useful to people, who drank from it, gave it to their animals and used it to irrigate their fields. A third part was barren and could neither hold the water nor bring out any vegetation. The first is the likeness of the one who understands the religion of Allah and takes benefit from what Allah sent him with, by learning it and teaching it to others. The last is the likeness of the one who pays no attention to it and does not accept the guidance with which Allah sent him.

### In short

- The rain is the same for everyone, and what the ground returns depends on the kind of ground it is.
- The good land yields its fruit easily by the permission of its Lord, and the barren land yields only a little that is worth nothing.
- The two lands stand for the believer who hears and takes benefit and for the disbeliever or the hypocrite who gains nothing from the teaching.
- Gratitude is the quality that opens a person to the message, and the verses are varied in their forms for such people.
- The Prophet ﷺ gave the same picture in the parable of the rain that fell on good soil, on hard ground that held the water, and on barren ground that held nothing at all.

59.text:
The chapter now leaves the general argument and begins the stories of the prophets. "Indeed, We sent Noah to his people. He said, “O my people! Worship Allah—you have no other god except Him. I truly fear for you the torment of a tremendous Day.”" The section opens the eighth ruku of the surah, and from here to nearly the end the subject is the messengers and the communities they were sent to.

### Phrase by phrase

**"Indeed, We sent Noah to his people"** marks the beginning of the stories. After Allah had mentioned the story of Adam at the start of this surah, He began to mention the prophets, one after another, and He began with Nuh, since he was the first messenger sent to the people of the earth after Adam.

His line is given in the books that record descent. He was Nuh bin Lamak bin Matushalakh bin Khanukh, and Khanukh, as they say, was the prophet Idris. Idris was the first person to write letters with the pen, and the descent runs from him through Barad and Mahlil, then Qanin, Yanish and Shith, and so to Adam, peace be upon them all. That descent is given by Muhammad bin Ishaq and by others of the imams who document lineage.

The beginning of the story is placed in the generations before him. Allah had mentioned the story of Adam first, and the decades after Adam are described in the reports as a long stretch in which the descendants held to the oneness of God. In a tradition from Abdullah ibn Abbas, the change began with the dead. When righteous people among them died, their people built places of worship over their graves and made images of them, so that the memory of their righteousness and their devotion would stay fresh and they could imitate them. As time passed they made statues of them, and later still they worshipped those idols, naming them after the righteous dead. The names given are Wadd, Suwa', Yaghuth, Ya'uq and Nasr. When this practice had spread and grown, Allah sent Nuh as a messenger, and it was through his mission that the new world was populated after the flood, which is why he is sometimes called the junior Adam.

The verse proves that his mission was to his own people and not to all the world. They lived in Iraq. They were outwardly civilised, and they were caught up in shirk. Disbelief as a public matter did not exist before them, since Adam was a prophet but his time was not the time for confrontation with error, and most of the injunctions given to him concerned the settling of the land and the management of human needs. The confrontation with kufr and with shirk began with Nuh. In terms of the mission of prophethood and of a code of laws, he is the first messenger of Allah, and his struggle with a crooked people lasted nine hundred and fifty years, at the end of which all but a few of them were drowned.

**"O my people! Worship Allah—you have no other god except Him"** is the call itself, and it is built of three parts. The first invites them to worship Allah, which is the essence of the matter. The second persuades them to leave off shirk and kufr, which had spread among them like an epidemic. The third warns them, as the next words do.

**"I truly fear for you the torment of a tremendous Day"** is the warning. The Day is the Day of Resurrection, and the torment spoken of is what awaits them if they meet Allah while they are joining others to Him. The words may also take in the punishment of this world, which for them came as the flood.

### How the story is placed in the surah

The surah up to this point has dealt with three things, the oneness of God, the messengership, and the life to come, which are the basic principles of the religion. They were proved and affirmed in many ways, people were urged to follow them, and they were warned against taking a stand against them. Then, as a natural sequel, the tricks of Satan that lead people away were described. What follows now is a description of some of the prophets and their communities, and it runs for about fourteen sections.

The pattern of those sections is the same in each. The messengers invited their communities to the same universal principles and to the same articles of faith. They gave good news of reward to those who believed and warned of punishment and a sad end for those who refused. Out of that come hundreds of rulings, major and minor, by way of corollary. The communities of the present are given the chance to learn from the end of the communities of the past, and for the Prophet ﷺ himself the record became a comfort, since this is how matters had gone with all the prophets before him.

The date of Nuh in relation to the other early figures is given in several reports. He is in the eighth generation of Adam. In a narration of Ibn Abbas that appears in the Mustadrak of Hakim there is an interval of ten generations between Adam and Nuh, and the same has been reported by Tabarani on the basis of a hadith of the Prophet ﷺ narrated by Abu Dharr. A generation is generally counted as a hundred years, which makes a thousand years between the two. Ibn Jarir reported that the birth of Nuh came eight hundred and twenty six years after Adam died. The Book states plainly that he reached the age of nine hundred and fifty, and a hadith gives the age of Adam as nine hundred and sixty. On those figures the span from the birth of Adam to the death of Nuh comes to two thousand eight hundred and fifty six years. Some narrations give his real name as Shakir, others as Sakan, and still others as Abd al-Ghaffar. Whether his time came before or after Idris is a matter of debate, and the majority of the Companions held that Nuh came before Idris, as is recorded in Al-Bahr Al-Muhit. A narration of Ibn Abbas in the Mustadrak of Hakim has the Prophet ﷺ saying that Nuh was given prophethood at the age of forty and lived for sixty years after the flood.

### What is drawn from the community and its end

The reason for their refusal is given plainly in the Book. It was very hard for them to accept that a man who looked like them had been chosen to deliver God's message on His behalf. Compared with the great figures of the past, whose religion they thought they were following and whose greatness history had settled, Nuh was a man of their own time with no glory attached to his name, and he looked ordinary to them. So they did not accept him, and they did not hesitate to call the prophet of their age foolish and misguided, since in their view he had turned away from the way of their great ones.

None of the things that should have moved them did so. His good will towards them, the strength of his arguments, his reasoning, and his firmness on the path of truth all left them where they were. Once he had conveyed the message in full and they had rejected it, the community was drowned in the great flood. The reason for the punishment was that they had called the signs of God false and denied them. What they wanted was for God's message to reach them through some established figure rather than an ordinary man. In the sight of God that was blindness. He has given human beings insight so that they may recognise the truth in the shape of signs, and not through something they can hold. Those who cannot do that are blind in the sight of God although their eyes are open, and such people have no share in His grace.

### In short

- Nuh was the first messenger sent to the people of the earth after Adam, and his call was the call of every prophet after him.
- The first idol worship began when images and places of worship were put up over the graves of righteous people, and the idols were named after them.
- His people were civilised in outward ways and sunk in shirk, and they were warned of the torment of the Day of Resurrection, and of the punishment of this world as well.
- Nuh is the junior Adam in the sense that the world was populated again through those who were saved with him.
- The stories that begin here all carry the same articles of faith, and they are set out so that later communities may take warning from the end of earlier ones.

60.text:
The first answer to the call comes from the men who held power among the people. "But the chiefs of his people said, “We surely see that you are clearly misguided.”" The word used for them means the chiefs, the headmen and the empowered elders of a community.

### Phrase by phrase

**"But the chiefs of his people said"** names the speakers. They are the leading men, and alongside them the general public and the great ones of the people are included by the same term in other readings of the verse.

**"We surely see that you are clearly misguided"** is the charge. What they meant by it was that he was trying to pull them away from the faith of their forefathers, and that the ideas he brought about rising on a last day and being rewarded or punished were nothing but superstition.

That answer carries a mark of its own. It is the manner of evil people to call the righteous misguided, as the Book will say of other communities in more than one place, since the call to abandon idols that their forefathers had worshipped strikes at everything they hold. The Book records the same attitude elsewhere. It says of one set of people that when they saw the believers they said that these had surely gone astray (83:32), and it records of another set that when they were not guided by the Qur'an they called it an ancient lie (46:11). Other verses carry the same theme.

It was also said of this community that the charge of foolishness and misguidance was not their only objection, since they had a further doubt about the man himself. That doubt is set out in Surah Al-Mu'minun, and it belongs with the answer given in the verses that follow.

### In short

- The leaders of the people were the first to answer, and their answer was an accusation rather than an argument.
- They charged Nuh with clear error, meaning that he had left the religion of their forefathers.
- Calling the righteous misguided is the habit of those who are themselves in the wrong, and the Book notes the same habit in other communities.

61.text:
The charge is answered without heat. "He replied, “O my people! I am not misguided! But I am a messenger from the Lord of all worlds"".

### Phrase by phrase

**"O my people! I am not misguided"** begins the reply with an address that keeps the bond intact. The word he denies is the more general of the two words for error, which makes the denial wider in its reach than a denial of the narrower word would have been.

**"But I am a messenger from the Lord of all worlds"** gives the ground of his standing. Nuh is not bound by the customs of his people, which rest on ignorance. What he brings them comes from the Lord of all that exists, the Lord and King of all things, and everything he tells them is under the guidance of his Lord.

### Answering a charge without heat

The way the answer is put is itself a lesson. The words carry the diction that belongs to a prophet. What he leaves behind is a trail for everyone who carries the call, for preachers and for reformers. He does not answer anger with anger. He takes the doubts they have and removes them in the simplest words he can find. His mission is to convey what Allah has sent him with, and what he conveys is for their good and not for any benefit of Allah and not for any personal interest of his own.

The phrase about the Lord of all the worlds also strikes at the practice of shirk, that is to say at the joining of any partner to Him. When the sense of that phrase is understood, no god or goddess of any kind stands as a valid object of worship. Their doubts about the punishment of the last day came from a lack of awareness on their part, and he, by contrast, had been given certainty about it.

The further doubt of the community is set out in Al-Mu'minun. There they argued that he was only a human being, a man like themselves who ate and drank and slept and woke as they did. They asked how they could take such a man as their leader, and said that if Allah had wanted to send them a message He should have sent angels with it, whose greatness would have impressed them. From where they stood, all they saw was one of their own community who wanted to set himself above them (23:24).

### In short

- The reply denies the charge and gives the reason for his mission in the same breath.
- He speaks to them as his people, and answers the accusation without matching it in temper.
- The phrase about the Lord of all the worlds by itself removes any partner from worship.
- The second line of objection, that he was only a man like them, is answered in the verses that follow and is set out at length in Al-Mu'minun.

62.text:
He then describes what the mission consists of. "conveying to you my Lord’s messages and giving you ˹sincere˺ advice. And I know from Allah what you do not know".

### Phrase by phrase

**"conveying to you my Lord’s messages"** is the first part of a messenger's work. What he passes on are the messages of his Lord, with the commands and the prohibitions of his Lord explained in them.

**"and giving you sincere advice"** is the second part. The counsel of Nuh is meant for their good, and he warns them of the torment and calls them to repentance and to faith.

**"And I know from Allah what you do not know"** is the third part. He knows from Allah what they do not know of the torment that waits for them if they do not believe, and that knowledge came to him by revelation.

### The testimony of the gathering at Arafah

Those three things are the description of a messenger, since he conveys the message in plain and eloquent words, offers sincere advice, and knows about Allah. Nobody else can compete with the prophets in that combination. To mark it, the Prophet ﷺ put a question to his Companions at Arafah, at the largest gathering of theirs there ever was. He asked them what they would say when they were asked about him. They answered that they would testify that he had conveyed the message and delivered it and given sincere advice. He then raised his finger towards the sky and brought it down towards them, saying, O Allah, bear witness, O Allah, bear witness. Muslim recorded that report in his collection.

The reply also settles the doubts about the last day. Their uncertainty came from a want of awareness, while he had been given certainty on the matter. In the same breath his call is cleared of any personal interest. The mission was for their good alone, and it served no benefit of Allah and no advantage of his own.

### In short

- The work of the messenger is summarised in three parts, the conveying of the messages, sincere counsel, and knowledge of Allah.
- The Prophet ﷺ asked his Companions on the Day of Arafah what they would testify about him, and called Allah to witness their answer, and that report is in the collection of Muslim.
- The doubts the people held about the last day came from their own ignorance, since the messenger had been given certainty about it.
- He sought nothing for himself, and everything he brought was for the good of the people he was sent to.

63.text:
He puts the wonder back to them as a question. "Do you find it astonishing that a reminder should come to you from your Lord through one of your own, warning you, so you may beware and perhaps be shown mercy?”"

### Phrase by phrase

**"Do you find it astonishing that a reminder should come to you from your Lord"** takes up their surprise directly. The answer is that the matter is not surprising at all. That Allah sends down revelation to a man among them is mercy, kindness and compassion towards them, since the warning is meant to save them from the torment, and that is why the reminder comes.

**"through one of your own"** touches the real objection, which was that the messenger was a man from among them. The point is worked out at length. Allah is the Absolute Master, and giving someone the rank of prophet or messenger is His own affair. He does it when He wills, and no one can have it otherwise. Beyond that, a little thought shows that the purpose for which a prophet is sent to guide human beings can be achieved only through a human being, and that this is a mission on which angels cannot be sent.

### Why the messenger had to be one of them

The reason is what prophethood is for. Its aim is to bring people to believe in Allah and obey Him, and to save them from the hard end that follows from opposing what He has laid down. That can only happen when someone of their own kind stands before them as a working model of the conduct asked of them, and shows them that it is possible to worship Allah and keep His injunctions while still living a human life with all its needs and desires. If angels had brought the call and set their own model before people, the answer would have been easy. Angels have no human desires, they do not go hungry or thirsty, they do not sleep and they do not tire, so how could people ever be like them? But when one of their own kind, with all the ordinary human traits and desires, walks among them as a perfect model of obedience, no excuse is left to them.

**"warning you, so you may beware and perhaps be shown mercy"** gives the purpose of the whole arrangement, that is to say the reason why a warner is sent at all. A warner whose warning can move people has to be one of their own kind, a human being with human qualities. So the answer here covers every community that raised the same doubt about the human character of its messenger. It is a matter for regret that in spite of the clarifications the Book gives, some people go so far as to deny the humanness of the Prophet ﷺ himself. The trouble with the ignorant is that they will not accept the superiority of anyone from their own kind, and so they nurse a grudge against the friends of God and the scholars of their own time and look down on them for being their contemporaries. That has always been the trademark of the ignorant.

Their other objection, that they were being asked to follow a man and not an angel, has been answered along the same lines. In Al-Mu'minun the doubt is given in their own words, and it is the doubt of a community that could not see how Nuh, a man like themselves, could be raised above them (23:24).

### In short

- The wonder they felt is turned back on them, since sending a man among them is a mercy rather than a strange thing.
- The rank of prophethood is given by Allah to whom He wills, and no one can take it or refuse it.
- A human messenger is the only kind who can serve as an example for human beings, since an angel's example would leave people an easy excuse.
- The warning comes so that the people may guard themselves and find mercy.
- The same refusal to accept a contemporary as a leader has been the habit of the ignorant in every age.

64.text:
The story closes with the response of the people and the end that came on them. "But they rejected him, so We saved him and those with him in the Ark, and drowned those who rejected Our signs. They were certainly a blind people".

### Phrase by phrase

**"But they rejected him"** records what the people did with all of that. They held to their rejection and their opposition, and only a few of them believed.

**"so We saved him and with him those in the Ark"** is the deliverance. When the flood came, the believers were kept from drowning and from the torment by being brought into the ship. The story in full, with the account of the drowning of the people, is given in Surah Hud and in Surah Nuh, and what appears here is the gist of it as the occasion requires.

**"and drowned those who rejected Our signs"** is the judgement. Their drowning is put down to the fact that they called the signs of God false. The Book says of them elsewhere that because of their sins they were drowned and then admitted into the Fire, and that they found none to help them instead of Allah (71:25).

**"They were certainly a blind people"** is the verdict on them. The blindness spoken of is blindness to the truth, since they could neither recognise it nor find the way to it.

The timing of the punishment carries a lesson. One of the early teachers said that when the flood overtook the people of Nuh they were at the peak of their numbers and their power, and the lands and mountains of Iraq were becoming too small for their growing population. It is the standing practice of Allah to give the disobedient time, and then to send the punishment at the moment when they have reached the highest point of their numbers, their power and their wealth, and have grown drunk with their own condition.

In this way the enemies were paid back, and the messenger was saved with those who believed in him, while the men who opposed him and denied him were destroyed. The Book says elsewhere that He will indeed make His messengers victorious (40:51). That is Allah's Sunnah with His servants, in this life and in the Hereafter, that the good end, the victory and the triumph belong to those who are mindful of Him.

The numbers of those who were saved are given in the reports. Eighty men were saved with Nuh in the ship, and one of them was Jurhum, who spoke Arabic. That statement came through Ibn Wahb on the authority of Ibn Abbas, and Ibn Abi Hatim collected it. It was also narrated with a continuous chain reaching Ibn Abbas. Some narrations say that the Ark held forty men and forty women. After the flood, the place in Mosul in Iraq where they came to settle became known as Thamanun, which means eighty.

### What the story of Nuh contributes

The brief account placed here carries three lessons. The first is that the call of all the prophets and their basic articles of faith were one and the same. The second is that Allah supports His appointed messengers in ways that are full of wonder, so that Nuh was in no danger to his safety even when a flood had risen as high as the peaks of the mountains around him. The third is that calling the prophets of Allah false amounts to inviting the punishment of Allah. That warning still stands. The communities of the past were overtaken because they treated the messengers as liars, and the same end can overtake those who take the same road now. The better course is not to become heedless and free of fear of that.

One more thing is marked by the closing words. The people wanted the message to be brought to them through some great and established figure rather than an ordinary man. In the sight of God that was blindness, since He has given human beings insight so that they may know the truth in the shape of signs, and not through anything they can see and touch. Whoever cannot do that is blind in the sight of God even with his eyes open, and such a person has no share in the grace of God.

### In short

- They held to their rejection, and only a few of their people believed.
- The believers were saved in the Ark, and those who called the signs of God false were drowned and then brought into the Fire.
- Their blindness was blindness to the truth, since they could not recognise it or find their way to it.
- The punishment came when the community was at the height of its numbers and power, which is the way of Allah with those who persist in denial.
- The account is placed here to show that the call of all the prophets was one, that Allah guards His messengers, and that treating them as liars brings down the punishment of Allah.

65.text:
The second community is now brought on. "And to the people of ’Âd We sent their brother Hûd. He said, “O my people! Worship Allah—you have no other god except Him. Will you not then fear Him?”" The sending is put the same way it was put for Nuh, and the call is the same call.

### Phrase by phrase

**"And to the people of ’Âd We sent their brother Hûd"** follows the pattern of the verse before. Just as Nuh was sent to his people, so Hud was sent to the people of Ad, one of their own brothers. He was among the noble men and the chiefs of Ad, since Allah chooses the messengers from the best and most honourable families and tribes.

Ad is the name of a man who stands in the fifth generation after Nuh, among the descendants of his son Sam. His descendants and his people after him came to be known by his name. Muhammad bin Ishaq sets out the line as Ad the son of Iram, who was the son of Aws, who was the son of Sam, who was the son of Nuh. They were arrogant in the land without any right, and they asked who among the creation was mightier than they were, while the One who had brought them into being was mightier than them, and they went on denying the signs (41:15). These are the ancient people of Ad whom the Book mentions, the children of Ad son of Iram, who lived in the deserts among lofty pillars. The Book asks whether the reader has seen how his Lord dealt with Ad, with Iram of the lofty pillars (89:7), a people whose like was never created in the land (89:6-8), and that greatness of theirs was in their might and their strength.

In the Book the people also appear as Ad al-Ula, Ad the First, and they are known in association with the name of Iram, which tells us that there is an Ad the Second as well. The better known position is that Iram is the name of the grandfather of Ad, and not of the people as a whole. This Ad belongs among the children of Aws, and he is known as Ad the First. The second son of Aws was Jathw, and he had a son named Thamud, who is called Ad the Second. So Ad and Thamud are two branches of Iram, and the name Iram is common to both of them.

Hud himself is also in the fifth generation of Nuh and among the progeny of Sam. The genealogies of the people of Ad and of Hud meet at Sam in that fifth generation, and that is why the verse calls him their brother.

**"He said, “O my people! Worship Allah"** is the invitation, and it rests on the same three parts as before. The people are called to worship Allah, which is the essence of the matter, and they are persuaded to leave off the practice of joining others to Him, which had spread among them.

**"you have no other god except Him"** removes every partner from the matter. The one to whom the call is made is the only God they have.

**"Will you not then fear Him?"** is the warning, and it is put shorter here than it was in the story of Nuh. The grave punishment that had come down on the people of Nuh was still fresh in the minds of the people of Ad, since it had happened not long before their own time, and so Hud had no need to describe the severity of what falls on disobedient people. It was enough to ask them whether they would not be mindful of Him now, by following His instructions and keeping away from what He has forbidden, so that they might be saved from His punishment.

### The country and the people of Ad

Their country lay in Yemen, in the area known as Ahqaf, which means sand mounds. Ibn Jarir recorded a report that carries the same point with it. It came from Abu At-Tufayl Amir bin Wathilah, who heard Ali bin Abi Talib put a question to a man of Hadramawt, asking whether he had seen a red sand mound in such and such a place there, a spot where a lot of Arak trees stood and lote trees grew. The man said that he had, and added that the description was as though Ali had seen it with his own eyes. Ali said that he had not seen it himself, but that it had been described to him. When the man asked what was there, Ali said that the grave of Hud stood in its vicinity. That report is useful for the same reason, since it indicates that Ad lived in Yemen, because their prophet was buried there.

The people had thirteen families, and their habitations were spread from Oman to Hadramaut and Yaman. Their lands were fertile, their gardens were abundant, and they built mansions and palaces to live in. They were tall and heavily built. Allah had opened the doors of His blessing upon them.

The people of Ad were mighty and strong in body, but their hearts were mighty and hard, and they were among the most denying of the truth of all the nations. The crooked turn of their thinking made the blessings they had into a curse for them. They grew so drunk with their power and their grandeur that they began to boast that nobody was greater than them in strength. What is strange is that they paid no attention to their Lord and to the Lord of all the worlds, in whose blessings they were bathed, and sank instead into the worship of idols cut out of the rocks. Their supplication was directed at those stones, and the supplication of their prophet before them had been the means by which the people of the earth were destroyed, as the Book notes when it reminds them whose offspring they are.

### Who the Arabs are, and what became of Ad

The famous authority on Arab genealogy, Abu al-Barak-at al-Jauni, wrote that the son of Hud was Ya'rub ibn Qahtan, who went to live in Yaman, and that the people of Yaman are his descendants. The Arabic language came from him, and it was from that connection with Ya'rub that the language was called Arabic and its speakers were called the Arabs. That is recorded in Al-Bahr Al-Muhit.

The truth of the matter is that Arabic was there from the time of Nuh, and that he had a companion in the Ark called Jurhum who spoke it. The populating of Makkah began from that same Jurhum. It is still possible that the origin of the language in Yaman came about through Ya'rub ibn Qahtan, and that this is what the genealogist meant.

For the people of Ad there came an end in two stages.
