When Hud urged them to leave the worship of idols, to take up the pure oneness of God, to give up injustice and oppression, and to deal in moderation and justice, they paid no attention, since they were drunk with power and with wealth. The first punishment that visited them was that the rains stopped for three years in succession. The land became desert and the gardens turned into dead wood. They held to their practice of joining partners to God and to the worship of idols through all of it. Then the second punishment came. A severe wind storm overtook them, and it held for seven nights and eight days together. Their gardens, their mansions and their palaces were levelled to the ground, and the men and the animals were lifted into the air and came back down to strike the floor on their heads. So the people of Ad were wiped out to the last man.

When the punishment came down on them for not listening to Hud and for holding to their disbelief and their shirk, the prophet took shelter with those who were with him in an open area enclosed with stakes. What was strange was this. The storm that was bringing the palaces down on their columns would change its pace at that enclosure and go in gently. Hud and his companions sat in peace where they were throughout the descent of the punishment, without having to face any inconvenience. After the destruction of the people of Ad they moved to Makkah and lived there until they died. That account is in Al-Bahr Al-Muhit.

### How the end was described in more than one way

That the punishment of the people of Ad came as a wind storm is stated plainly in the Book. There is also a statement that follows the story of Nuh in Surah Al-Mu'minun, that after them another generation was brought forth (23:31), and it seems clear that this other generation is the people of Ad. After their words and deeds have been set out there, it is said that a harsh and horrifying sound took them (23:41). On the strength of that statement some have held that the punishment that came on Ad was that sound, which is called As-Saihah. There is no contradiction between the two accounts, since it is possible that both of them came to pass.

The point of the mention here is that this was a brief account of Ad and of Hud, of the same shape as the account of Nuh before it. What it shows is the way of the Lord with the communities that are sent messengers and refuse them.

### In short

- Hud was sent to the people of Ad as one of their own, and the call he gave was the same call Nuh had given before him.
- The people of Ad were descended from Ad son of Iram, and they were known for their great strength and their lofty buildings.
- Their home was Yemen, among the sands, and the report about the grave of the Prophet Hud in Hadramawt points to the same place.
- They had every blessing of fertile land, gardens and palaces, and their power turned them away from the One who had given it to them.
- The warning was put briefly because the punishment that had fallen on the people of Nuh was still a living memory among them.
- Their end came in two stages, first three years without rain and then the storm that left nothing standing, while Hud and his companions were kept safe in their enclosure.

66.text:
The chiefs make the same answer their kind made before. "The disbelieving chiefs of his people responded, “We surely see you as a fool, and we certainly think you are a liar.”"

### Phrase by phrase

**"The disbelieving chiefs of his people responded"** names the speakers. The word covers the general public and the chiefs, the masters and the commanders of the people, and the ones speaking here are those among them who had disbelieved.

**"We surely see you as a fool"** is the charge of folly. What they meant was that he was misguided, since he was calling them to leave off the worship of their idols in order to worship Allah alone.

**"and we certainly think you are a liar"** adds the second charge. They did not merely think him mistaken. They judged him a liar in the claim he was making, which is to say in his claim to have been sent by Allah.

This answer is the same in substance as the answer the people of Nuh gave. Their stand against the messenger resembles that one, and the only difference between the two is a matter of some words. The chiefs of Quraysh were to wonder at the same thing later, when the call to worship One God was put to them.

### In short

- The leaders who rejected the message were the ones who spoke, and they brought two charges at once, folly and lying.
- The charge of folly meant that he had left the way of the forefathers, and the charge of lying struck at his claim to be sent by God.
- The answer of this community is the answer of the community before it, differing only in some of its words.

67.text:
The answer comes back in the same manner as before. "Hûd replied, “O my people! I am no fool! But I am a messenger from the Lord of all worlds"".

### Phrase by phrase

**"O my people! I am no fool"** takes the first charge away. What they accused him of was folly, and the word in the Arabic suggests ignorance, which is what they laid at his door.

**"But I am a messenger from the Lord of all worlds"** gives his standing, and with it the second charge is answered as well. He is not as they claim. What he brought them is the truth from Allah, who created everything and who is the Lord and the King of all things. He brought it from the Lord of all that exists, for them.

The reply that appears in this verse and the one after it is nearly the same as the reply Nuh gave to his own people. That is what the two stories are for, since the messengers of Allah were sent with one message and met with one kind of answer.

### In short

- The accusation of folly is denied at once and without qualification.
- The ground of his mission is given in the same words the earlier messenger used, that he comes from the Lord of all the worlds.
- The reply follows the pattern of the replies before it, which is the point of the two stories being told one after the other.

68.text:
He goes on to describe the work itself. "conveying to you my Lord’s messages. And I am your sincere advisor".

### Phrase by phrase

**"conveying to you my Lord’s messages"** is the first part of the work. What he passes on are the messages of his Lord, with the commands and the prohibitions of his Lord explained in them. What he is asking of the people is belief in the oneness of Allah and in His sacred law, and he delivers what he was instructed to deliver, no less and no more.

**"And I am your sincere advisor"** is the second part. He warns them of the torment of Allah and calls them to repentance and to faith, and he is trustworthy in conveying the message of his Lord. Another sense is carried by the same words, that they used to consider him a trustworthy person, and that it is a strange thing for them to be accusing him now.

The wording shows what the relation between the one who calls and those he calls to should be. It is not the relation of a rival or a competitor. It is a relation of good will and of trust. The one who calls should have nothing in his heart but good wishes for the people he is addressing. However rude and unpleasant their behaviour towards him becomes, he should remain their well-wisher to the last moment.

There is a further point in it. When he delivers the message, he should not carry the feeling that he is handing over something that belongs to him, and that he is doing them a favour. He should feel rather that what he holds belongs to them. His part is the part of a trustee, and the delivery of it discharges him of a great responsibility. That is the standard the verse sets for everyone who takes up the same task after him.

The charges the people made against him, folly and lying, have both been taken away by this point, since the one who carries the messages of his Lord and advises them for their own good is neither a fool nor a deceiver. The third of the qualities of the prophets is joined to the other two here, so that conveying the message and sincerity and honesty stand together.

### In short

- The work of the messenger has two sides, the conveying of the messages and the counsel offered to the people.
- The counsel comes from good will, and the messenger is trustworthy in what he carries.
- The one who calls is not a rival but a well-wisher, and he holds the message in trust for those he addresses rather than owning it himself.
- The people had taken him for a trustworthy man before this, which makes their present charge strange as well as unjust.

69.text:
The wonder is turned back on them, and then the favours they have been living on are put in front of them. "Do you find it astonishing that a reminder should come to you from your Lord through one of your own so he may warn you? Remember that He made you successors after the people of Noah and increased you greatly in stature. So remember Allah’s favours, so you may be successful.”"

### Phrase by phrase

**"Do you find it astonishing that a reminder should come to you from your Lord through one of your own so he may warn you?"** takes up the objection that runs through all of these stories. They thought it strange that a man like themselves should be sent to them. The answer is that they should not wonder because Allah sent a messenger to them from among themselves to warn them about the days of Allah and about the meeting with Him. Instead of wondering, they should thank Allah for the bounty.

The objection itself is the one the people of Nuh had raised before them, which was how they could take a human being like themselves as their superior, and whether an angel would not have been better. The answer given here is the answer that was given there. A human being coming to people as the prophet or messenger of Allah, to put the fear of Him in their hearts, is nothing to be surprised about, because the one who can convince other human beings effectively is one of their own kind. The Book puts the same point in another place where the disbelievers are said to have wondered at the call to worship One God (38:5).

**"Remember that He made you successors after the people of Noah"** is the first favour named. They were established on the earth as successors to the people of Nuh, who had been destroyed because of their disbelief, and the reminder is that they should thank Allah and praise Him for that standing.

**"and increased you greatly in stature"** is the second favour. The words mean that they were made taller than other people and stronger in body. The same expression is used in the Book of Talut, of whom it is said that he was given abundance of knowledge and of bodily stature (2:247). The people of Ad were tall and heavily built, and their buildings and their gardens answered to that. One reading of the increase gives the measure of their height. The tallest of them reached a hundred feet, and the shortest came to sixty.

**"So remember Allah’s favours, so you may be successful"** draws the conclusion. Remembering the favours was for their own good, and the outcome held out to them is that they might escape the wrath and the torment, and attain what they desire while avoiding what is feared.

### What the call of the prophets rests on

The basis of the call of the prophets has always been to remind people of the bounties conferred on them, and to warn them that if they did not remain grateful to God they would suffer the scourge of God. Communal and material questions are never made the subject of their preaching. They take care that in the discussion between them and their hearers nothing comes up but the truths that really concern the hearers, so that the community sees them as preachers of the cause of the one God and of the Hereafter, and in no other form.

The line about remembering the favours so as to prosper carries the same weight. It shows that the bounties of the Hereafter are earned by the one who has acknowledged the grace of God in this world. Paradise is the greatest expression of the grace and bountifulness of God, and so the Paradise of the Hereafter will be reached by one who has come to know and recognise that attribute of grace and generosity in his Lord. That recognition is the real price of Paradise.

The wickedness of the people lay in their failure to see it. Their blessings had been opened to them, and their crooked thinking turned those blessings into a curse, since they grew drunk with power and grandeur and took no notice of the Lord in whose blessings they were sitting.

### In short

- The wonder they felt at being sent one of their own is the same wonder the earlier community felt, and the answer is the same, that a human messenger is what the task requires.
- They were reminded of the two great favours, that they had been made successors to the people of Nuh and that they had been given great bodily strength.
- The same expression about stature is used elsewhere of Talut, who was given abundance of knowledge and of body.
- Remembering the favours of Allah is the road to success, and gratitude for grace in this world is the price of the grace of the Hereafter.
- The call of the prophets rests on the favours of God and the warning of His scourge, and never on communal or material questions.

70.text:
The invitation is pushed back at him. "They said, “Have you come to us so that we would worship Allah alone and abandon what our forefathers used to worship? Then bring us what you threaten us with, if what you say is true!”"

### Phrase by phrase

**"Have you come to us so that we would worship Allah alone and abandon what our forefathers used to worship?"** puts their refusal in their own words. Hud was trying to pull them away from the faith of their fathers, and to bring them round to belief in one God, and that was a thing they would never do. What they were being asked to leave behind was what their fathers had worshipped, and the weight of their fathers' practice was the whole of their argument.

**"Then bring us what you threaten us with, if what you say is true!"** takes up the warning. Since he was telling them of punishment, they invited him to produce it there and then, if he was telling the truth. The same challenge was put to the Prophet ﷺ by the people of Quraysh, who asked that the sky be brought down on them or that a painful torment be brought, and the Book records their words (8:32).

### What the challenge looked like when it came

The answer to their demand is given in the verse that follows, and something of how it looked when it arrived is preserved in a report from that generation. The story of the emissary of Ad was told by a man who came to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ and found himself in a position similar to the one the man of Ad had been in.

Al-Harith Al-Bakri said that he went to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ to lay a complaint before him about Al-Ala bin Al-Hadrami. On the way, in the district of Ar-Rabdhah, he came upon an old woman of Bani Tamim who was alone there. She asked him to take her to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, since she had needs to put before him, and he took her along. When they reached Al-Madinah he found the mosque full of people, and a black flag raised high, with Bilal holding a sword before the Messenger of Allah ﷺ. He asked what was happening and was told that the Prophet ﷺ meant to send Amr bin Al-As on an expedition.

He sat down, and when the Prophet ﷺ went to his house he asked permission and was let in. He greeted him, and the Prophet ﷺ asked whether there had been a dispute between him and Bani Tamim. He said there had been, and that they had got the better of them. He mentioned the old woman of Bani Tamim whom he had passed by and brought, and she was let in. Then he asked the Prophet ﷺ whether he would put a barrier between them and Bani Tamim, such as the desert of Ad-Dahna. The old woman grew angry and opposed him, and he said then that his case was like that of a sheep that carried its own destruction, since he had brought the woman along without knowing that she would turn out to be an opponent, and he sought refuge with Allah and with His Messenger from becoming like the emissary of Ad.

The Prophet ﷺ asked him about the emissary of Ad, though he knew the story better than the man did, since he liked to hear it again. So he told it. A famine once came on Ad, and they sent a man to get them relief. His name was Qayl. For a whole month his host was Mu'awiyah bin Bakr, who supplied him with drinks while two female singers sang to him. When the month was over, Qayl went to the mountains of Muhrah and prayed that Allah knew he had not come to cure a sick person or to ransom a prisoner, and he asked Him to give Ad water as He used to. Black clouds came, and he was told to choose which of them he wished to be sent to Ad, and he pointed at one of them. He heard a voice proclaiming from it that it should be taken as ashes that would leave none of Ad alive. It was conveyed that the wind sent to them was no more than would pass through a ring, and it destroyed them all the same.

Abu Wa'il said that this was true, and that when a man or a woman sent an emissary, they would tell him not to be like the emissary of Ad, who brought disaster and utter destruction on them instead of relief. Imam Ahmad collected that story in his Musnad, and At-Tirmidhi recorded it in similar wording, as did An-Nasa'i and Ibn Majah.

### In short

- The people refused the call on the ground that it asked them to abandon what their forefathers had worshipped.
- They answered the warning with a challenge, demanding that the punishment be brought down on them if the messenger was telling the truth.
- The same challenge was put to the Prophet ﷺ by the people of Quraysh, and the Book records it.
- The report of the man who came to Al-Madinah and told the story of the emissary of Ad preserves how that challenge ended for the people of Ad.
- The emissary chosen by Ad asked for rain and was given the cloud that destroyed them, which is why his name became a proverb for bringing ruin on those who send you.

71.text:
The answer comes at once, and it is not the answer they were expecting. "He said, “You will certainly be subjected to your Lord’s torment and wrath. Do you dispute with me regarding the so-called gods which you and your forefathers have made up—a practice Allah has never authorized? Then wait! I too am waiting with you.”"

### Phrase by phrase

**"You will certainly be subjected to your Lord’s torment and wrath"** tells them that the thing they were daring him to bring had already been decreed. The torment and the wrath had fallen on them in the sense that they were settled and on their way, and it may come sooner than they expect.

**"Do you dispute with me regarding the so-called gods"** turns to the ground of the quarrel. What they were contending about were names. The people of Hud, as Muhammad bin Ishaq reports, used to worship a number of idols, among them Suda and Samud and Al-Haba, and it was these that he was answering when he spoke of the terror and the wrath. Ibn Abbas said that the terror meant scorn and anger.

**"which you and your forefathers have made up"** shows how much weight the argument from the forefathers carries. The names were given by them, and the thing they were worshipping had no more behind it than the naming. A man is able to picture qualities through names. When a good word is fastened to a person he appears good, and when a bad word is fastened to him he appears bad, and the beings other than God that people come to fix their attention on come to be what they are through these names. Certain people come to be called by titles of that sort, and in time the titles stick so firmly to the persons that people begin to believe the man who is called the hearer of plaints really does hear plaints, and that the one called the solver of difficulties really does solve them. The truth is that names of that kind are invented by human beings, and that there is no one behind them who carries those names, and no argument from religion or from reason in their favour.

That is the plain form of the habit among ordinary people. There is a more polished form of it among educated people, in which unusual words are attached to particular people as well, and in time those words become a fixed part of the names, and people begin to take the persons to be as extraordinary as the titles conferred on them say. Whatever has acquired, through long standing custom, the holiness that attaches to the past takes on a great weight and loftiness in the eyes of people. Set beside it, the call of the preacher of today looks a small thing, so they pay him no attention and take him for an unimportant man. They are confident that nothing will harm them, since they count themselves the heirs of the glory of their forefathers. Recklessness where God is concerned makes a person insensitive by degrees, until the language of admonition and of remembrance can no longer reform him. Only when the verdict of divine retribution is pronounced does he become aware of his own shortcomings.

**"a practice Allah has never authorized?"** is the second part of the charge. No scripture and no proof has come down from Allah for the worship of these names. The Book makes the same point in another place, where the people of Hud are said to have been arrogant in the land without any right and to have asked who was mightier than them, when the One who gave them their being was mightier than they were, and they used to deny the signs (41:15).

**"Then wait! I too am waiting with you"** closes the verse. They had asked him to bring the punishment, and he tells them to wait for it, and says that he will wait with them. So the whole matter was one of waiting.

### How the answer was put

The provoking reply of the people drew a suitable answer from the prophet, and that answer carried the news that the punishment they were looking for was on its way. But he was a prophet, and his fatherly care and his wish to do them good forced him to say, in the course of the same reply, that he was sorry his people had taken senseless things as objects of worship, with no proof from reason and no proof from revelation behind the position they had taken. By that point they had become so fixed in their devotion to what was false that they had begun to quarrel with a prophet of Allah over it.

The Book describes the same end in another place, where it says of them that they were arrogant in the land without right (41:15). And in Surah Al-Mu'minun, in the passage that follows the story of Nuh, the same generation is said to have been taken by the harsh sound (23:41), which shows that the wind and the sound were both part of what came down on them.

### In short

- The prophet tells them that the torment and wrath they were daring him to bring were already decreed and on their way.
- The quarrel was over names that they and their forefathers had invented, and the worship built on them had no warrant from Allah.
- Names acquire weight over long custom until people believe that the titles they give each other carry real powers, and the whole of it is human invention.
- Recklessness about God hardens a person by degrees, until admonition and remembrance no longer reach him.
- He does not match their temper. He tells them to wait, and says that he will wait with them, and his regret at their state comes through even in the answer to their challenge.

72.text:
The story closes with the deliverance and the end of the deniers. "So We saved him and those with him by Our mercy and uprooted those who denied Our signs. They were not believers".

### Phrase by phrase

**"So We saved him and those with him by Our mercy"** is the deliverance, and it is named as mercy rather than as anything earned. Hud and those who had believed with him were kept safe from the punishment, and it was by a mercy from Allah that they were kept.

**"and uprooted those who denied Our signs"** is the judgement on the others. What is meant by the cutting off is that those present at that time were totally destroyed, and some have said that it also means that the line of the people of Ad was cut off for the future as well, so that no root of them remained to grow.

### How the destruction came

The Book returns to the end of this people in several places, and each time it says that Allah sent a barren wind that destroyed everything it passed over. One passage gives the manner of it. As for Ad, a furious violent wind destroyed them. Seven nights and eight days together were laid on them without a break, until men could be seen lying overthrown as though they were the hollow trunks of date palms, and the question is put whether any remnant of them can be seen (69:6-8). When Ad rebelled and went past the limit, the strong wind carried them up into the air one by one and brought each of them down on his head, smashing the skull and severing it from the body, and that is why the Book likens them to hollow trunks of date palms (69:7).

It was the same people whose prophet had spoken to them about the way they lived. On every high place they were putting up palaces where nobody lived. They took fine buildings for themselves as though they were going to remain in them for ever. And when they seized someone, they seized him as tyrants do. What he asked of them was that they should have taqwa of Allah and obey him (26:128-131). Part of that address is given in full elsewhere. There he calls Allah to witness, and calls them to witness with Him, that he is free of everything they join to Him. He tells them to plot against him if they can, and to give him no respite. He has put his trust in Allah, his Lord and their Lord. There is no creature that moves but He holds it by its forelock, and his Lord is on a straight path (11:53-56).

The Book also records the answer they gave him in that same place. They had seen no evidence from him, they said, and they would not leave their gods on the strength of his word alone, and they did not believe him. All they could say was that one of their gods had seized him with an evil, which is to say with madness. That was the state of a people whose prophet had offered them the plainest of all arguments, and who answered him by saying that their stones had struck him mad.

**"They were not believers"** states the ground of it plainly. Those who were destroyed were disbelievers, and they were not of those who would have believed. Some of them had followed Hud, but they were few and they had to conceal their faith. The struggle of Hud against the stubbornness of the people of Ad came to this end. He was kept safe from the punishment, and so were those who had believed in him, and the root of those who had called him a liar was cut off.

### What the story leaves behind

The account leaves a trail of good counsel behind it. For heedless human beings it is a reminder to keep remembering Allah and to take up a way of life marked by obedience to Him. For those who choose to reject honest advice and refuse to learn from what they see, it shows what they may expect at the end. And for the preachers and the reformers who come after, it holds up a mirror, in which the prophetic way of carrying the message and of setting things right can be seen.

### In short

- Hud and those with him were saved by the mercy of Allah and not by anything of their own.
- Those who called the signs of God false were rooted out, and one reading of the words is that their line was cut off for the future as well.
- The reason is given plainly, that they were not believers.
- The story leaves three things behind, a reminder to the heedless, a warning to those who reject advice, and a model of the prophetic way of carrying the message.

73.text:
A third community is brought on, and with it the first sign that comes as a proof. "And to the people of Thamûd We sent their brother Ṣâliḥ." He is sent to them with the call of the messengers before him. "He said, “O my people! Worship Allah—you have no other god except Him." Then the proof is put in front of them. "A clear proof has come to you from your Lord: this is Allah’s she-camel as a sign to you." And the proof comes with a command. "So leave her to graze ˹freely˺ on Allah’s land and do not harm her, or else you will be overcome by a painful punishment." The verse carries the call, the proof and the warning in one breath.

### Phrase by phrase

**"And to the people of Thamûd We sent their brother Ṣâliḥ"** follows the pattern of the two stories before it, and the Prophet Salih who is named here is the third of the messengers whose story the surah tells. In the account of the people of Ad it was said that Ad and Thamud are the names of two persons descended from the same grandfather. The children of those two took the names of their forebears, and so the two groups became two separate peoples. One group was known as the people of Ad, and the other group was known as the people of Thamud.

Salih, in his lineage and in his country, was one of the people of Thamud, since he too came of the progeny of Sam. That is why the Book calls him their brother. In the books of tafsir and of genealogy the tribe is traced to Thamud bin Athir bin Iram bin Sam bin Nuh, and he was the brother of Jadis son of Athir, and of the tribe of Tasm as well. They belonged to the ancient Arabs, who were called Al-'Aribah, and their time came after that of Ad, before Ibrahim.

Their country lay in the north-western part of Arabia, between the Hijaz and Ash-Sham. Their chief city was called Hijr, which is known now as Mada'in Salih. Like the people of Ad they were wealthy, powerful, brave and inclined to art. They were skilled in sculpture and in building. They made palaces in the open plains, and they were known for cutting living spaces and structures into the mountains and inside them. In his survey of the Qur'an's geography, Maulana Sayyid Sulaiman Nadvi noted that their architectural remains still stand, and that Iramic and Thamudic inscriptions are carved on them.

The Messenger of Allah ﷺ passed by their ruins on the way to Tabuk in the ninth year of the hijrah. The report of that journey is given in full below, and it carries the lesson of the place, and the basis of that report is given in the Two Sahihs.

**"O my people! Worship Allah—you have no other god except Him"** is the call, and it is the call that every messenger from Adam to the last of them has given. What Salih asked of his people was that they should profess the divine oneness and turn from every other object of worship. The Book says it plainly, that among every ummah a messenger was raised to tell its people to worship Allah and to keep away from every false deity (16:36), and the same is put in another place (21:25). What Salih asked of his people is what the prophets before him asked of theirs, and the reason for it is that the community of human beings is one community in its basic articles of faith.

**"A clear proof has come to you from your Lord"** introduces the sign. It came about in a particular way, and the account of it belongs with the call, because the call was resisted and the demand was made.

**"this is Allah’s she-camel as a sign to you"** names the proof. The detail of this animal appears elsewhere in the Book, and its background is given in the reports. It was a great creature with a strikingly beautiful appearance, and it used to pass through their valleys by one pass and come out by another, since it needed to move easily, and it drank a lot of water. Salih began to preach when he was a young man, and he kept at his duty until the marks of age began to show on him, and still he did not give it up. His people grew impatient with his repeated efforts to bring them to belief in one God, and they decided to put a demand to him that he could not possibly meet, so that they would come out of the confrontation as the winners. What they asked for was that a she-camel should come out of Katibah, the hill of theirs, in its tenth month of pregnancy, strong and healthy.

The first thing Salih did was to take a pledge from them. He asked whether, if the demand were met, they would all believe in him and in his call, and they all entered into a compact with him on it. Then he prayed two cycles of salah and made his supplication, that nothing was difficult for Allah, and that their demand should be granted. Soon after the supplication there was a rumbling in the hill, a great rock burst open, and out of it came the she-camel as they had described her.

Some of the people believed at once when they saw this. As for the rest, they too made up their minds to enter the faith they had been refusing until then, but some of their chiefs, who were the real patrons of the worship of idols, talked them out of it.

In the text the animal is called the she-camel of Allah. That is because it stood as a proof of the perfect power of Allah and had come about in an extraordinary way as a sign of the prophet's truthfulness. The words about leaving it to graze on the earth of Allah carry the point that it was to be left free to eat and drink because what it would take was not the property of the people. The earth belonged to Allah, and He was the one who brought out what grew on it. So the animal was to be left to feed, unhindered, on the natural grazing of His earth, and was not to be harmed in any way, whether by hamstringing it or by striking it.

**"So leave her to graze ˹freely˺ on Allah’s land and do not harm her"** is the command that goes with the sign. When Salih saw that his people had broken the pledge, he was anxious for them, since the danger was that punishment would come on them for it. He advised them, out of care for them, not to touch the animal and to keep it safe, since in that case they might stay out of the reach of punishment, and otherwise they might be seized at once.

**"or else you will be overcome by a painful punishment"** is the warning that closes the verse, and the warning was not idle.

### The water and the turn

The well from which the people drew their water was the same one the she-camel came to. She was an extraordinary creature, and when she drank her share she took the whole of the water in it. So it was settled, as the divine will had it, that the animal would have the water on one day and the people of Thamud would have it on the next.

What happened on the day she drank was reported as part of the same arrangement. On that day the people were given milk from her instead of water, in such quantity that they filled their water containers with it.

The two turns are given in the Book in more than one place. In one passage the prophet is addressed and told that the water is to be divided between them, one day for her and one day for his people, and that the division will be watched, so that nobody goes against it (54:28). In another place the same camel is described as belonging to Allah, with one day of water fixed as her right and the other day fixed for the people (26:155).

### The journey that passed by their ruins

The report of the Tabuk journey is carried by Al-Bukhari, and by Ahmad in his collection. Abdullah bin Umar said that when the Messenger of Allah ﷺ travelled to the area of Al-Hijr in Tabuk with his people, he camped near the homes of Thamud, at Al-Hijr. The people brought water from the wells that Thamud had used before them, and they used that water to make their dough and set their pots on the fire to cook.

The Prophet ﷺ gave orders that the pots should be emptied and the dough given to the camels. Then he moved on with them from that place to another, near the well that the camel used to drink from, and he forbade the Companions from going into the area where the people had been tormented, and said that he feared what had befallen them might befall them too, so they should not go in upon them.

The same instruction is given in another report of the same journey. He told them that nobody should enter the land of the punished settlement, and that nobody should use the water of its wells.

### Where the story stands in the surah

The account of the people of Nuh and of Hud has gone before, and the same pattern runs on from here to the end of the surah. Prophets are sent to communities, they give the call of truth, the communities deny them, and a terrible end follows. The main subject of the remaining part of the surah is that sequence.

A general observation belongs to the story. Worldly wealth and high living tend to estrange people from the remembrance of their Creator and from the meeting with Him in the Hereafter, and to push them towards the ways of error, and that is what happened among the people of Thamud. The punishment of the flood that came on the people of Nuh had not been forgotten by the world of that time, and the destruction of their neighbours the people of Ad was current history for them. Wealth and power, however, pull people by a force of their own. When one wealthy structure comes down on its foundation, along come other people, or another group, who raise a higher structure on that same foundation, paying no attention at all to what happened there before. Their own families had come into the mansions and the lands of Ad once Ad was destroyed, and it was on the very spots where their kin had met destruction that they raised their own places of luxury. Not content with that, they went into the same deeds that the people of Ad had done. They too became careless of their Creator and unmindful of the Hereafter, and stooped to the worship of idols and to joining others to the divinity of Allah. So Allah, in the way He always deals with such people, sent Salih as His messenger to guide them back to the straight path.

A further observation comes from the shape of their story. After the destruction of the community of Ad, certain righteous people whom God had saved settled in the district of Hajr, in the north-west of Arabia. Their number grew, and they made great progress in farming and in building. They put up palaces on the plains and cut stone houses out of the hills. In time they fell into the evils that commonly follow on a community's material development and worldly comfort, which are debauchery, forgetfulness of the Hereafter, heedlessness about the limits God has laid down, self-conceit, and disregard for the greatness of God. At that point God raised up Salih to warn them of His chastisement, and they would not accept the warning and would not mend their ways.

In a universe where everything else lives in complete obedience to God, they chose to live in arrogance and to disobey Him. Where everything kept strictly to the limits set for it, man wanted to live by going past them. Their transgression created disorder in a world that had been set right, and so they were held unfit to live in it. Yet the trial given to them was not what they feared. God assigned them a she-camel and commanded them not to harm her, on pain of destruction. He could have assigned them a terrifying lion for the purpose, and He assigned a she-camel instead. The reason is that the test of a person's fear of God is taken at the level of the she-camel, and not at the level of the lion. In every society there are people who are like the camel of God. They are the weak, who have no material strength that could hold oppression in check. Through such people God tests the faith of a community, and the certificates of Paradise and of Hell are issued on the basis of how that test turns out.

### In short

- Salih was sent to Thamud as one of their own, and the call he gave is the call every messenger has given.
- The tribe was descended from Thamud bin Athir, among the ancient Arabs, and their land lay between the Hijaz and Ash-Sham, with Hijr as their chief city and their ruins still standing when the Book was sent down.
- The she-camel was the proof, and the one command attached to it was that it should be left to graze and not be harmed. The Book answers that deed twice over, saying that they called the sign a lie and killed it, and so their Lord destroyed them for their sin and levelled them (91:14), and that the she-camel was given to Thamud as a clear sign, and they did her wrong (17:59).
- The whole people was held responsible for the deed of the one who did it, since none of them condemned it and the whole tribe agreed to it.
- The water of the well was divided between the camel and the people by turns, and the division is recorded in the Book.
- The Prophet ﷺ passed by their ruins on the way to Tabuk, and forbade his Companions to enter the dwellings of the punished or to use the water of their wells.

74.text:
The reminder turns to the blessings they have been living on. "Remember when He made you successors after ’Âd and established you in the land—˹and˺ you built palaces on its plains and carved homes into mountains. So remember Allah’s favours, and do not go about spreading corruption in the land.”"

### Phrase by phrase

**"Remember when He made you successors after ’Âd"** is the first blessing named. The word for successors is the plural of the word for a deputy, and what is meant is that after the people of Ad were destroyed, Allah brought Thamud in to settle in their place and gave their lands and their homes to them as the new owners.

**"and established you in the land"** is the second. They were lodged in the country, and they could enjoy it and satisfy their needs from it.

**"you built palaces on its plains"** is the third. The word for palaces is the plural of the word for a large building. In one reading the palaces are taken as the summer dwellings, built on open ground from its mud.

**"and carved homes into mountains"** is the fourth. The word for carving is the one used of sculpture and of cutting stone, and the reading given for it is that they cut the mountains into dwellings for the winter.

**"So remember Allah’s favours"** draws the conclusion from all of it. The blessings of Allah in this world are directed to disbelievers as much as to anyone else, as they were given to the people of Ad and of Thamud in great wealth and power, and a people who have received them are asked to acknowledge them.

**"and do not go about spreading corruption in the land"** is the command that comes with the reminder. They were not to commit transgressions on the earth, and not to call others to anything besides Allah.

### What the verse teaches

Four matters come out of the command. The first is that all the prophets are at one on the articles of faith, and that their revealed codes stand together on the same ground. Every one of them calls people to the pure oneness of God as the basis of worshipping Him, and every one of them warns against the contravention of that oneness, which brings punishment in this world and in the next.

The second is that the pattern of past communities has been that the wealthy and the traditional holders of social standing have been the ones who said no to the call of the prophets, and that in consequence they were disgraced and destroyed here and made deserving of punishment in the life to come.

The third, in the reading that al-Qurtubi gives, is that the blessings of Allah in this world are shared by disbelievers as well, as they were shared by the people of Ad and of Thamud, who were given great wealth and power.

The fourth, again from al-Qurtubi, is that palaces and mansions are among the blessings of Allah, and that building them is allowed. It is a different matter that the noble prophets and the men of God have not favoured them, since they make people careless, and the sayings of the Prophet ﷺ about high rising buildings are of this kind.

### In short

- The verse reminds them of four blessings, that they were made successors to Ad, that they were settled in the land, that they built palaces in its plains, and that they cut homes out of its mountains.
- Blessings of this world are not a mark of divine approval, since they are given to disbelievers as well.
- Palaces and fine dwellings are among the permitted blessings of God, even though the men of God have held back from them because of the carelessness they breed.
- All the prophets agree on the oneness of God, and all of them warn against going past that oneness.
- The community that receives the blessings is asked to remember them and to keep away from spreading corruption.

75.text:
The people split into two parties, and the exchange between them is recorded. "The arrogant chiefs of his people asked the lowly who believed among them, “Are you certain that Ṣâliḥ has been sent by his Lord?” They replied, “We certainly believe in what he has been sent with.”"

### Phrase by phrase

**"The arrogant chiefs of his people asked the lowly who believed among them"** brings out the two parties. One of them had come to believe that Salih was a prophet, and the other was made up of the deniers. The arrogant put their question to those they counted weak, which is to say to those among the people who had believed.

Imam Razi drew attention to the way the two groups are described in the sentence. The trait of the disbelievers is given in the active voice, that they were arrogant, while the state of the believers is given in the passive, that they were the weakened ones. The arrogance of the first group was what they chose to do of their own accord, and it was a blameworthy thing, and in the end it was the cause of their punishment. As for the state ascribed to the believers, it was the description the others fastened on them. It had nothing to do with their actual condition, and there was nothing in it that could be held against them. What is blameworthy is the attitude of the people who called them weak and low, and took them for such, with no reason for it.

**"Are you certain that Ṣâliḥ has been sent by his Lord?"** is the question. The word they stopped to ask about is whether he really is what he is. Another reading of the verse puts the question in terms of knowledge, asking whether the believers really knew that Salih had been sent from his Lord.

**"We certainly believe in what he has been sent with"** is the answer. The believers do not enter into the question of his person at all. They state their faith in what he brought, and they act in agreement with it.

The wonder of that answer is worth noting, since it gives the difference between the two parties in a single line. All the debate of the arrogant, about whether he is a messenger or not, is not worth debating, because the matter is settled and certain, and what he says is a message brought from Allah. If there is anything worth talking about, it is who believes in him and who does not. On that question the believers have their answer ready, that they believe in every word of guidance he brought.

### What the two replies show

The contrast between the two parties tells the reader where the difference lies. Those who deny the truth look at the person of the prophet, and since no outward glory surrounds him and he holds no important seat of the time, they pass him by and discount him. The believers look at the message, and when they catch sight of the truth in what he says, they accept it at once and become his companions.

That is the reason a prophet is a controversial figure in his own time rather than an established one. He comes without worldly trappings, he is not the occupant of any of the leading positions of the day, and it is hard for his contemporaries to believe that the one they know as an ordinary man is the one God has chosen to carry His message. Truth makes itself known through proofs and not through worldly glory. Those who are able to see it in the form of a proof find it at once, while those who are always overawed by outward splendour stay in doubt and never receive the guidance that would make them supporters of the truth.

### In short

- The community divided into those who were proud and those they counted weak, and the proud party put the question.
- The wording of the verse marks the arrogance as their own choice, while the weakness was a label they pinned on others.
- The believers answered by speaking of the message rather than the man, and they said plainly that they believed in what he had been sent with.
- Those who reject a prophet look at his person and find nothing impressive, while those who accept look at the message and see the truth in it.
- Truth is recognised through proofs, and not through the standing a person holds in the world.

76.text:
The answer of the other party is short and cold. "The arrogant said, “We surely reject what you believe in.”"

### Phrase by phrase

**"The arrogant said"** keeps the same description of them as before, that the pride was theirs and of their own choosing.

**"We surely reject what you believe in"** is their whole reply. They had heard an answer of the plainest kind, and it left them where they were. In another reading the words are put as a rejection of that which the believers had faith in, with the added sense that they would neither enter it nor act in agreement with its laws.

The exchange ended there. The eloquence of the believers did not soften the people of Thamud, and the arrogant came back with a cold refusal. The lust of worldly life is merciless, and so is the intoxicating elation that comes with wealth and power. Both of them become invisible curtains before a human being's eyes, so that eyes which are open no longer see what is plain in front of them.

### In short

- The proud party answered with a flat rejection, and they kept the pride that the verse had already named as their own doing.
- The answer of the believers, clear as it was, made no difference to them.
- Love of the world and pride in wealth and power work like a curtain over the sight, hiding what is plainly in front of a person.

77.text:
The matter comes to the point of the deed itself. "Then they killed the she-camel—defying their Lord’s command—and challenged ˹Ṣâliḥ˺, “Bring us what you threaten us with, if you are ˹truly˺ one of the messengers.”"

### Phrase by phrase

**"Then they killed the she-camel"** records the act that settled their fate. The Book attributes it to the whole tribe, and that carries a lesson of its own, which is set out below.

**"defying their Lord’s command"** gives the character of the deed. What they refused was the command of their Lord that Salih had laid on them, and the act was done insolently.

**"and challenged Ṣâliḥ"** begins the taunt. They mocked him over what he had promised, and asked how the punishment would come and from where, and what the signs of its coming would be.

**"Bring us what you threaten us with, if you are ˹truly˺ one of the messengers"** is the challenge in full. They dared him to produce the punishment, and they said it as a jest, since they doubted what he had told them.

### How the animal was killed

The account of the killing is given in the reports. Two beautiful women of Thamud set a prize. Each of them swore to give herself, or one of the girls of her house, to whoever would kill the she-camel. Both of them were of noble family, and one of them, Umm Ghanm Unayzah the daughter of Ghanm bin Mijlaz, had the deepest hatred of Salih among the whole people. She had wealth and beauty in her house, and her husband was Dhu'ab bin Amr, a leading man of Thamud. The other was the noblewoman Saduf bint Al-Muhayya bin Dahr bin Al-Muhayya, married to a Muslim man of Thamud whom she had left.

Saduf summoned Al-Habbab, a man of the tribe. She put the offer to him that she would give herself if the deed were done, and he refused it. So she turned to a cousin of hers, Musaddi' bin Mihraj bin Al-Muhayya, and he agreed to it. As for Unayzah bint Ghanm, she sent for Qudar bin Salif bin Jundu, a short man with red-blue skin, whom they counted a bastard, since he was not the son of the man whose name he carried but of a man called Suhyad, though he had been born in Salif's house. Unayzah said to him that she would give him whichever of her daughters he wished if he killed the camel. Qudar bin Salif and Musaddi' bin Mihraj got together and gathered a number of troublemakers from Thamud for the purpose. Seven more joined them, and the group came to nine, which is the number the Book gives when it says that there were nine men in the city who made mischief in the land and would not set it right (27:48).

Those nine men were chiefs of their people, and they drew the whole tribe into agreeing to the killing. The two of them waited for the camel to leave the well, with Qudar beside one rock on her path and Musaddi' beside another. When she passed Musaddi', he shot an arrow at her that went through her leg. Unayzah came out then and told one of her daughters, who was among the most beautiful of the women, to uncover her face for Qudar, and that gave him the encouragement to swing his sword and bring it down on the animal's knee. She went down on the ground, and one scream came from her to warn her young. Qudar stabbed her in the neck and cut her throat.

Her young one climbed a high rock and screamed. Abdur-Razzaq recorded from Ma'mar that a report reached Al-Hasan Al-Basari that the young one said, "O my Lord, where is my mother?" It was also said that the young one screamed three times and went into a rock and vanished in it, or that they followed it and killed it along with its mother. Allah knows best.

The Book calls the man who did the deed the most wretched of the people (91:12), since it was his act that brought mass punishment down on them all.

### What is drawn from the killing of one animal

The killer of the she-camel was one arrogant member of the community, and the action is nevertheless attributed to the whole community, and it was said that they hamstrung her. That shows that when one person among a group does a bad deed and the others do not condemn it, all of them are counted as parties to the crime. It is the same with the people of a community who are given over to their desires, since they are not moved by plain speech and will not stand behind anyone who calls them to serious and sincere action.

The Book makes the same point when it states that the whole tribe shared in agreeing to the crime. Qatadah said that he was told that the man who had been marked out to do the killing went round to all of them, to the women in their rooms and to the children, and found that every one of them consented to it.

The Book also records the reason the camel had become so hated. She took the water of the well, and the people wanted it for themselves every day. They did not dare to kill her, for fear of what divine punishment would follow, and so they laid a plot instead. It is also worth noting what the Book says of the nine men who made the plan, that they plotted a plot while a plan was being made for them and they did not perceive it (27:49-50).

### The three days of respite

When the animal had been finished off and the news reached Salih, he came to them where they were gathered. When he saw the camel, he wept and proclaimed that they had three days to enjoy themselves in their homes, and that the promise was not going to prove false (11:65).

The nine who had killed the animal did the killing on a Wednesday, and that same night they conspired to kill Salih. Their reasoning was that if he was telling the truth, they should finish him off before they themselves were finished, and if he was lying, they would make him follow his camel. The Book gives their oath and their plot, and how a plan was made against their plan while they were unaware (27:49-50).

They came to his house for the purpose, and the might of Allah that guards His messengers brought a hail of stones down on them, which smashed their heads before the rest of the tribe. That is the plan that was made and the plan they did not perceive.

Then came the signs Salih had told them about. On the Thursday, the first of the three days, the people woke and found their faces a deep yellow. On the Friday, the second day, the faces had turned dark red. On the Saturday, the third day, they woke with their faces black. Men and women, old and young, nobody was exempted. On the Sunday they put on the fragrance used for the dead and waited for the torment and the revenge of Allah, not knowing what would be done to them, or how, or from where it would come. When Salih saw his people breaking the pledge he had been anxious for them, and the danger he had feared was what came to pass.

In this condition, with no way left to them, a severe earthquake struck them from below the earth while a terrible sound tore down from above. The cry and the quaking of the earth killed them all at once, and they fell headlong like a bird coming down on its breast.

Instead of repenting and asking forgiveness when they heard the signs described to them, those people decided that their better course was to kill Salih himself. Their reasoning was that if he was truthful and the punishment was coming, then they should finish him before the punishment finished them, and if he was a liar, let him have the punishment that belongs to lying. That intention is given in detail elsewhere in the Book. A group of them set off for his house with the purpose of killing him, and while they were on the way they were killed by the hailstones, as the Book says of them, that they planned a plan and a plan was made, and they did not perceive it (27:50).

### In short

- The killing of the she-camel is the deed that settled the fate of the community, and it was done in defiance of the command they had been given.
- Two noblewomen set a prize for the killing, and the men they recruited were joined by others until the group came to nine, the number the Book gives for the mischief makers in the city.
- Qudar struck the animal down and cut her throat, and the Book calls him the most wretched of the people, since it was his act that brought the punishment on them all.
- The verdict of the Book is that the whole tribe shared in agreeing to the crime, and the confirmed reports say the same.
- They were given three days of respite, and the signs Salih told them about came one after another, until the faces of the people turned yellow, then red, then black.
- They conspired to kill their prophet instead of repenting, and the plot they made was answered by a plan they never saw.

78.text:
The punishment arrives, and it arrives from both sides at once. "Then an ˹overwhelming˺ earthquake struck them, and they fell lifeless in their homes".

### Phrase by phrase

**"Then an ˹overwhelming˺ earthquake struck them"** is the judgement from below. The word is the word for the shaking of the earth. In another reading the sound that announced their torment is joined to it as As-Saihah. The two came together, the noise from the sky and the severe tremor from the ground. The Book gives that sound in another place, where the cry takes them and morning finds them prostrate in their dwellings (15:83), and the word for the cry carries the sense of a shrill sound or a severe one.

**"and they fell lifeless in their homes"** is the state they were left in, and the same word is used of them in the other verse that speaks of the cry (15:83). The word used for it is a form that means being brought to a standstill, senseless and motionless, at a single spot, as Al-Qamus gives it, and the sense is that every one of them lay dead exactly where he was. The Book uses the same word of them in another place, where the cry takes them and morning finds them prostrate in their dwellings (15:83).

### How the two punishments came together

The verses of the Book brought together show that two kinds of punishment converged on the people of Thamud at the same moment. The earthquake came from below and the sound came from above, and the souls were taken and the bodies left without life in a single hour. None of them escaped it, whether young or old, man or woman.

The end of the story is given in the witnesses that were preserved. Those who studied the story said that none of the offspring of Thamud remained except Salih and those who had believed with him.

One man escaped the first stroke. He was a disbeliever called Abu Righal, and he was inside the sacred area, the Haram of Makkah, at the time, and the torment that came on his people did not touch him. When one day he left the Haram, a stone fell from the sky and killed him. Abdur-Razzaq narrated from Ma'mar, who had it from Isma'il bin Umayyah, that the Prophet ﷺ passed by the grave of Abu Righal and asked the Companions whether they knew whose grave it was. They said that Allah and His Messenger knew better. He told them that it was the grave of Abu Righal, a man of Thamud, who had been inside the sacred area of Allah and had been saved from His torment by that, and that when he left the sacred area what had befallen his people befell him as well, and that he had been buried here with a branch of gold. The people went at the grave with their swords, looking for the golden branch, and found it. Another report from Abdur-Razzaq, through Ma'mar from Az-Zuhri, says that Abu Righal is the ancestor of the tribe of Thaqif.

The reports of the Prophet ﷺ speaking in this way about a man long dead belong with the other report on the same subject, which is given in the entry for the next verse.

The account is also carried in a report of the journey to Tabuk, in the collection of Al-Bukhari, that the Prophet ﷺ and his Companions passed by Hijr, the place where the people of Thamud had met their punishment. There he gave the instruction that nobody should enter the land of the punished settlement, and that nobody should use the water of its wells. The reports of the same journey have been given already in this passage.

### What the place was left for

Allah in His wisdom allowed the settlements of the punished peoples to remain as signposts of warning for the generations that came after. The Book warns the people of Arabia again and again that the places which lay on their travel route to Syria should teach them the essential lesson of the rise and fall of peoples, and it says of those dwellings of the ungrateful that they were not lived in after their people, except a little (28:58).

### In short

- The earthquake seized them, and the Book describes them as left motionless on the spot where each of them stood.
- The earthquake and the cry came at the same hour, one from below and one from above.
- None of the people of Thamud remained except the prophet and those who had believed with him.
- Abu Righal was spared because he was inside the sacred area of Makkah, and was killed by a stone from the sky once he left it, and his grave and the golden branch buried with it are given in the reports.
- The Prophet ﷺ passed by Hijr on the way to Tabuk and forbade his Companions to enter the punished dwellings or to use their water.
- The settlements were left standing as signposts, so that later peoples would read the lesson of the rise and fall of nations on their own travel routes.

79.text:
The story closes with the prophet speaking over the people who are past hearing. "So he turned away from them, saying, “O my people! Surely I conveyed to you my Lord’s message and gave you ˹sincere˺ advice, but you do not like ˹sincere˺ advisors.”"

### Phrase by phrase

**"So he turned away from them"** gives his leaving. After the punishment had come on his people, Salih and those who had believed with him left the place and went elsewhere. According to some narrations there were four thousand believers with him. He went with them to Hadramaut in Yaman, and it was there that he passed from this world. Others report that he went to Makkah, and that it was there he died.

**"O my people! Surely I conveyed to you my Lord’s message"** is the content of what he said as he left. He had delivered the message of his Lord to them, with its commands and its prohibitions explained.

**"and gave you ˹sincere˺ advice"** is the second part. He had warned them of the torment of Allah and called them to repentance and to faith, and he had wished them well.

**"but you do not like ˹sincere˺ advisors"** is the verdict he left with them. They did not listen to those who advised them, and they took no benefit from what he brought, because they did not love the truth and did not follow those who offered them sincere counsel.

These words are put as an admonition and a reproach addressed to a people who had already perished by the time they were spoken, and they heard him, which was a miracle granted to their prophet by Allah.

### The same manner of speech at Badr

What is recorded in the Two Sahihs gives the parallel. After the Messenger of Allah ﷺ had defeated the disbelievers at Badr, he stayed in that area for three days. Then he rode his camel, which had been made ready for him in the latter part of the night, and went on until he stood by the well of Badr, into which the bodies of the disbelievers had been thrown. He called out to Abu Jahl bin Hisham, and to Utbah bin Rabi'ah, and to Shaybah bin Rabi'ah, and asked whether they had found what their Lord had promised them of torment to be true, since he had found what his Lord had promised him of victory to be true.

Umar said to him, "O Messenger of Allah, why do you speak to people who have rotted?" He said, "By the One in whose hand my soul is, you do not hear what I am saying any better than they do, but they cannot reply."

So it was with Salih and his people. The words were spoken over them after they had perished, and the point of them is not that the dead should benefit but that the living should take the lesson.

### Why he addressed them when they were gone

A question is put against the outward arrangement of the text, since the people had been destroyed by the punishment and there is no use in addressing them afterwards. The answer is that one good may come out of it, which is that people in general should learn their lesson from it, and that this form of address resembles the address of the Prophet ﷺ when he said a few words over the dead disbelievers of Quraysh at Badr.

It is also possible that the saying of Salih belongs to the time before the punishment came and his people were destroyed, even though it stands later in the order of the text. From the outward arrangement, it appears that he said it as he was departing, telling them that he had delivered the message of his Lord and wished the best for them, but that they did not seem to like honest advisers.

### What the last words of the story show

The community that gives way to its desires is not moved by plain speech at all. It is not prepared to support anyone who calls it to serious and sincere action. On the contrary, great crowds gather around people who say pleasant things and trade in false promises. Such a community is not drawn to the true well-wishers, and it rushes instead towards those who will use it.

### In short

- Salih left his people after they had been destroyed, and he went with the believers to Hadramaut, or according to other reports to Makkah.
- What he said over them was that he had conveyed the message and given sincere counsel, and that they did not like sincere advisers.
- The same manner of speech was used by the Prophet ﷺ at the well of Badr, and Umar asked him why he spoke to those who had rotted.
- The address was not meant for the dead to benefit from it, but for the living to take the warning.
- The saying may also have come before the punishment, though it stands last in the order of the text.
- A community that gives itself to its desires turns away from serious counsel and gathers instead around those who flatter it.

80.text:
The fourth story opens, and it opens on a deed that had never been seen in the world. "And ˹remember˺ when Lot scolded ˹the men of˺ his people, ˹saying,˺ “Do you commit a shameful deed that no man has ever done before"". The verse puts the question to the people, and the question is the beginning of the story.

### Phrase by phrase

**"And remember when Lot scolded the men of his people"** names the messenger and the people. His call was the same call to the oneness of Allah that every messenger brought. Lut was the son of Haran, who was the son of Azar, and his uncle was Ibrahim, peace be upon them both. The original homeland of the two of them was known as Babel, near Basrah in western Iraq. The worship of idols was common there, and even the family of Ibrahim was caught up in it.

In the whole family of Ibrahim, only two entered the faith at first, his wife Sarah and his nephew Lut, as the Book says of him, that he believed in him (29:26). It was with those two that Ibrahim left his homeland behind and moved to the land of Sham. After reaching the river Jordan he settled in the land of Canaan near Bayt al-Maqdis, in obedience to a divine command. In his own country his people had opposed him, and the opposition ended in the well known fire of Nimrud, and his father threatened to drive him out of the house.

Then Allah made Lut a prophet as well, and sent him to Sadum, near Bayt al-Maqdis, for the guidance of the people there. The area took in five chief cities, called Sadum, Amurah, Admah, Sububim and Bali or Sawghar, and the Book refers to their centre by several names. Those details are given in the reports of the place, among them Al-Bahr Al-Muhit. Sadum was counted the capital and the centre of the group, and it was there that Lut stayed. The land was fertile and green, with all kinds of grain and fruit growing in it.

**"Do you commit a shameful deed"** names the offence. The people of that district did things that no one among the children of Adam had ever done, and that had not even crossed anyone's mind. What they did was to go after males rather than females, and the practice was not known in the world before these people invented it. Amr bin Dinar said of the words that no male had ever lain with a male before the people of Lut.

The word used here is the word for an indecency, and it is given in the verse with the definite article. Where the Book speaks of adultery it uses the word for a shameful act in the indefinite form, as in the verse that calls it a shameful act (17:32), and here the word is made definite. The hint carried by that is that the unnatural practice of this community was, as it were, the collection of all indecencies together, and a far graver crime than adultery itself.

**"that no man has ever done before"** is the ground on which the offence is condemned here. The manner of a people is usually to fall into a sin because of the conditions they live in, or because they are following their ancestors without thought. That is no legal excuse in the sacred law, yet a person caught in it can in ordinary practice be allowed some measure of excuse. But when it is a sin that nobody has ever committed before, and one that carries no compulsion of its own, it becomes a curse of the highest order. The second ground is that such an act becomes a channel for making others accursed with the one who did it. A person who invents an evil act or an evil custom carries the sin and the punishment of his own deed. Along with him, all those who sink into the same sin through his example are affected, down to the last day, and their curse and their punishment sit on the shoulders of the one who started it. That is what Abd al-Malik, the Umayyad ruler, gave voice to when he said that if this affair of the people of Lut had not been mentioned in the Book, he would never have suspected that a human being could do such a thing.

An ordinary look at the matter gives the same verdict. In the habit of a human being, as the Book puts it, when he finds freedom from need he begins to go past the limits (96:6-7). On these people too the doors of blessing had been opened. Driven on by that pattern of behaviour, drenched in wealth and possessions, they went to the farthest ends of luxury and desire. What they lost first was the sense of honour, of dignity and of modesty, which is among the most essential things a human being has, and with it went the very ability to tell the good from the bad. In the end they got themselves caught up in acts of unnatural indecency. Such acts are abominable apart from being forbidden and sinful, and they stir hatred and distaste in the heart of anyone whose taste is sound and decent, to the point that even animals keep away from such things.

### The three kinds of indecency, in one reading

One strand of teaching reads the question of the verse against the state of the person who hears it. Each person's indecency fits the days and the states he is in. Look at where a man stands on the road he is travelling, and his indecency will take its measure from his own mortal nature at that point. When it comes to the creatures of this world, there are three groups and no more. They are the common people, then the elect, and then the elect of the elect.

For the common people, the indecency is the one the sacred law explains, and its penalty is the whip or the stoning. For the elect, the indecency is to look at the pleasures and the appetites of this world with the eye in the head, to see their enjoyment and their adornment, and to let them into oneself, even where they are permitted and far from anything doubtful. In the case of such people, the harm that comes from the permitted delights of this world is greater than the harm that comes from what is forbidden in the case of ordinary people. The penalty for that indecency, in the words of the master of the sacred law, is the command to lower the eyes and hold back the hands.

For the elect of the elect, the indecency is that they should look at anything other than the Real with the awareness of the heart. The declaration has come from the Real, "Say, God, then leave them" (6:91). The sense of that is that the servant should not look at himself, but see everything as the act of his Lord. He should not put his Lord under an obligation by his own acts, but look at the success that is given to him. He should flee from his own marks and see only the love that comes to him. What has someone seized by that love to do with anything else? The heart is to be kept turned towards Him and the rest let go. The tumult of the world is all this talk of you and me, and if a person gives up the me, the whole world becomes his garden. And the word from God is that it is a wonder how anyone who has faith in Him can depend on anything other than Him. If such people were to look at the subtleties of His kindness, they would not worship anything but Him.

### In short

- Lut was the nephew of Ibrahim and believed in him, and he left his homeland with the two who remained faithful to the call.
- He was sent as a prophet to Sadum and the cities around it, near Bayt al-Maqdis, a fertile district of five towns.
- The offence of his people was one that had never been committed before them by any creature, and it was the first appearance of that practice in the world.
- The verse carries the word for the shameful act in its definite form, which suggests that the offence gathers into itself every kind of indecency.
- The verse condemns it on two grounds, that nobody had ever done it before and that such an inventor of evil carries the sin of all who follow him.
- Their wealth and comfort had carried them past the limits, until they lost the sense of shame and the ability to tell good from bad.

81.text:
The offence is named plainly. "You lust after men instead of women! You are certainly transgressors.”"

### Phrase by phrase

**"You lust after men instead of women"** states the deed without dressing it up. What is meant is that they left the women whom Allah had created for them and went to men instead. This behaviour is evil and ignorant, since they had put things in a place that was never meant for them.

What the line hints at is that Allah has appointed marriage with women as the lawful way for the natural satisfaction of human desire. To walk around that way and choose an unnatural one is plain ugliness in the human self and a proof of a dirty mind.

**"You are certainly transgressors"** is the verdict. In one reading the word for wantonness is tied to the practice of idolatry, meaning that they crossed from the lawful into what is forbidden. The real disease of the people was that they went beyond the limits Allah had set in everything, and in their case the limit they jumped over was the very boundary of humanity. The same thing happened with desire, since they went past the bounds appointed by Allah and reached for a taste that runs against nature.

### What the community's scholars drew from it

The Companions, those who followed them, and the leading jurists have declared this crime to be far graver than other shameful acts. Imam Abu Hanifah said that the punishment given to the one who commits it should match the punishment that came upon the people of Lut by the command of Allah, when rocks rained down from the sky and the floor of the earth was turned over. His view was that such a person should be pushed down from a high mountain, and rocks thrown down on him from above.

In a narration of Ibn Abbas that Ahmad, Abu Dawud, At-Tirmidhi and Ibn Majah all carry, the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said of the people who commit this act that both the doer of the deed and the one it is done to are to be killed. The Book lays the same weight on the matter when it speaks of the act among the sins of a later people.

### In short

- The verse names the offence plainly, that they went after men instead of the women who were created for them.
- Marriage with women is the lawful way appointed for natural desire, and taking another way is a defect of the human self.
- The verdict is that they had gone past the limits, since they crossed from what is lawful into what is unlawful.
- The jurists have counted this crime graver than other shameful acts, and the Prophet ﷺ ordered that both parties to the act be put to death.
- The punishment the lawgiver prescribed for it matches the way the punishment came on the people of Lut themselves.

82.text:
The answer of the people is not an argument at all. "But his people’s only response was to say, “Expel them from your land! They are a people who wish to remain chaste!”"

### Phrase by phrase

**"But his people’s only response was to say"** shows how little they had to offer. They could not find a suitable rejoinder to what Lut had said, and they were stubborn all the same.

**"Expel them from your land"** is their decision, and they spoke it among themselves. What they answered him with was the intention of driving him and those who believed with him out of their town, and that is what they set about doing.

**"They are a people who wish to remain chaste"** is the taunt that came with it. They turned the one thing that should have been praised into a charge against them, and they worked themselves up over it. Qatadah said of them that they shamed Lut and the believers with what was not a shame at all.

Mujahid gave the sense more bluntly, and said that the people were saying of Lut and those with him that they wanted to keep themselves pure, and one early authority gave the wording as they said it. A similar report is narrated from Ibn Abbas.

What their answer actually shows is the state of a majority that has power and wealth behind it, since they had the boldness to say such a thing because they were the larger body and held the material advantage, and so they thought themselves safe. The few who had faith in Lut were the only ones on the other side, and the rest were sunk in their course.

### In short
