- The people could answer the prophet's warning with nothing but a plan to drive him out of their town.
- They fastened on the purity of the believers as though it were a fault, which is a charge without substance.
- Their confidence came from their numbers and their material superiority, not from any argument they had.
- Only a few people close to Lut had any faith in him.

83.text:
The deliverance comes before the punishment. "So We saved him and his family except his wife, who was one of the doomed".

### Phrase by phrase

**"So We saved him and his family"** is the rescue. Allah saved Lut and his household, since only his household believed in him, and the Book says in another place that the believers were brought out of that place, and that no household of the Muslims was found there except one (51:35-36).

### Who was saved with him

Who belongs to the family spoken of here is a matter on which the scholars differ. Some say that the two women who had become believers were included in it, while the wife was not. Other verses on the same subject are given as proof, that in those habitations there was no home of the Muslims except one (51:36), and the report of Ibn Abbas on this carries the same point, that the people saved from the punishment were only from the household of Lut, and that his wife was not among them. Others take the word broadly, so that it covers his own family and also those who had joined him by entering the faith.

The command given to him was to take those who were with him and to leave that settlement in the night, with the warning that none of them should look back, since the punishment would come down on those inside once they were out of it.

**"except his wife, who was one of the doomed"** is the exception. She did not believe. She held to the religion of her own people, and she used to conspire against Lut with them, telling them who came to visit him, by signals they had agreed on between themselves. That is why no word about her was given to him when he was ordered out of the town by night with his household, and she was left behind with her people and shared their end.

Two reports are given about her. One is that she simply did not go out with them. The other is that she did set off with them and walked on for a while, and because she was eager to see what became of the people she had left behind, and against the command that had been given, she was seized by the punishment along with them.

The word used for the doomed means those who stayed behind, and it is also taken to mean those who were destroyed, which is the more obvious reading. The case of the wife shows how even-handed the justice of God is in the matter of reward and punishment. His scales give no weight to relationship or to friendship. His judgement was even-handed enough that it spared neither the son of Nuh, nor the father of Ibrahim, nor the wife of Lut, nor the uncle of the Prophet ﷺ. And on the other side, when the wife of Pharaoh did righteous deeds, she was admitted to Paradise.

### In short

- Lut and his household were saved, and the Book records elsewhere that no believing household was found in that place except one.
- The household saved was a counted few, and those who wrote on the verse differ on whether the word covers only his family or also those who joined him in the faith.
- He was told to leave by night and not to look back, since the punishment would fall once they were clear of the town.
- His wife was not among the saved, since she held to the religion of her people and passed on information about his visitors.
- One report says she never left, and another says she turned back to watch and was caught by the punishment.
- Her case shows that the justice of God is even-handed, since ties of family do not shield anyone, while righteous deeds can raise anyone.

84.text:
The punishment is described in a few words, and then the reader is sent to look at its end. "We poured upon them a rain ˹of brimstone˺. See what was the end of the wicked".

### Phrase by phrase

**"We poured upon them a rain"** names the judgement. What came down on them was a rain of stones, and the stones are described in another passage where the Book gives the details, that when the command came the uppermost part of that place was made its nethermost part, and stones of hard clay were rained on it, one after another, marked from the Lord, and that they are not far from the transgressors (11:82-83).

**"See what was the end of the wicked"** turns the account into a lesson. The words are addressed to the Prophet ﷺ, and the sense is that he should see the end of those who dared to disobey Allah and to deny His messengers. One reading of the line put it as a question to the idolaters: see what the outcome was for those who went against the truth.

### How the punishment came

Taken together with the other passages, the punishment has several parts. Rain of stones came from above, and the ground itself was turned over, as the angel raised the crust of that land and cast it back topsy-turvy. The stones that rained down came one over the other, so ceaselessly that they collected one on top of the next. The stones were marked, and some hold that each stone carried the name of the person it was destined for.

The order of the punishment is given in more than one way. In the verses of Surah Al-Hijr, the account mentions that a sound seized them at sunrise (15:73). That shows a harsh sound coming first from the skies, with the other punishments after it. From the outward arrangement of the words it appears that the earth was turned over after the sound, and then the stones were rained down on them to set a stamp on their disgrace. It is possible too that the stones came first and the turning of the earth after them, since the Book is not bound to give events in the order they happened.

Among the punishments sent on the people of Lut, the turning over of the surface of the earth has a particular correspondence with their act of shame. They were guilty of perversion, and the ground under them was turned upside down.

The Book warns the people of Arabia at the end of the passage in Surah Hud where these things are described, telling them that the overturned habitations were not far from the wrongdoers. They pass by those places on their journeys to Syria, and it is a strange thing that they take no lesson from them.

They are not limited to the time when the Book was being revealed. They are still there, between Bayt al-Maqdis and the river Jordan, and the area carries the name Sea of Lut, and the Dead Sea as well. It lies far below the level of the sea, and in one particular stretch the water is unusual, so that no life of the sea survives in it, which is where the name comes from. That place is said to be the Sodom of the story, and the story of its people stands as a warning against the practice that brought it down.

### In short

- The punishment was a rain of stones of hard clay, marked from the Lord and sent one after another.
- The ground was turned over as well, with the highest part of the town made its lowest, and the stones came so thick that they collected one on top of another.
- The verses of Al-Hijr add that a sound seized them at sunrise, and the order in which the parts of the punishment came is given in more than one way.
- The turning over of the earth corresponds to the perversion of the people, who had put things in a place not meant for them.
- The Book tells the people of Arabia that these overturned dwellings are on their travel route and not far from them, and that they should take warning from them.
- The site is still marked, between Bayt al-Maqdis and the Jordan, and the water there is such that no sea life survives in it.

85.text:
The fifth story opens. "And to the people of Midian We sent their brother Shu’aib." He brings them the same call as the messengers before him. "He said, “O my people! Worship Allah—you have no other god except Him." Then the proof is named. "A clear proof has already come to you from your Lord." And with it come the commands about dealings between people. "So give just measure and weight, do not defraud people of their property, nor spread corruption in the land after it has been set in order." And the close of it. "This is for your own good, if you are ˹truly˺ believers". The story is the last of the series in this surah, and it joins the call of the prophets to a matter of plain dealing between people.

### Phrase by phrase

**"And to the people of Midian We sent their brother Shu’aib"** names the messenger and the people. Shu'ayb, as Muhammad bin Ishaq said, is among the progeny of Madyan the son of Ibrahim, and he is also related to Lut. The descendants of Madyan the son of Ibrahim came to be known by the name Madyan as well, and the place where they lived took the same name, so that Madyan is the name of a people and of a city at once. The city still stands near Ma'an, on the way to the Hijaz from Sham. When the Book tells the story of Musa elsewhere and says that he arrived at the water of Madyan (28:23), it is speaking of that same place.

Shu'ayb was known for eloquent speech, and because of it he was called the orator of the prophets.

The people he was sent to are given in the Book both as the people of Madyan and as the people of Al-Aykah, and the word for Al-Aykah means a forest. Some of the authorities hold that these were two separate peoples living in separate settlements, and that Shu'ayb went to one of the two first. Once that people had been destroyed, he went to the other. The punishment that came on the two is described in different words in the Book. The punishment of the people of Madyan is given in some places as the sound and in others as the earthquake, while the punishment of the people of Al-Aykah is given as the shade of a cloud. In that form of it, intense heat struck the people of Al-Aykah first, and it almost roasted them in their own district. Then a dense cloud came over the forest nearby and cast its shade across the whole of it. Drawn by the shade and the cool breeze, all the people of the district came together under that cloud, and there, walking on their own two feet, they arrived at the very spot where they were to be destroyed. Once they were all gathered, fire rained from the cloud and the earthquake shook the earth, and that killed them all.

Others hold that the people of Madyan and the people of Al-Aykah were one and the same people, and that the three kinds of punishment named in the Book converged on them, the fire from the clouds first, then the piercing sound with it, and then the earthquake. That is the view preferred in the reports that carry the story.

Whichever it is, what matters is the message of truth that Shu'ayb brought them, and that is what the verses give. Before turning to it, there is a principle to be seen. The essence of the religion, which is the combined call of all the prophets, is the fulfilling of rights, and rights are of two kinds. There are rights owed directly to Allah, on whose fulfilment or neglect no visible human gain or loss depends, and prayer and fasting are of this kind. There are also the rights of the servants of Allah, which is what human rights mean in ordinary speech, and they have to do with other people. This community was heedless of both kinds, and was working against both.

By refusing belief in Allah, and in the messengers He sent, they were taking away what was owed to Him, and on top of that, by cutting down weights and measures, they were slicing away the rights of human beings. It went further than that with them, since such people would sit at the entrances of roads and streets and frighten everyone passing, rob them of what they carried, and warn them of worse to come if they believed in Shu'ayb. In that way they had made disorder the settled order of God's earth. It was to correct these things that Shu'ayb was sent to them.

**"O my people! Worship Allah—you have no other god except Him"** is the first of the three things he said to them. This is the call to the oneness of Allah that all the prophets have given down the ages, and it is the spirit of all true belief and all true action, and it is the road that the whole line of the messengers walked. These people were sold to the worship of what had been created, and were in consequence heedless of the sacred Being and His attributes, and neglectful of His rights. So this was the first message put to them.

**"A clear proof has already come to you from your Lord"** is the second. The clear proof means the miracles manifested at the hands of Shu'ayb, and the different forms those miracles took are given in Al-Bahr Al-Muhit. The sense is that Allah has set out the proof and the evidence for the truth of what he brought.

**"So give just measure and weight"** is the third, and it lays down a major rule of just conduct. The word kail covers measuring by volume, and the word mizan covers the weights, and the word for making short means to bring loss on someone by giving less than what is due. Rights of this kind, owed to other people, are what the scholars call the rights of the servants, the huquq al-Ibad, as against the rights owed to Allah. So the instruction is to give full measure and full weight, and to hold back from causing loss to people in what belongs to them.

The particular crime of giving short measure and short weight in buying and selling is prohibited in the first part of the verse, and then the prohibition is made general by what follows. What was being done to them in the markets was that merchants would avoid giving full weight and measure, and the Book gives the same warning elsewhere when it speaks of those who give less than is due in measure and weight (83:1), and asks its question about them before the Lord of all that exists (83:6). Those verses carry a stern warning and a sure promise.

**"do not defraud people of their property"** generalizes the command, and now it covers every kind of cutting back on what is due to others, whether the right in question concerns property or honour or anything else. In the same way that it is forbidden to give less than is due in weighing and measuring, it is forbidden to cut back on the rights of other people. Attacking the honour of a person, failing to give him the respect that his station calls for, falling short in the obedience owed to those who must be obeyed, and failing to show respect to those who must be respected, all of these fall under the crime that the people of Shu'ayb used to commit. In his famous khutbah at the farewell pilgrimage, the Prophet ﷺ declared that the honour of people deserves the same respect and defence as their blood, and that stands as a wider confirmation of the view.

These things are covered by the words for giving short measure wherever they occur in the Book. The leader of the community saw a man hurrying through his ruku and his sujud, the bowing and the prostration of the prayer, and said to him that he was guilty of giving short measure. What he meant was that the man had not given the prayer its due. So the shortcoming in an act of worship is described there with the same word that is used of a cheat in the market. That word, and the name given to those who deal in that way, is the one the Book uses when it speaks of the mutaffifin (83:1).

**"nor spread corruption in the land after it has been set in order"** carries the same command that appeared earlier in the surah, and the meaning is the same. The physical good order of conditions on the earth depends on using things properly, in the right measure and place, keeping to limits and holding to moderation, fairness and justice. The spiritual good order of it depends on the tie with Allah and on obedience to His commands. The opposite of that, which is disorder of both kinds, appears when these principles are set aside or abandoned. The people of Shu'ayb had done exactly that. They had let go of all of it, and the earth among them had become a hotbed of disorder both outward and inward. That is why they were told to hold back from the deeds that would carry corruption across the whole earth.

**"This is for your own good, if you are ˹truly˺ believers"** closes the verse, and the words that come after it in verse 86 take up the same call from another side. The sense is that if they turn back from what they were doing, nothing but good waits for them, here and in the life to come. The call to the oneness of Allah, and the giving of full measure and weight, are better for them than the state they were in. As for the life to come, success in it plainly depends on obeying what Allah has commanded. As for this world, once people find that there is someone who is honest in his weights and his measures and careful about the rights of those who deal with him, his standing and his good name in the market become established, and his trade grows in volume and in trust.

### What the scholars drew from the market and the road

The words about giving full measure and weight and not making people short of their things were read as carrying a wider rule, and the instruction covers all kinds of reducing, slicing and short-changing of rights.

The command about the roads was explained in two ways. Some said the two statements carry the same sense, since these people used to stop and threaten those who came to Shu'ayb, and they were ordered not to do that. Others said the crimes were two separate ones. They sat on the thoroughfares, robbed and snatched what people had, and also prevented people from believing in Shu'ayb. On that reading the first statement describes the first crime and the second describes the other, and it is this view that Al-Bahr Al-Muhit and other works relied on.

Under the same command against robbing and snatching fall the checkpoints set up on the roads to collect taxes that are not permitted by the sacred law, and the words about blocking the road are understood by some as the prevention of people from the path of Allah. Al-Qurtubi said that the men who sit on the thoroughfares and make people pay taxes that the sacred law does not allow are criminals of the same kind as the people of Shu'ayb, and more oppressive and tyrannical than they were.

The moral state of the community is spelled out in the same passage. These people traced themselves to Ibrahim and professed his religion, and they were a trading community, so their wrongdoing came out in their dealings. They did not keep to honesty in weights, measures and transactions. Injustice in dealing with others goes against the balanced system that God has enforced, since the system of this world is made to work on the basis of perfect justice. Nothing in it takes more from others and gives less in return. Everything in it runs on principles of justice to the point of mathematical exactness, and when that is not the case, what has happened is a disturbance in the well-balanced world of God.

### In short

- Shu'ayb was sent to the people of Madyan, a people descended from Madyan the son of Ibrahim, and the town itself still stands on the route between Sham and the Hijaz.
- The people are also called the people of Al-Aykah, which means the forest, and the early authorities differ on whether these were one people or two, while the punishments given for them in the Book are the fire from the cloud, the piercing sound and the earthquake.
- The essence of the religion is the fulfilment of rights, both the rights owed to Allah and the rights owed to other people, and this community was failing in both.
- The three things Shu'ayb said were the call to the oneness of Allah, the proof that had come to them, and the command to deal justly in measure and weight, and the whole of it was put as being for their own good.
- The command against making people short of their due covers property, honour, respect and every right, and the road command covers both highway robbery and the checkpoints that collect taxes the sacred law does not permit.

86.text:
The call of Shu'ayb turns to the roads, where his people had made a trade of the travellers. "And do not lie in ambush on every road—threatening and hindering those who believe in Allah from His Path and striving to make it ˹appear˺ crooked. Remember when you were few, then He increased you in number. And consider the fate of the corruptors". The verse names the practice, forbids it, and then puts two motives in front of them.

### Phrase by phrase

**"And do not lie in ambush on every road"** takes up the sittings themselves. The people used to set themselves on the roads at the entry points leading to the town, and the verse forbids it.

**"threatening"** gives the first thing done there. As-Suddi said that what they threatened people with was death if they would not hand over their money, since they were bandits. The first of the two readings of the passage is that it is about robbing travellers, and that reading is the better one, since Shu'ayb first names the sitting on every road, and then adds the second matter separately.

**"and hindering those who believe in Allah from His Path"** gives the second thing done there. Ibn Abbas, Mujahid and several others read the words the other way round, and said that the people sat on the road threatening the believers who came to Shu'ayb to follow him. So on that reading the road was blocked precisely against the people who wanted to hear him.

**"and striving to make it ˹appear˺ crooked"** is the further charge. They wanted the path of Allah to be twisted and turned aside, and they hunted for anything in it to misrepresent, so that people could be drawn away from the true religion with doubts and objections of their own making. The words about sitting at the roadside and charging a toll are also taken by some as an excise tax, which is the other face of the same crime.

**"Remember when you were few, then He increased you in number"** is the first motive put to them, and it belongs to persuasion. They had been weak because they were few, and afterwards they became mighty because of their numbers. They were asked to remember the favour of Allah, whether it lay in numbers that grew from small beginnings, or in an economic weakness that turned into freedom from need.

**"And consider the fate of the corruptors"** is the second motive, and it works by warning. The sense is that they should look at the sad end of peoples who had made disorder on the earth before them, and that the peoples of Nuh, of Ad, of Thamud and of Lut stood in front of them as examples of the different forms of punishment. What happened to those peoples should have been enough to show them their own situation, and to bring them to correct themselves. A further reading of the same words turns them to the idolaters before them and asks what the end of those people was.

### What the community's story leaves behind

When the people of Madyan went to the furthest end of their wrong ways, God sent Shu'ayb to them with His message. He urged them towards the way of righteousness and towards honesty in their dealings, and with clear arguments he made them aware of why honesty was needed. They were not willing to take the admonition. More than that, they would not accept his mission at all. They twisted what he preached, they made trouble between him and the people, and they turned to violent means to keep people from supporting him. In the end the retribution of God came down on them and they were destroyed.

What their case shows is the weight God gives to the rights of human beings and to honesty in dealings between people. A community was destroyed in spite of laying claim to belief, and the judgement of God cannot be swayed, since He is the best of judges.

### In short

- The people of Shu'ayb used to sit on the roads and rob and frighten the travellers who passed.
- On the other reading, they were blocking the road against those who came to believe.
- They also sought to make the path of Allah look crooked, so as to turn people away from it with invented doubts.
- They were reminded of the favour of Allah, who raised them from a small and weak people to numbers and strength.
- They were sent to look at the end of those who had made corruption before them, since the peoples of Nuh, Ad, Thamud and Lut each carried a lesson.
- The ruin of a people who claimed belief shows how heavily God weighs honesty in dealings and the rights of other human beings, and with that the words at the end of verse 86 have said all they have to say.

87.text:
The call comes to the division that had opened in the town. "If some of you do believe in what I have been sent with while others do not, then be patient until Allah judges between us. He is the Best of Judges.”"

### Phrase by phrase

**"If some of you do believe in what I have been sent with while others do not"** describes the state the community had been brought to. Some of them had taken the call and others went on refusing it, and no outward difference had opened between the two.

**"then be patient until Allah judges between us"** is the answer to what they made of that. The people had raised a difficulty out of the division in their ranks, since both sides were living comfortably, and the argument they put was that if disbelief were a crime, the criminal would have been punished already. The answer given here addresses the same doubt. They were told not to make haste, and to wait, and the waiting was to last until Allah judged between them.

**"He is the Best of Judges"** gives the ground of the patience. Allah is forbearing and merciful, and He grants respite to those who do wrong. His decree begins to move against them only when they have gone past every limit in their wickedness and their high-handedness. So the state the two sides were living in was not evidence that the denial was of no account. If they held to it, the time was not far off when the decisive punishment would overtake the deniers.

The two groups are also put in the plainest terms, that when the judgement comes it will be made clear which side stood on the truth and which were the liars, and that those who stood on the truth will be saved while the liars will be destroyed. What Allah will give is the best end to those who are mindful of Him and obey Him, and He will destroy those who deny Him.

### In short

- The division in the town is named plainly, with some believing and some refusing.
- The people treated the comfortable state of both sides as an argument, and the answer is that they should not hurry.
- Allah grants respite to wrongdoers, and His decree moves when the wrong has gone past every limit.
- The judgement will show which side held the truth, and the outcome will be deliverance for one and destruction for the other.
- The end given to those who fear Him and obey Him is the better end, and the deniers are the ones who will be destroyed.

88.text:
The chiefs lose patience and turn to the threat they had been holding in reserve. "The arrogant chiefs of his people threatened, “O Shu’aib! We will certainly expel you and your fellow believers from our land, unless you return to our faith.” He replied, “Even if we hate it"". The verse records the threat and the first words of the answer.

### Phrase by phrase

**"The arrogant chiefs of his people threatened"** names the speakers. They are the council of the people, the ones who looked down on belief, and they are described by their pride, as the chiefs of the earlier community were.

**"O Shu’aib! We will certainly expel you and your fellow believers from our land"** is the first arm of the threat. Not convinced by the answer they had been given, they set out the choice they had always intended to force, and there was nothing else they could say. Either Shu'ayb and the rest of the believers returned to the fold of the old faith, or they would be thrown out of the town.

### Why the demand was made at all

**"unless you return to our faith"** is the second arm, and it is worth a look. In the case of the other believers, a return was possible to imagine, since they had all been part of the faith and the way of the disbelievers and had come to Islam later. The case of Shu'ayb was different, since he had never followed their false faith even for a single day, and a prophet of Allah cannot follow a faith that runs against the pure oneness of God. What explains the demand is the way matters looked to them. Before prophethood was given to him, Shu'ayb kept quiet about their sayings and their doings and went on living among the people as one of them, and so his people took him for one more of their own, a fellow traveller and a follower of their faith. It was only when he gave the call to true faith that they discovered that his religion was not theirs, and from that they concluded that he had turned away from the old way. So the words are addressed to him in the plural, and the plural in their address takes in the rest of the believers as well, since Shu'ayb had never been part of their religious community.

**"Even if we hate it"** is what he said first. It is put as a question in the original, and the question is meant as a refusal. The sense is whether they were trying to make the believers go back to a faith they disliked and knew to be false, and the manner of asking says plainly that such a thing can never be.

### In short

- The chiefs of the people, who were proud, demanded that Shu'ayb and the believers return to the old faith or leave the town.
- The demand could be imagined for the others, who had once followed that faith, but not for Shu'ayb, who had never followed it.
- His people had taken him for one of themselves because he had lived quietly among them before his prophethood.
- The plural in their address takes in everyone who believed with him.
- His answer begins as a question, which is the strongest form of refusal, and asks how they could return to something they hate.

89.text:
The answer continues and becomes a prayer. "We would surely be fabricating a lie against Allah if we were to return to your faith after Allah has saved us from it. It does not befit us to return to it unless it is the Will of Allah, our Lord. Our Lord has encompassed everything in ˹His˺ knowledge. In Allah we trust. Our Lord! Judge between us and our people with truth. You are the best of those who judge.”"

### Phrase by phrase

**"We would surely be fabricating a lie against Allah if we were to return to your faith after Allah has saved us from it"** gives the first reason. Allah had rescued them from that faith, and to go back to it would be to invent a falsehood against Him. The lie would be twofold. To treat disbelief, and the shirk that joins partners to God, as though they were faith would mean saying that Allah had commanded it, which is forging a lie against Him. Beyond that, after a person has believed in the revealed truth and has come to knowledge and insight about it, a return to disbelief amounts to saying that the first way was false and mistaken and the later one true and correct. That is a compounded lie, since it takes the true for the false and the false for the true.

### The claim and its correction

**"It does not befit us to return to it unless it is the Will of Allah, our Lord"** qualifies the claim. There was a flavour of assertion in saying that they could never go back, and making such a claim sits awkwardly with the spirit of selfless submission that belongs to a servant of Allah. It does not suit those who are near to the presence of their Lord and have come to know Him. So he added the condition of the divine will, and the sense of it is that nothing is theirs to guarantee. Another reading of the same words takes them as a way of saying that the matter is not theirs at all, since the knowledge of it belongs to Allah, and if He were to take that knowledge from their hearts they would have nothing to hold to.

**"Our Lord has encompassed everything in ˹His˺ knowledge"** states the ground of that submission. His knowledge takes in all things, including the situation of Shu'ayb and the situation of his people, and there is nothing hidden from Him. He knows what is right for His servants.

**"In Allah we trust"** takes the answer one step further. The words are a mirror of humility, an affirmation of tawakkul, the trust in Allah, and a confident handing over of the affair to Him, and those three are among the master virtues of the prophets. What they come to is this, that a person is nothing and has no claim of his own to do a thing or to hold away from it, and that being able to do good and being able to keep away from evil are nothing but the grace of Allah. There is no strength in which a servant may say that he will stand on his own. The Prophet ﷺ gave the same sense in the words that had there not been the grace of Allah, people would not have been guided, nor have been able to give in charity, nor to perform the prayer. The trust Shu'ayb put in Allah was over all his affairs, over what he did and over what he left alone, and its point is that his Lord would keep him firm on the right path and guard him from the ways that lead down.

**"Our Lord! Judge between us and our people with truth. You are the best of those who judge"** is the supplication, and it comes at the moment when he saw that nothing would move those people. He stopped addressing the arrogant chiefs and turned to his Lord. Ibn Abbas said that the word used here means to decide, which is how the word for a judge takes its sense in the language.

What the prayer asked for in reality was the destruction of those among his people who disbelieved, and the destruction came when they were overtaken by the earthquake. So the supplication of a prophet against a people who had been given every chance was answered, and the answer is the subject of the verses that follow.

### In short

- The believers could not go back, since that would be inventing a lie against Allah after He had delivered them from that faith.
- The lie would be twofold, since it treats what God never commanded as His command, and takes the true for the false and the false for the true.
- The claim that they would never return is made subject to the will of Allah, which is the manner of a servant who does not bind his own Lord.
- The Lord's knowledge takes in all things, and nothing of their situation is hidden from Him.
- Trust in Allah is stated as the foundation, and it is coupled with humility, since guidance and the strength to obey are the grace of Allah alone.
- The supplication asked Allah to judge between them and their people with truth, and what it asked for in reality was the undoing of the deniers, which came in the form of the earthquake.

90.text:
The chiefs make one last attempt to hold their people. "The disbelieving chiefs of his people threatened, “If you follow Shu’aib, you will surely be losers!”" The word is a warning put out among themselves, and it is aimed at the people who might still be listening.

### Phrase by phrase

**"The disbelieving chiefs of his people"** names those who spoke. They are the leading men of the community who had refused the call to believe in the oneness of Allah, and the word for chiefs is the word for the leading men and the notables.

**"If you follow Shu’aib, you will surely be losers"** is what they said among themselves, and it is also taken as what they said to their followers. In one report the words were spoken by the chiefs privately to one another, and the account of it stands in Al-Bahr Al-Muhit on the authority of Ata. What they meant by being losers was that the person who followed him would be ignorant and duped.

Another reading of their words is that they were warning the people against him openly, telling them that if they took the path of Shu'ayb and left the way of life their ancestors had followed, ruin would certainly come to them through it.

Their words are a misleading statement, and the thing they were attacking was the faith they had been given every chance to see. The mockery they had made of the prayer of their prophet is recorded elsewhere, when they asked whether his salah commanded him to do the things he called them to (11:87). The verse brings their warning forward and leaves the answer to the verse that follows it, which is verse 91 of this surah, where the punishment itself is named.

### What the case of this community shows

The community of Shu'ayb was not guilty of denying God outright. Its guilt was that it represented Him falsely, since it had attributed to God a religion that God had never sent. That has been the position of the communities of the prophets generally. Such communities were not unlike those to whom God had revealed His religion earlier, but by means of changes and additions of their own making they turned it into something else. In that way they changed the religion of God into the religion of their own desires, and then went on calling it the religion of God.

The religious leaders of later times, who have the support of the people and hold power, are in the same position. They know very well that they cannot argue with the prophets and win, but they do not want anyone to take their importance from them, so they look for a way to silence those who speak. Allowance can be made for a person so long as the truth has not become clear to him. Once it has been made clear and a man still chooses to be arrogant, he has lost any claim to sympathy. The punishment in this world is given on that basis, and the punishment in the Hereafter will be decided on the same basis, according to the guilt of the people.

### In short

- The leading men of the community, who had refused the call, warned the people that following Shu'aib would end in ruin.
- One report has them saying it privately among themselves, and another reading has them warning the people openly against him.
- What they meant was that a follower of Shu'ayb would be ignorant and taken in.
- Their community's guilt was not a plain denial of God but a false representation of Him, since they had made a religion of their own desires and called it His.
- Men in power who cannot answer the prophets try instead to silence them, and the punishment of this world and the next is measured by what a person does once the truth has been made clear to him.

91.text:
The answer to their threat comes at once. "Then an ˹overwhelming˺ earthquake struck them and they fell lifeless in their homes".

### Phrase by phrase

**"Then an ˹overwhelming˺ earthquake struck them"** names the punishment in the opening of the verse. The ground shook under them, and in one reading the loud noise that announced their torment is joined to it.

**"and they fell lifeless in their homes"** describes the state they were left in. The word means that they were brought to a standstill where they were, prostrate and motionless, keeled over on their knees. The morning found them dead in their dwellings, in the town and in the encampments around it.

### Why the earthquake came, and how it fits with the other accounts

The earth shook them as the punishment for the threat they had made to drive out Shu'ayb and those who believed with him. What they had said of the believers was the opposite of the truth, and what came to pass was that the loss fell on nobody but them.

The end of this people is told again in Surah Hud. It says there that when the command of Allah came, Shu'ayb and those who had believed with him were delivered by a mercy from their Lord. The wrongdoers were seized by the cry, and they were left lying in their own houses, dead (11:94). The cry is named there in that context because the people had mocked Shu'ayb over his prayer. It was fitting that the cry should be named as the thing that silenced them. Their challenge is recorded by the same account, since they had asked him to make a piece of the sky fall on them if he was one of the truthful (26:187). In Surah Ash-Shu'ara the answer is given with the punishment of the day of the shadow, Yawm az-Zullah. A gloomy cloud came over them and seized them, and the verse says that it was the punishment of a great day (26:189).

The reconciliation of the two accounts is given in a report from Ibn Abbas. The people of Shu'ayb were first subjected to such intense heat that it was as though the door of the fire had been thrown open at them. It choked them. Shade and water gave them no relief. Driven by the heat they went down into their cellars, and it was hotter there, and with nothing left to try they ran out of the town into the forest nearby. There Allah sent a thick cloud with a cool breeze passing underneath it, and, their senses gone under the heat, they all rushed for shelter under its shade. At that point the whole cloud turned into a cloud of fire raining down on them, and the earthquake came as well and turned them to ashes. So the punishments of the earthquake and of the shade converged on those people at the same time, and that account is recorded in Al-Bahr Al-Muhit.

Others said that it is possible the people were split into different groups. On that view one part of them met the shaking of the ground, while the other part met the fire that rained out of the cloud. Either way, the shade they had run to for relief was the thing that came down on them.

### In short

- The earthquake came on them as the answer to their threat to expel Shu'ayb and his followers.
- They were left prostrate where they stood, dead in their dwellings, and the morning found them so.
- The same end is given in Surah Hud, where the cry seizes the wrongdoers and the believers are saved by a mercy from Allah.
- The challenge they had put to Shu'ayb, that he should make a piece of the sky fall on them, is answered by the punishment of the day of the shadow.
- On the reconciliation given in the reports, intense heat drove them out of the town to the shade of a cloud, and the cloud turned to fire on them while the ground shook.
- The shade they ran to for relief was what destroyed them, and some hold that the people were split so that the earthquake took one part and the shade the other.

92.text:
The verse states what became of them, and then states the verdict twice. "Those who rejected Shu’aib were ˹wiped out˺ as if they had never lived there. Those who rejected Shu’aib were the true losers".

### Phrase by phrase

**"Those who rejected Shu’aib were wiped out as if they had never lived there"** describes the emptiness left behind. One sense of the word used here for dwelling is to live in a place in peace and comfort, and that is the sense intended. The houses where they had lived at ease were left so desolate after the punishment that it was as if that peace and comfort had never been there at all.

**"Those who rejected Shu’aib were the true losers"** gives the verdict. The words are repeated, and the repetition has a purpose of its own, since it is meant as a refutation of what the chiefs had said at the beginning. They had warned the people that anyone who followed Shu'ayb would be a loser. The answer comes back in the same words turned round, that the loss fell on the people who called him a liar. They lost themselves and what they had, while those who had faith did not fail in the least, which is the opposite of what the disbelievers had claimed.

The naming of the people as those who rejected him is also deliberate, since it is the rejection that explains the punishment and makes the sentence fit. In the Arabic of the verse the words alladhīna kadhdhabū Shu'ayban, those who denied Shu'ayb, are repeated as the subject of both sentences, and the repetition is aimed at the warning the chiefs had put out.

### What the verse is for

The fate of the people of Shu'ayb is set out here as a lesson, and the lesson is the real purpose behind the whole account. It was the people who had threatened to throw Shu'ayb and his believing companions out of their city who were themselves removed from the land, and the very place they had wanted to keep for themselves was left as though no one had ever lived in it. So the verses close the story of the community with a picture of what the threat came to, and of the end of those who made it.

### In short

- The places where they had lived at ease were left so empty that it was as if they had never been there.
- The verdict is repeated to overturn the threat the chiefs had made, since the losers were the ones who denied the prophet.
- They lost themselves and their possessions, while the believers lost nothing.
- Their rejection of Shu'ayb is named as the reason for what came on them.
- The whole account is given as a lesson, and the people who tried to drive the messenger out were the ones removed from the land.

93.text:
The messenger is left looking at the ruin of his people. "He turned away from them, saying, “O my people! Indeed, I have delivered to you the messages of my Lord and gave you ˹sincere˺ advice. How can I then grieve for those who chose to disbelieve?”"

### Phrase by phrase

**"He turned away from them"** describes his leaving, and it happened before the punishment came down. He went apart from them with the sentence of his Lord in sight. The greater number of the early authorities hold that he and those who had believed with him left that country for Makkah, and that they stayed there until their lives came to their end.

The turning away was also the moment he spoke over them. With the torment, the punishment and the destruction having struck them, he addressed them once more in the way of an admonition and a rebuke, and that is the sense of his words here.

**"O my people! Indeed, I have delivered to you the messages of my Lord and gave you ˹sincere˺ advice"** is the summary he gives of his own work among them. He had conveyed what he was sent with. He had warned them of the torment of Allah, called them to repent, and called them to believe, and he had wanted good for them in all of it.

**"How can I then grieve for those who chose to disbelieve?"** is put as a question that expects no answer. It was the depth of his disappointment with a people who were sunk in disobedience and stubbornness that had moved him to ask his Lord to chasten them. When the punishment then came, and it came as the answer to his prayer, his heart was distressed for them, as the heart of a prophet who carries affection for his people is distressed. The words here settled his own heart. He had done what a messenger does, and there was no room left for grief over the state they had chosen for themselves.

### The place this leaves the story

The prayer of Shu'ayb is answered and the community of Madyan is finished. The account closes with the messenger leaving, with the testimony of a task fully done, and with the refusal of the people standing as the reason for everything that came on them.

### In short

- Shu'ayb left the country before the punishment fell, and the greater number of the early authorities hold that he went to Makkah and stayed there.
- He spoke over his people one last time, as an admonition and a rebuke.
- He had delivered the messages of his Lord, warned them, invited them to repent, and wished them well.
- His prayer against them had been answered, yet his heart was pained for them, since a prophet carries affection for his people.
- The grief is set aside in these words, since a people who refused belief after the message had reached them left him nothing to grieve over.

94.text:
The story of Madyan closes and the surah draws the general rule out of it. "Whenever We sent a prophet to a society, We afflicted its ˹disbelieving˺ people with suffering and adversity, so perhaps they would be humbled".

### Phrase by phrase

**"Whenever We sent a prophet to a society"** widens the frame. The lesson is not tied to the people of Nuh, or of Ad, or of Thamud, or of Shu'ayb on their own. The way described here is the usual way of Allah with the peoples He has sent messengers to, and the verse states it as a rule.

**"We afflicted its ˹disbelieving˺ people with suffering and adversity"** names the first treatment. The affliction is said in the words Basa and Darra. Basa is taken to mean hunger and poverty, and Darra to mean illness, and the two expressions have these senses in other places in the Book as well. Abdullah ibn Masud confirmed these meanings for the two words. Some of those who study the language said that the first word refers to hardship in wealth and the second to the loss of health, and one account has the pair the other way round, with the physical sicknesses and ailments of the people under the first word and the poverty and humiliation they went through under the second.

**"so perhaps they would be humbled"** gives the purpose. The affliction was sent so that they would call on Him, humble themselves before Him, and ask Him to lift what had come on them. The turning of a man to his Lord when he is pressed is a human thing, and the distress was therefore a mercy in disguise, sent for the good of the people it fell on. So the verse carries its own warning for the people who heard it. The fate of suffering that the earlier verses had described was not a thing set apart for those who had gone before, and the people of Quraysh and every other people who refuse the way of Allah were being told plainly what treatment attends a message that is denied.

The complaint of a man against his own time is put in verse by that meaning, that people are made to behave badly towards you so that you turn back to your Lord in tears. Verse 94 ends on that note, and the verse that follows it, verse 95, takes the second half of the same treatment.

**Where the surah is going.** The stories of five messengers and their peoples have now been told. The sixth account, that of Musa and his people, is taken up after a few more verses, and the warning given in these verses covers the ground between the two.

### On the way the Book tells a story

The usual way of the Book with historical events differs from the way of the books of history. It does not set out to give an event in full or in its order of time. It chooses the part of it that carries the purpose in hand, and then it puts the weight on the lesson or the moral that part contains. What the reader is meant to carry away from the stories of the peoples is the manner in which Allah deals with those who deny what He sends, and that manner does not change from one generation to the next.

### In short

- The verse widens the account, since what happened to the earlier peoples was not reserved for them alone.
- The messengers came to their societies first with a call, and the affliction came to those who denied them.
- Basa and Darra name the two sides of that affliction, hunger or want on one side and illness or loss of health on the other.
- The point of the affliction was that the people would humble themselves and turn back to their Lord.
- The people of Quraysh were warned in the same words that this way of Allah still holds.
- The Book tells such events by selecting the part that carries the lesson, not by setting down the whole of the history in order.

95.text:
The second half of the treatment is put in front of them. "Then We changed their adversity to prosperity until they flourished and argued ˹falsely˺, “Our forefathers ˹too˺ had been visited by adversity and prosperity.” So We seized them by surprise, while they were unaware".

### Phrase by phrase

**"Then We changed their adversity to prosperity"** turns the condition round. In this verse the word for the evil condition refers to the hardship, and the word for the good condition means prosperity, and the word used for the increase means growth. The hardship was changed into ease, the illness and sickness into health and well-being, and the poverty into richness of provision. So the drought and the want of fruit were replaced with fertility, abundance and comfort.

**"until they flourished"** gives the result of that turn in their fortunes. They increased in number, in wealth and in children.

**"and argued ˹falsely˺, “Our forefathers ˹too˺ had been visited by adversity and prosperity.”"** is how they read what had happened. The intended end of the whole turn was that they would be thankful to their Lord and turn back to Him, and instead they said that hardship and ease had come to their fathers before them just as they had come to these people. On their reading there was nothing to learn in either, since it was only the habit of time, a matter of the usual ups and downs that people pass through, and no consequence of anything they had done. They held firmly to what they were on and took their fathers as their example.

The effect was that they were shut off from learning anything from either state. Trouble came, and they said that it was bound to happen. When it lifted and they were given good days instead, they settled deeper into their misunderstanding. So the first set of circumstances taught them nothing, and neither did the second.

The words of the verse have nothing more to say about them after that point. **"So We seized them by surprise, while they were unaware"** gives the end of it. The punishment took them suddenly, while they were not expecting it, and before they perceived that its time had come.

### Why the second test is the heavier one

The two states were set as tests, and the people failed both. Neither the affliction nor the ease moved them to change their ways, and the failure in the second is the more dangerous of the two. To be given progress even after a person has been guilty of arrogance is a serious thing, since it is a sign that God has left the culprit to be taken at the point where he has become most fearless of the punishment of God.

Understanding of wisdom and of the testing itself is what the two conditions call for. A believer gives thanks to Allah in good times and practices patience in hard times. A report in the Sahih says that the affair of the believer is a wonder, because nothing that Allah decrees for him is anything but good for him. If harm strikes him he is patient, and that is good for him, and if prosperity is given to him he gives thanks, and that is good for him.

Other reports carry the same lesson. A believer goes on being tried by afflictions until he comes out purified of sin, and the likeness given for the one who plays a part is that of a donkey that does not know why its owners tied it up or why they let it go. Another report says that death coming suddenly is a mercy for the believer and a painful punishment for the one who disbelieves.

The reward of a life lived in awareness of God is in the Hereafter. If God wishes, He gives a part of it in this world as well, in well-being and in respect, and both are from His favour and not from the merit of the one who receives them.

### In short

- When the hardship did not humble them, their condition was turned round, and the hardship was replaced with ease, health and wealth.
- They increased in numbers and in what they owned, and the turn should have brought gratitude and a return to their Lord.
- They reasoned that hardship and ease had visited their fathers too, and took the whole of it for the ordinary movement of time.
- They were caught in that state, and the punishment took them suddenly while they were unaware of its coming.
- Being given ease after arrogance is the more dangerous of the two tests, since it can leave a person fearless of the punishment of God.
- The believer is the one who thanks in prosperity and is patient in hardship, and the reward of that life is with Allah.

96.text:
The surah names the condition that would have changed everything for those towns. "Had the people of those societies been faithful and mindful ˹of Allah˺, We would have overwhelmed them with blessings from heaven and earth. But they disbelieved, so We seized them for what they used to commit".

### Phrase by phrase

**"Had the people of those societies been faithful and mindful ˹of Allah˺"** sets the condition on two things, iman and taqwa. The first is that the hearts accept what the messenger brought, believe him and obey him, and the second is that they carry out what was commanded and keep away from what was forbidden.

**"We would have overwhelmed them with blessings from heaven and earth"** gives what the two would have brought. The blessing spoken of is barakah, and the word means increase and growth. The blessing of the heaven is the rain that comes down from it, and the blessing of the earth is the vegetation and the fruit that come up out of it. Beyond the rain and the produce, the expression covers every means of prosperity, and above all a carefree enjoyment of what a person owns, with no anxiety spoiling the pleasure of it.

Barakah shows itself in two ways, and the reports of the Prophet ﷺ carry an instance of the first of them. Jabir ibn Abdallah reported that on the day of the trench a thousand of the companions were at work and had no food with them. He told the Messenger of Allah ﷺ that there was a small measure of barley and one sheep, and asked what he was to do. The instructions were to grind the barley and make it into dough, to slaughter the sheep and clean it, and to set a pot on the fire. Mustafa ﷺ then placed his blessed hands on the dough, moistened a finger with his mouth and passed it over the top of the pot. The companions were then called group by group, and bread was cooked with the dough. They ate from the pot until a thousand men had eaten, and there was still some left over. The point of the report is that barakah gets the work done and not quantity. In one of them the thing itself grows in quantity, as is reported of the Prophet ﷺ, that a large number of people drank their fill from a small pot of water, and a whole army ate to satisfaction from a small amount of food. In the other the quantity stays as it is and the usefulness of the thing is multiplied many times over. A single morsel of food can become a source of great strength and health, while on another occasion a large amount of food does nothing. A person can do a great deal of work in one short hour, and at another time the same work cannot be finished in four or five hours. In such cases the food and the time have not increased, and what has increased is their effect.

What the words of the verse say is this. Barakah in the things of heaven and of earth comes by faith in Allah and by taqwa, and where the two are absent the barakah is withheld. Faith is set here against kufr, and a town that believed was given good in this world on account of what it believed.

There is a case for that in the stories of the messengers. No town believed as a whole after seeing the punishment, except the town of Yunus. When his people believed, the torment of disgrace was lifted from them in the life of this world, and they were allowed to enjoy themselves for a while (10:98). The Book says of that messenger that he was sent to a hundred thousand or more, and that they believed, and so they were given their enjoyment for a time (37:147-148). Every other township that was sent a warner took the same road, and the warners were denied (34:34). So the opening of this verse is not an empty supposition. The people of one town did what the others did not, and the difference in their end is on record. Take the world as it stands. The produce of the earth is greater than it has ever been, and inventions serve our comfort in ways past generations could not have imagined. Yet a man in the middle of all that abundance is worried, low and dissatisfied, and further from peace and comfort than those who came before him. Nothing explains that except that barakah has gone out of these things.

**"But they disbelieved, so We seized them for what they used to commit"** states the outcome. They gave the lie to the messengers and the Books, and they were seized on account of what they used to earn, with drought, with a lack of fruit and with punishment.

### Wealth as favour and wealth as anger

Prosperity, good health and possessions are not always a sign that Allah is pleased with a person. They are sometimes given out of anger, which is what verse 44 of Surah Al-An'am says, that when the people forgot what they had been reminded of, the doors of everything good were opened to them, and then they were caught suddenly by the punishment of Allah (6:44). So wealth and ease are not reliable signs of favour, and they can be a sign of wrath.

What this verse adds is that barakah in the things of heaven and earth is a sign of favour. Wealth given against a person's sins is usually short-lived and marks displeasure, while wealth given to a reward of iman and taqwa carries lasting benefit. The two look so much alike that telling them apart is difficult. The men of knowledge have given signs for it. When prosperity and good health make a person more grateful to Allah and more given to worship than before, that is a mark of favour. When they push him deeper into sin, that is a mark of wrath, and shelter is sought from that state.

### In short

- The verse makes the coming of good things conditional, and the two conditions are faith and taqwa.
- Barakah means increase and growth, and it works either by growing the thing itself or by multiplying the good it does.
- Blessings from heaven and earth cover the rain from above, the produce from below, and a settled freedom from anxiety over what one owns.
- The report of the Prophet ﷺ shows a whole army fed from a little food, which is the first kind of barakah.
- Where faith and taqwa are absent, abundance can still be given, and that is the wealth that comes as anger rather than as favour.
- The sign that separates the two is what the wealth does to a person, since gratitude marks favour and deeper sin marks wrath.

97.text:
The next two verses take up the false confidence of the same people. "Did the people of those societies feel secure that Our punishment would not come upon them by night while they were asleep"

### Phrase by phrase

**"Did the people of those societies feel secure"** addresses the people of the towns, and in the plainest reading it is the people of Makkah who are meant, since they were the ones being warned by these stories. The question carries a rebuke, and the mention of the towns recalls the peoples whose end had just been told, of Nuh, of Ad, of Thamud and of the rest.

**"that Our punishment would not come upon them by night while they were asleep"** names one of the two times a man is most helpless. The word used here for the coming by night is bayatan, which is the arrival of a thing on a people in the darkness while they are unaware of it. Verse 97 of this surah puts that half of the question, and the verse that follows it, verse 99, gathers both halves into one and answers them. The word used for coming by night carries the sense of a raid in the dark. The picture is of people lying asleep and completely unaware of anything approaching.

**Where the surah is going with the question.** The verse is a warning put to the world. The words say the same to every generation that follows, and to the people of the Prophet's own time first of all. The residents of those towns lived unmindful of one fact. The punishment of Allah can take a people at any hour, when they are sleeping at night or when they are taken up with their affairs. The peoples described in the verses before were destroyed by night and by day. What happened to them should have been enough to teach those who came after them to avoid the things that brought death and disaster on those who went before.

### In short

- The question is put to the people of Makkah and to the people of the world, since the warning belongs to all who live after those towns.
- One of the two hours named is the night, and the word used for it carries the sense of a raid in the dark.
- The picture is of people asleep and unaware of anything coming towards them.
- The verse rebukes a false confidence, since what the earlier peoples suffered shows that the punishment of Allah comes at any hour.
- The lesson is that a person should take warning from what happened to others and keep away from what destroyed them.

98.text:
The second half of the question follows. "Or did they feel secure that Our punishment would not come upon them by day while they were at play"

### Phrase by phrase

**"Or did they feel secure"** puts the same rebuke a second time, and the two questions together close off every hour of the day.

**"that Our punishment would not come upon them by day"** names the daytime, and the word here is the forenoon, the part of the morning when a person is at his work.

**"while they were at play"** describes the state they were caught in. It covers the people busy with their own affairs and unaware of anything else, and it covers the part of it that is play, since the verse says of some that they were amused forgetfully, taken up with the life of this world and its falsehood.

So the two verses cover sleeping and waking, the night and the day, and no hour is left in which a person may consider himself beyond reach. The question is put as a rebuke of the feeling, and the answer is implied in the fact that whole nations had been taken in exactly those hours.

### In short

- The second question completes the first, so that the two together cover the whole of the day.
- The daytime named here is the forenoon, the hours of work and busyness.
- The state described is one of being at play, whether in the sense of being absorbed in one's own affairs or in the sense of being taken up with amusement and falsehood.
- No hour is left unmentioned, and the earlier nations were taken in just such hours.
- The rebuke falls on the false confidence itself rather than on the hours.

99.text:
The two questions are now drawn into one and answered. "Did they feel secure against Allah’s planning? None would feel secure from Allah’s planning except the losers"

### Phrase by phrase

**"Did they feel secure against Allah’s planning?"** is the summary of both. The word for planning is used of His drawing people on by degrees, through favours and ease, and then seizing them suddenly. That is why the increase of a people's wealth and strength was never safe ground for confidence. The favours arrive as a test and not as a warrant.

**"None would feel secure from Allah’s planning except the losers"** is the answer, and it turns the confidence back on the person who holds it. Al-Hasan Al-Basri said that the believer performs acts of worship while he is in fear, in fright and anxiety, and that the wicked one commits acts of disobedience while feeling safe from the punishment of Allah.

The point was put even more sharply in another place. Nasrabadi said that a sinner has no ground for feeling secure from the drawing on by degrees, and asked which sin is greater than the sin of the man who takes note of something of his own acts. He meant that such a person is laying claim to a share in what belongs to the Lord alone, and that is a contention with His oneness.

So fear is the mark of the one who believes, and the sense of safety is the mark of the one who has lost. What the words of the verse say is plain enough on its face. The people who were given strength and abundance in this world are the ones who should look at those gifts as a test, and the ones who succeed are those who are not made proud by what they are given, but see the generosity of Allah in it and give thanks.

### In short

- The word for planning here means drawing a people on by degrees with favours and then taking them suddenly.
- The two earlier questions are gathered into one and the false confidence itself is answered.
- No one is safe from that drawing on except the people who are lost, since safety from it is itself the mark of the losing side.
- The believer worships in fear and anxiety, while the wicked one disobeys while feeling safe.
- The man who feels secure is claiming something that belongs to the Lord alone, which is the sharpest form of the sin.
- The blessings given to a people are a test, and the successful ones are those who see the generosity behind them and give thanks.

100.text:
The lesson is put to the people who now stand where the destroyed peoples stood. "Is it not clear to those who take over the land after ˹the destruction of˺ its former residents that—if We will—We can punish them ˹too˺ for their sins and seal their hearts so they will not hear ˹the truth˺"

### Phrase by phrase

**"Is it not clear to those who take over the land after ˹the destruction of˺ its former residents"** addresses the inheritors of the land, and the plainest instance of such inheritors in the time of the Prophet ﷺ were the people of the land of Makkah. Verse 100 of this surah puts the question to them. The words say that the events just told should have carried the lesson home. The word used here carries the sense of guiding or informing, and the events that have just been told are made the subject of it. The verse means that those events should serve as a lesson and as a means of guidance for the generations who took the land over from those who held it before.

**"that—if We will—We can punish them ˹too˺ for their sins"** is the teaching itself. The people who came after can be caught by the punishment of Allah just as their ancestors were caught, and for the same reason. Ibn Abbas explained the words as asking whether it had not been made clear to them that if Allah willed, He would punish them because of their sins, and Mujahid and several others said the same.

Abu Ja'far bin Jarir At-Tabari set out the sense at length. Allah asks whether He has not made it clear to those who succeeded the earlier nations on the earth. Those successors followed their own ways, and they behaved as those before them had behaved. If He willed, He would bring on them the same end that was decreed for those who preceded them.

**"and seal their hearts so they will not hear ˹the truth˺"** names the further punishment. To seal is to place a cover over the heart. The ones who take no lesson from what happened to those before them are made unable to listen to the truth, so that words of advice and reminder do not reach them.

### What the inheritors of the land should see

The pattern repeats itself, and it should be read as a sign. A community reaches a high level of honour and prosperity, and then it declines, is removed from the scene, and another community takes the same place it had. That rise and fall is a sign of God. It should remind a person of His supremacy, since all the strings of gain and loss are in the hands of a supreme being. He may give good fortune to one and take it away from another.

The powers of observation and of thought that a person has been given are enough to draw the conclusion. If the real source of power were in any other hands, the group that had once reached ascendancy would never have allowed others to replace it. A person who learns this finds nourishment in the rise and fall of nations.

What happens instead is that the new community takes its own rise as proof about itself. When one community falls and another rises in its place, the members of the rising one assume that what happened to the previous community was a fate particular to that community, and that it will never happen to them. Those are the people the verse addresses, since they are not learning from the ruin they have walked past, and in some cases they are copying the very behaviour that brought it about.

The contrast between the two groups runs through the whole passage. On one side are those who walk through the dwellings of the destroyed peoples without understanding, and on the other are those who take the lesson. The Book makes the point in another place, that there is guidance in the many generations destroyed before them, in whose dwellings they walk about, and it asks whether they will not then listen (20:128 and 32:26). The same point is carried in the words addressed to a people who lived in the houses of men who had wronged themselves (14:44-45). It is carried again in the question of whether any of those generations can still be seen, or whether the least whisper of them can be heard (19:98). So the ruins the people passed each day were the plainest sign, and the warning came to them in the very ground they walked on.

### In short

- The verse turns the lesson on the people who inherited the land from those who were destroyed.
- If Allah wills, He can punish the later people for their sins just as He punished the earlier ones.
- The sealing of the heart comes after a people refuse the lesson, and it leaves them unable to hear the truth.
- The rise of one community as another falls is a sign that all gain and loss is in the hand of God.
- The rising community tends to take the fate of its predecessor as a fate peculiar to them, and the Book points out the error.
- Ruins the people walked past every day were the plainest warning they had, and the Book asks whether any of those generations can be seen or heard.

101.text:
The surah gathers the five stories it has told and draws the meaning out of them. "We have narrated to you ˹O Prophet˺ some of the stories of those societies. Surely, their messengers came to them with clear proofs, but still they would not believe in what they had already denied. This is how Allah seals the hearts of the disbelievers"

### Phrase by phrase

**"We have narrated to you ˹O Prophet˺ some of the stories of those societies"** points back to what has been told. The word used for a story or tiding carries the sense of great news. The small word meaning from or of, together with it, makes plain that what these verses describe is only a part of a far larger number of events carrying the same lesson. The Book has given a handful of them, and the handful is enough to make the point.

The stories are those of the peoples of Nuh, of Hud, of Salih, of Lut and of Shu'ayb. The account of each ended with the destruction of those who disbelieved, the deliverance of those who believed, and the warning given to the nations by the truth set out with the evidence that the messengers brought.

**"Surely, their messengers came to them with clear proofs"** is the first half of the charge against them. The signs and miracles that the messengers came with were a definite means of deciding between right and wrong. The tiding was brought down with Gabriel as the angel of revelation, and the proofs were sent in the words of the messengers.

A further point belongs here. It is known from this verse that miracles were given to every prophet. The miracles of some have been told in the Book and the miracles of most have not been mentioned in it, and the silence about them is no ground for saying that those prophets had none. The people of Hud said to him that he had not brought them any clear sign. This verse makes plain that their statement came out of plain obstinacy, and it may also be that they thought his miracles were of little weight compared with what they wanted to see.

**"but still they would not believe in what they had already denied"** is the second half, and the hardest of it. The sense given by Ibn 'Atiyyah is that they were not the kind of people to believe afterwards in what the messengers brought them, since they had already denied the truth when it first came to them, even though they recognized it. That reading is sound, and another verse supports it, where Allah says that when the signs come they will not believe, and their hearts and their eyes will be turned away from the guidance as they refused to believe in it the first time (6:109-110).

So the denial recorded here is not a single act that a man might take back. It is a settled refusal that a person grows into, and once it is settled the door of belief is closed from the inside.

### The justice of the warning before the punishment

The Book states elsewhere that Allah never punished a people until He had sent a messenger to warn them (17:15). The same principle stands in the words about the towns of which the story is related, where it is said that some of them are still standing and some have been reaped, and that they were not wronged, but they wronged themselves (11:100-101). The proof had come to each people in its own language and its own way, and the warning had been delivered by a man from among them. What came afterwards was the fruit of what they had chosen.

### The habit that this verse warns against

There is a trait of the disbelieving peoples that the verse lays bare, namely that a people will hold stubbornly to the path of ignorance with no regard for clear signs and proofs, only to prove that what they once said was true. That trait is not confined to the peoples of the past. Many Muslims, and even some of the religious scholars, are seen to hold to a wrong position in the face of clear proofs of the truth, and that habit is a usual cause of a person's falling under the anger of Allah.

### How the hearts come to be sealed

**"This is how Allah seals the hearts of the disbelievers"** states the law of it. The sealing is put on those who disbelieve and reject the truth, and the result is that they can no longer accept the good as good.

The way it comes about is plain. Man has been given the powers of observation, of hearing and of thinking, so that he may learn lessons and come to understand the signs of God through them. When a person does not use those powers for the purpose they were given for, the sensitivity of his heart keeps fading until his feelings grow blunt, and the seal of insensitivity is fixed on his heart and his mind. His state then is that of a man who does not see though he has eyes, does not hear though he has ears, and does not understand though he has a mind, and for all that he is counted among human beings, he has lost the humanity that was meant.

The record of the human race bears the same pattern. It began with the followers of Adam. When those followers went astray, the prophets of God came to remind them. Those who put themselves right at the coming of a prophet were saved, and those who refused to be put right were destroyed. The generations after them forgot the vows of submission they had made, and they met what the earlier generations had met. The same state of affairs has come round again and again, until for the greater part of the human race the record has become one of disobedience and broken pledges.

### What a covenant implies

The last part of the charge against the peoples was the breaking of the covenant, and the verse that follows takes it up on its own. The hearts of these peoples were sealed because they denied the truth when they saw it, and no fresh sign was going to help them after that. The mercy of the warning had been spent, and the sealing was the settled consequence.

What the verse establishes for the reader is a line between the one who turns and the one who will not. The towns whose stories were told are a warning to the people who came after, and the same words hold for a people who reject the messenger in front of them. The hearts of those who reject are sealed in the same way, and they are not guided to the faith, and the justice of it lies in this, that the truth had reached them with its proofs and they turned away.

### In short

- The verse gathers the stories of the five peoples already told, and the word used for them means great tidings, of which only a part has been related.
- The messengers came to each people with clear proofs, and miracles were given to every prophet, whether the Book has mentioned them or not.
