- Their denial was a settled refusal, and the sense of the words is that they would not believe later in what they had already denied.
- The warning came before the punishment, and no people was destroyed until a messenger had been sent to them.
- The sealing of the heart follows the refusal, and it leaves a person unable to see, hear or understand what the signs are for.

102.text:
The subject of the covenant is taken up in the same breath. "We did not find most of them true to their covenant. Rather, We found most of them truly rebellious"

### Phrase by phrase

**"We did not find most of them true to their covenant"** is the opening of verse 102, and it states the failure. It was not the warning that was lacking, and it was not the proofs. What was lacking was loyalty to a commitment they had already made.

Which commitment it was has been answered in more than one way. Ibn Abbas said that the covenant meant here is the one that Allah made with the spirits of all creatures before they were created, when the question was put to them, that He was not their Lord, and all the human spirits entered into the covenant by answering that He was. Most of the people forgot that covenant after they came to the earth, and they fell to worshipping false gods instead of Allah.

Abdullah ibn Masud said that the covenant meant here is the covenant of iman, the faith itself, and the Book has spoken of a man who entered into a covenant with the Most Merciful. On this reading the verse says that most people turned away from their covenant with Allah. The everyday shape of that is easy to see. Take what happens to nearly every person. When distress catches him, he turns to Allah. He makes a promise, in words or in his heart, that if he is relieved of what has come on him he will be faithful, obedient, and will keep away from disobedience. Once he is out of it, he goes back to what he desires, with no regard for the covenant he made.

Another answer takes the covenant as the one bound up with the first nature of the human being. It is the fitrah that Allah placed in them while they were still in the loins of their fathers, together with the taking of the covenant that He is their Lord and King and that no deity but He is worthy of worship. All of them affirmed this, and they testified against themselves to it. Then they defied it, threw it behind their backs, and worshipped others besides Allah, with no proof and no argument, and with nothing from reason or from the sacred law to support them. The pure fitrah refuses such a thing, and every one of the honoured messengers, from the first of them to the last, forbade it. A hadith collected by Muslim carries the point. It says that Allah created His servants as hunafa, turned to Him alone, and that the devils came to them and turned them from their religion and forbade them what He had allowed them. It is recorded in the Two Sahihs that every child is born on the fitrah, and the parents are the ones who turn him into a Jew or a Christian or a Zoroastrian.

**"Rather, We found most of them truly rebellious"** is the second half of the finding. In this reading the words mean that most of the nations of the past were found disobedient, turning away from obedience and from compliance.

### The word most and what it allows

It is worth noticing that the verse says most of them and not all of them. The reason is that there are people so perverted that they do not turn to Allah even in their distress. They never think of making any promise to Him at all. There are others who fulfil what they promised and stay obedient to Him. So the exception in the wording keeps the door open, and it keeps the description honest.

Junayd said that the most beautiful of the servants in state is the one who halts with God in preserving the limits and in being loyal to what he has covenanted. The whole of the verse is that standard applied to the nations that have gone before.

### Where the surah goes next

The five accounts of the earlier peoples have now been closed so that those who read may take the lesson from them, and the next event is the account of Musa, which is told at length in the verses that follow. His miracles were greater in number and more striking in their nature than what was given to the prophets before him, and his people, the Children of Israel, were more stubborn and more ignorant than the other peoples of the world. The verses from 103 to 110 carry that account, and they carry some rulings and points of discussion along with it.

### In short

- The failure of those peoples was not a want of warning, but a want of loyalty to a covenant they had already made.
- One answer takes the covenant as the pact made with all human spirits before creation, when they affirmed that Allah was their Lord.
- Another takes it as the covenant of faith, which most people break as soon as the distress that made them promise is lifted.
- A third takes it as the fitrah that was placed in them, and the affirmation that went with it, which they threw behind their backs to worship others.
- The wording says most and not all, since some people turn in their distress and some keep what they promised, and the account of Musa follows next with more of its signs.

103.text:
The five stories close and the longest account in the surah opens. "Then after them We sent Moses with Our signs to Pharaoh and his chiefs, but they wrongfully rejected them. See what was the end of the corruptors"

### Phrase by phrase

**"Then after them We sent Moses with Our signs"** names the messenger who follows the five already told. The Book sent, after Nuh and Hud and Salih and Lut and Shu'ayb, Musa, with proofs and clear evidences. The signs may refer to the verses of the Torah that were given to him, or to the miracles that were placed in his hand, and in one reading they are counted as nine tokens.

**"to Pharaoh and his chiefs"** names the people he was sent to. The word Pharaoh was the title of the kings of Egypt, and the Pharaoh of the time of Musa is said to have been Mernephtah. His chiefs were the leading men of his people, the Copts of Egypt.

**"but they wrongfully rejected them"** states the answer they gave. The word used here for the wrong they did carries the sense of putting a thing to a use opposite to the one it was made for. Instead of being grateful to Allah for His verses and having faith in them, they turned cold towards them and refused them. Another verse describes the same response, that they belied those signs wrongfully and arrogantly, though they were themselves convinced of them (27:14).

**"See what was the end of the corruptors"** is the closing call to look. It was these very people who turned others away from the path of Allah and gave the lie to His messengers. What came to them was drowning, all of them together, while Musa and his people stood watching. That public drowning added disgrace to the punishment of Pharaoh and his people, and it added comfort to the hearts of the party of Allah.

The Ayah that carries this, verse 103 of this surah, asks the reader to look at how they were punished. The whole account that follows is set out as the answer to that call.

### In short

- Musa was sent after the five messengers already named, and he was sent with proofs and clear evidences.
- The signs given to him are taken either as the verses of the Torah or as his miracles, counted in one reading as nine tokens.
- Pharaoh was the title of the kings of Egypt, and the one of his time is named as Mernephtah by the historians.
- His people rejected the signs wrongfully and arrogantly, though they were convinced of them in their hearts.
- Their end was drowning in public, while Musa and the believers watched, and the verse calls the reader to look at it.

104.text:
The words of the messenger to the king are given now. "And Moses said, “O Pharaoh! I am truly a messenger from the Lord of all worlds"

### Phrase by phrase

**"And Moses said, “O Pharaoh! I am truly a messenger from the Lord of all worlds"** is his opening declaration. The One who sent him is the Creator, the Lord and the King of all things, and there is nothing outside His dominion. The account describes a debate that took place between Musa and Pharaoh, and the plainest of the matters raised in it was this claim of a message from the Lord of everything.

**"from the Lord of all worlds"** is the whole of the argument in a few words. A messenger does not come with a private word or with a claim of his own. He comes from the one who owns everything he is speaking about, and that is why the demand that follows carries weight.

Pharaoh did not accept the claim. In the report of his answer given in the Book, he told Musa plainly that he was lying, and the debate then turned on the proof rather than on the words. The matter was raised in the presence of Pharaoh and his people, and that is why the account insists on the open and public nature of everything that came next.

### In short

- Musa opened with a plain statement of who had sent him, the Creator and Lord of all things.
- The claim to a message from the Lord of all worlds is the foundation of everything he demands afterwards.
- Pharaoh met the claim with a flat denial and called him a liar.
- The exchange happened in front of Pharaoh's people, so the proofs that followed were seen by many.

105.text:
The demand that goes with the message is stated. "obliged to say nothing about Allah except the truth. Indeed, I have come to you with clear proof from your Lord, so let the children of Israel go with me.”"

### Phrase by phrase

**"obliged to say nothing about Allah except the truth"** carries the sense of a duty laid on him by his position. Since the message given to the prophets is a sacred trust, it is a great sin to tamper with it, and every one of the prophets is free of sin and cannot do such a thing. What he says of Allah is therefore only what he was given to say, and no part of it can be adjusted to please a listener.

**"Indeed, I have come to you with clear proof from your Lord"** moves from the claim to the evidence. The proof he brought was an unequivocal sign that Allah had given him, and it stood as evidence that what he was conveying was the truth. Musa argued from two directions at once. His truthfulness was beyond question, since he had never spoken a lie in his life, and the miracles in his hand were a clear proof of the claim to prophethood.

To Pharaoh in the land of Egypt, **"so let the children of Israel go with me"** is the thing he asked for, and it is the demand that runs through the whole account. The demand was that they be released from slavery and from the treatment they had been under, and that they be allowed to leave with him. In one reading the words include their property, both the greater part of it and the smaller, and in another the destination is named as Syria. They were the offspring of an honourable prophet, Isra'il, who is Ya'qub the son of Ishaq the son of Ibrahim, the intimate friend of Allah, and the command was simply that they be allowed to worship their Lord and his Lord.

The children of Israel had spent a long time under the hand of the Egyptians. In one account the call of Musa in the land lasted forty years before the command came for the migration, and the request for their release was the first step of it.

### In short

- Musa states the duty that binds him, that a prophet says nothing of Allah except what he was given.
- The message is a sacred trust, and tampering with it is a sin the prophets are kept free of.
- He brings a clear proof, and he argues both from his own truthfulness and from the sign in his hand.
- He asks for the release of the Children of Israel from slavery so that they may worship their Lord.
- They were the descendants of Ya'qub, called Isra'il, the son of Ishaq and the son of Ibrahim.

106.text:
The answer of the king is obstinacy dressed as an offer to be convinced. "Pharaoh said, “If you have come with a sign, then bring it if what you say is true.”"

### Phrase by phrase

**"Pharaoh said"** introduces the reply of the king of Egypt to everything that had been said. He would not believe what he had heard, and he would not entertain the request that had been put to him.

**"If you have come with a sign, then bring it if what you say is true"** turns the matter into a test he sets. The words are the speech of a man who wants the proof produced so that he can judge the claim for himself, and the demand came out of his stubbornness rather than out of any readiness to accept the answer. There was no interest in the message itself, and no thought of the release that had been asked for. All that remained was the challenge, and the signs that followed were given in answer to it.

### In short

- Pharaoh refused both the message and the request that went with it.
- He demanded the sign be produced, so that he could judge the claim himself.
- The demand came out of obstinacy, not out of any readiness to believe.
- The proof that followed was given in direct answer to his challenge.

107.text:
The first sign is given in the sight of everyone present. "So Moses threw down his staff and—behold!—it became a real snake"

### Phrase by phrase

**"So Moses threw down his staff"** records the response to the challenge. He did what was asked of him and cast the staff on the ground.

**"and—behold!—it became a real snake"** describes what happened to it. The word used for the creature here means a huge serpent, and it is used of a male snake. Ibn Abbas explained it that way on the authority of Ali bin Abi Talhah, and As-Suddi and Ad-Dahhak said the same.

The description given of it was reported at length. On one account the staff became a serpent of great size. It opened its mouth and rushed towards Pharaoh. When he saw the snake coming at him, he jumped from his throne and cried out to Musa for help, asking him to take the creature out of his way, and Musa did so. As-Suddi gave the scene in more detail. The snake opened its mouth and headed for Pharaoh to swallow him, and it put its lower jaw on the ground while its upper jaw reached the top of the wall of the palace. At the sight of it Pharaoh was so frightened that he jumped up and lost control of himself, which had never happened to him before that moment. He cried out that Musa should take it away, and that he would believe in him and release the Children of Israel to him. Musa took the snake, and it turned back into a staff.

In the historical traditions reported on the authority of Ibn Abbas, the movement of the serpent towards Pharaoh was so violent that many of the courtiers around him died of extreme fear.

**Why the miracle was described as clear.** The word used as the description of the snake means clear or prominent, and the choice of it is telling. The event took place openly before the eyes of the people of Pharaoh, and it was not performed in a hidden place in the manner of the magicians. The transformation of a staff into a real serpent is not in itself impossible, and what makes it astonishing is that it is unusual. A miracle has to be an act beyond the power of an ordinary person, and Allah shows such acts through His prophets so that people may understand that they carry a divine support and are true prophets of Allah.

### In short

- Musa cast down the staff as the answer to the challenge, and it became a huge male serpent.
- Ibn Abbas, As-Suddi and Ad-Dahhak all described the creature as a male snake, and the reports are agreed on its size.
- On the reported account the serpent rushed at Pharaoh, whose terror made him jump from his throne and call on Musa to remove it.
- In As-Suddi's report its lower jaw rested on the ground while its upper jaw reached the palace wall, and Pharaoh promised to believe and to release the Children of Israel.
- The word describing it means clear, since the sign was worked openly before the eyes of the people and not in the manner of the magicians.

108.text:
The second sign follows at once. "Then he drew his hand ˹out of his collar˺ and it was ˹shining˺ white for all to see"

### Phrase by phrase

**"Then he drew his hand"** uses a word that means pulling something out of another thing with force. Musa applied some strength as he brought his hand out. The verse does not name the place he drew it from, and other verses supply it. In one place the command is to put the hand under the robe (27:12), and in another to put it under the arm (20:22), so the hand came out from under his arm or from under his shirt.

**"and it was ˹shining˺ white for all to see"** describes the state of the hand. The word means white, and whiteness of the hand can also come from a disease. That is why the Book says in two other places that the hand comes out white without hurt, which removes any suspicion of leprosy (27:12 and 28:32). Ibn Abbas said that the words without hurt mean that the change was not caused by leprosy, and Mujahid and several others said the same. Musa put his hand back into his sleeve and it returned to its normal colour.

A tradition reported from Ibn Abbas adds what kind of whiteness this was. It was not the whiteness of an ordinary change of colour. It carried a light that lit up everything around it, and the word used for those who saw it means the onlookers, which shows how striking the sight was, since people gathered to look at it.

**The two signs together.** Musa performed two miracles at that meeting in answer to the demand of Pharaoh. The first was the change of the staff into a serpent, and the second was the drawing out of his hand with light coming from it. The first worked as a warning for those who would not believe, and the second was set out as an invitation to the truth, since it showed that the message of Musa was a light, and that following it would lead people to lasting success.

### In short

- The word for drawing out the hand carries the sense of pulling it out with force.
- Other verses place the hand under the robe or under the arm, and the Book leaves the exact place unstated here.
- The whiteness was not of an ordinary kind, since the reports from Ibn Abbas say it carried a light that lit up the surroundings.
- The Book adds the words without hurt in other places to remove the thought of leprosy, and the hand returned to its normal colour afterwards.
- The serpent served as a warning and the shining hand as an invitation, and the two together showed that the message was light.

109.text:
The court takes up the challenge and puts a name to what it has seen. "The chiefs of Pharaoh’s people said, “He is indeed a skilled magician"

### Phrase by phrase

**"The chiefs of Pharaoh’s people said"** names the speakers. The word used for them means the influential chiefs and the leading men, and the noblemen of his people agreed with the judgement Pharaoh had passed.

**"He is indeed a skilled magician"** is the verdict they reached. They were ignorant of the divine power of Allah and had seen nothing in their lives but the charms of the sorcerers, so there was nothing else they could say. Their addition of the word meaning knowing shows the impression the signs had made on them, since they were admitting that what Musa had done could not be performed by an ordinary magician. They were saying that he was a sorcerer of great knowledge.

**How a miracle differs from sorcery.** The two are distinct in their nature and their effect, and the difference does not need much explaining to anyone who applies common sense. The sorcerers usually live in impurity, and the more unclean and impure they are, the more successful they are held to be in their sorcery, while the prophets are by nature the cleanest and purest of people. Another clear distinction is that a sorcerer never succeeds when he makes a claim to prophethood. Then there is the working of the acts themselves. What is done under sorcery does have physical causes like everything else, and the only difference is that those causes are hidden from ordinary people, who then take the effect to be happening without any cause at all. Miracles are a direct manifestation of the power of Allah and have nothing to do with physical causes. That is why the Qur'an ascribes them directly to Allah and not to the prophets, and why it says of the pebbles thrown at Badr that it was Allah who threw them.

So the people of Pharaoh themselves felt that the signs of Musa were not like the ordinary acts of sorcerers. They went on accusing him of sorcery, and in the same breath they admitted that he was of great knowledge. That admission means they knew his act was not on the level of what the sorcerers did.

### What the chiefs did next

After Pharaoh had recovered himself and returned to his throne, he said to the leading men of his people that Musa was a well-versed sorcerer, and they agreed with him. They then took counsel among themselves about what should be done. They conspired to put out the light he had brought and to bring his word down. They plotted to present him as a liar and an impostor, and what they feared was that he would draw people to his side by what they called his magic, and so overcome them and drive them out of their land. What they feared came to pass, exactly as another verse says, that Allah let Pharaoh and Haman and their hosts receive from them the very thing they were afraid of (28:6).

### In short

- The leading men of Pharaoh agreed with his judgement and described Musa as a sorcerer of great knowledge.
- Their word knowing shows they admitted the act was beyond what an ordinary magician could do.
- Sorcery works through hidden physical causes and sorcerers live in impurity, while miracles are the direct power of Allah with no cause behind them but His will.
- No sorcerer has ever succeeded in making a claim to prophethood, and the Book ascribes miracles to Allah alone, as with the pebbles at Badr.
- The chiefs made common cause with Pharaoh on the matter, and what they feared most was that Musa would take the people and the land from them.

110.text:
The verdict is given its political shape, and the king turns to his advisers. "who seeks to drive you from your land.” ˹So Pharaoh asked,˺ “What do you propose?”"

### Phrase by phrase

**"who seeks to drive you from your land"** is the charge they built on the name of sorcery. The land is Egypt, and the claim was that Musa intended by his magic to drive them all out of it. In one reading the thought was put more plainly still, that he wanted to remove them from the land and take it for himself and his people.

**"What do you propose?"** is Pharaoh's question to the chiefs, and in another reading the words are what do you command, which is the speech of a king who wants his advisers to name the measure rather than decide it themselves. The consultation that followed was the planning of a plot, and the verses that come after this one report what they settled on.

### What the passage shows about the leaders of a people

A prophet's discourse is addressed first to the leaders of the day, to those who hold the leadership of thought in their surroundings. Such people are often better placed than anyone else to understand the message in its depth, since they have the minds for it. What history shows instead is that they are almost always set against the call.

The way they work is worth setting out. They use their talents to put a wrong meaning into the message. A sign that came by the intervention of God is declared to have come by the force of magic, and to turn people further away, the whole movement is given a political colour, with the claim that these preachers are simply seeking power. The general public cannot examine such talk on its own, and the result is that they grow suspicious of the truth they were being offered.

To raise such points against the messenger of the truth is a great crime. The leading men of a people may hold on to their leadership by it, but the price they pay is the Hereafter, since God is the Truth, and a man who comes forward in the name of God has no room to speak of anything else. Such a man is bound to truth and to justice. Whoever does otherwise has lost the right to represent God and deserves punishment rather than reward.

Musa had been sent to the Children of Israel and also to Pharaoh and his community of Copts. The Children of Israel had many weaknesses at that time, but they stood with Musa in the main. Pharaoh and his people, apart from a few of them, refused him. At the end of the whole struggle, after the years of calling them, Musa was commanded to leave Egypt with the Children of Israel, and he asked Pharaoh to let them go so that they could pray to the one and only God in the open air. Musa was the bearer of the truth, and Pharaoh counted him a mere worker of magic and set out to overcome him through his own magicians.

### In short

- The charge against Musa was that he wanted to drive the Egyptians out of their own land.
- Pharaoh put the question of a measure to his advisers, and the consultation was the beginning of a plot.
- A prophet speaks first to the leading men of his people, since they are the ones best placed to weigh what he says.
- Those leaders usually meet the call by twisting it, calling the sign magic, and giving the movement a political colour.
- The general public, unable to examine the charge, is left suspicious, while the leaders keep their standing at the cost of the Hereafter.
- Musa was sent to the Children of Israel and to Pharaoh's people together, and Pharaoh set out to meet him with his own magicians.

111.text:
The advisers give their answer, and it is a delay rather than a judgement. "They replied, “Let him and his brother wait and send mobilizers to all cities"

### Phrase by phrase

**"They replied"** records the answer of the chiefs and the noblemen to the question Pharaoh had put to them. They did not speak of the message, and they did not speak of the signs, and they did not speak of the Children of Israel. The whole of their answer was a proposal about how to handle the two men.

**"Let him and his brother wait"** is the first part of it. The sense given by Ibn Abbas is that the words mean delay him for a time, and in one reading the instruction is not to kill them. The brother named here is Aaron, and in the Arabic the two are named together as Musa and his brother, since Aaron was his brother in blood and his partner in the mission.

**"and send mobilizers to all cities"** is the second part. The cities meant are the areas and the provinces of the kingdom, and the men to be sent into them are summoners or soldiers, whose work was to gather the magicians from the different lands and bring them in.

**What they were counting on.** The land of Egypt at that time was a place where magic was the trade of the day. What the words of their counsel say is that the whole trade could be gathered in one place, widespread and followed with honour, and the sorcerers held a high standing among the people. The men around Pharaoh had the idea that what Musa had brought was a kind of magic like the magic their own sorcerers practised. That assumption was wrong from the beginning, and because of it they gathered the whole trade together in order to defeat what he had shown them. In their thinking the difficulty was one of skill, and a greater skill would settle it.

The verses of this passage tell the remaining part of the account of Musa, which reaches its end forty years after he first came to the land. What had happened should have been enough to convince Pharaoh and to bring him to believe, since a staff had turned into a serpent and a hand had come out shining white. Instead the wrongdoers turned to false readings of what they had seen, so that they could cover the truth up. Pharaoh and his people gave the lie to Musa and said to the people that he was a great sorcerer who wanted to drive them out of their homes and take the rule of the country for himself.

The Book records their proposal in the words of those who made it, and it records where the plan led, since the appointment for the contest was set as the whole of this passage goes on to describe.

### In short

- The advisers answered with a plan and left the message and the signs untouched.
- Their first counsel was to delay the matter, and in one reading not to put the two men to death.
- The brother named with Musa is Aaron, who shared the mission with him.
- They asked for summoners to be sent through the provinces of the kingdom to gather the magicians of every land.
- Their hope rested on the strength of the magic of their time, and on the belief that what Musa had brought was magic of the same kind.

112.text:
The purpose of the gathering is stated in the closing words of the passage. "to bring you every clever magician.”"

### Phrase by phrase

**"to bring you every clever magician"** gives the errand of the men sent out. The word for the magician here carries the sense of one who is cunning and practised in his craft, and a variant reading makes it stronger still, so that the sense is a sorcerer who outdoes the rest. The whole of the kingdom's skill was to be brought to one place.

**What Musa was given, and why.** The signs that Musa was sent with belong to a pattern. The practice of Allah with His prophets follows a rule. Each is given miracles that answer the demand of his own time. In the time of the prophet Isa, the Greek thought and the sciences of medicine stood at their highest, so his signs were of that kind. He opened the eyes of those born blind, and a leper was cured the moment his hand touched him. When the Holy Prophet ﷺ came, the Arabs took their pride in eloquence and in what they could do with the language. The Qur'an was therefore given as the greatest of all his miracles. The time of Musa in Egypt was ruled by sorcery and by the repute of the sorcerers, and what he was given was greater than all of the spells they could gather, so that the people might see for themselves that the master of the craft could not stand against the messenger of Allah.

Their own account of the appointment is given in the Book. They said that they could produce magic the like of what he had shown, and they asked for a meeting between them, to be kept by both sides, in an open place where neither would have an advantage. Musa named the day of the festival, with the people assembled when the sun had risen, and Pharaoh withdrew, devised his plot and came back (20:58-60).

**What the two verses leave in place.** The scene is set for the contest between the messenger and the gathered magicians, and the gathering itself had been ordered by the very men who claimed his proof was only magic. The two verses close by putting every skilled sorcerer in the land under one roof, and the next verses show what came of it.

### In short

- The men sent out were to bring every cunning and practised sorcerer from the lands of the kingdom.
- A variant reading carries the sense of a sorcerer who surpasses the others, which is what the contest required.
- Prophets are sent with miracles that answer the demand of their own time, as Isa was given the cure of the blind and the leper when medicine stood at its height.
- The Arabs took pride in eloquence, so the Qur'an was given as the greatest of the miracles of the Prophet ﷺ.
- The Book reports their own claim that they could match his magic, and the meeting was set for the festival day at sunrise (20:58-60).

113.text:
The whole trade is assembled and the first thing its masters do is bargain. "The magicians came to Pharaoh, saying, “Shall we receive a ˹suitable˺ reward if we prevail?”"

### Phrase by phrase

**"The magicians came to Pharaoh"** records the gathering that the summons through the provinces had produced. They were seventy in number by one count, brought in from the towns and the districts of the kingdom, and they came to the king at his call.

**"saying, “Shall we receive a ˹suitable˺ reward if we prevail?”"** is what they said when they arrived. The question is a plain request for a wage, and the words put it as a condition, that there would be a gift for them if they came out of the contest as the victors.

Pharaoh met them with what he could offer without giving away anything of his own. He told them that they would have their reward, and that he would give them tremendous provisions. He set that hope before them, and he added the promise of a place among his private audience and his closest associates, which in a court of that kind carried more weight than the money did.

What their opening words say is that the outcome was to them a matter of business. The day set for the meeting was the day of the festival, with the people gathered when the sun had risen (20:59). One report adds a conversation that took place before the contest. Musa spoke with the chief of the sorcerers and asked him whether they would accept the faith if he defeated them. The man answered that there was no question of their being defeated, since their powers were such that no one could overcome them, and he added that if the outcome went the other way, they would declare their faith openly in the presence of Pharaoh. The bargain struck with the king and the wager offered by the messenger were both on the table before a single staff had been thrown.

### In short

- The magicians gathered at Pharaoh's call, and one count gives their number as seventy.
- Their first words were a bargain, since they asked what reward would be theirs if they won.
- Pharaoh promised them a reward, generous provision, and a place among those closest to him.
- One report has Musa asking their chief beforehand whether a defeat would bring them to the faith.
- The chief answered that defeat was not a thing he could imagine, and that if it came they would declare their faith openly before the king.

114.text:
The king's answer is given in one short sentence. "He replied, “Yes, and you will certainly be among those closest to me.”"

### Phrase by phrase

**"He replied, “Yes"** settles the bargain without any haggling. He confirmed the reward they had asked about, and the promise was given in full.

**"and you will certainly be among those closest to me"** goes past the money. The words mean that they would belong to the circle brought near, and the Book describes the whole exchange in a few sentences. In another account the promise was put in the same terms, that they would surely be among those brought near (26:109). The point for the record is the weight of the offer and the smallness of what it was offered for, since a court place and a private standing were being used to buy a verdict in a matter of truth.

**What his promises were for.** Pharaoh had collected the magicians to defeat Musa, and everything he said to them was directed at that end. He told them there would be a reward and gave them large assurances, so that their hopes would be fixed on what they wished for, and he made them among his closest associates and his best companions, so that their standing in the court would be tied to his project. When they were assured of his promises, they went to the contest with the whole of their craft and with the whole of their ambition in the same scale.

The matter was the easier for him to arrange because the land had already decided what it thought of the signs. The people of Pharaoh had given the lie to Musa, had called him a great sorcerer, and had said that he wanted to take the rule of the country from them. So the man who set the reward was the man who had already framed the charge, and the magicians were brought in to confirm a verdict that had been reached before they arrived.

### The sign in the bargain

There is a lesson in the shape of this exchange. The truth came to those people with proofs that no craft could match, and the men who were asked to answer it were offered money and rank to speak against it. The offer worked on them, and the reason it worked is written plainly in the account of what happened afterwards. A person who sets his hope on what a king can give him will meet the clearest proof in the world and still stand against it.

### In short

- Pharaoh granted the reward at once, without any negotiation.
- He added a place among those brought near him, which was worth more in that court than the money.
- The promises were made for one purpose, to secure a victory over Musa.
- He gave them long assurances so that their hopes would be fixed on what they wished for.
- The men who promised the reward had already called Musa a sorcerer and accused him of wanting the kingdom, so the verdict was bought in advance.

115.text:
The two sides meet, and the courtesy of the messenger gives the first move away. "They asked, “O Moses! Will you cast, or shall we be the first to cast?”"

### Phrase by phrase

**"They asked, “O Moses! Will you cast"** puts the choice to him. The word used here for casting means to drop something down, and the question is about which side would drop what it carried first.

**"or shall we be the first to cast?”"** is the other half of the question, and in another place the same words are given as or we be the first to throw (20:65). Their manner of speaking shows what was in their minds. They were certain they would win, since their pride in their craft had made the result a settled thing in their eyes, and the question was put as one who expects to be answered in his own favour. The wording also shows that they wanted to begin. By putting the choice to their opponent, they kept up the appearance of giving him the honour of the first move, while the flow of the sentence made their own wish plain.

**The size of the thing they were about to throw.** On the day of the meeting they threw down their ropes and their staffs, and the count given in one account is seventy staffs and seventy ropes. The same number is given again in the account of the staffs alone, seventy of them thrown at once. Their hope was that the mass of them, moving together, would settle the matter before Musa had even begun.

**What a prophet does when he is opposed.** The answer Musa gave is treated as a model in the account. A prophet does not take the first step in a hostile action against the people who oppose him. Even at the last moment he gives his opponents the chance to open the fighting, and once they have taken that responsibility on themselves, he uses the power he has been given to bring them down. It is worth putting the two sides of that side by side, since it applies to the message as much as to the contest. In setting out the religion and calling people to it, the prophet is the one who begins, and he takes the first step every time. When the matter turns into an attack, the first move is left to the other side.

### In short

- The magicians put the choice to Musa, of who would drop what they carried first.
- The phrasing shows both their confidence and their wish to begin.
- Their pride in their art had made victory a settled thing in their own minds.
- One count of what they threw comes to seventy staffs and seventy ropes.
- A prophet does not start a fight, and he leaves the first hostile move to the other side, though in calling people to the truth he is always the one who begins.

116.text:
The messenger gives way, the craft puts on its full display, and then everything is answered. "Moses said, “You first.” So when they did, they deceived the eyes of the people, stunned them, and made a great display of magic"

### Phrase by phrase

**"Moses said, “You first.”"** is the answer, and it is a command that lets them go before him. Musa behaved towards them with courtesy by inviting them to take their turn first, and the effect of that courtesy was that they accepted the faith after they were defeated. So the giving of the first move was not a concession made out of weakness. It was the manner of a man who had nothing to fear.

A question comes up at this point. Sorcery is an unlawful act, and when it is used against a prophet sent by Allah it becomes an act of disbelief. How then did Musa give permission for magic by telling them to go ahead? The answer follows from what the contest was. It was certain that they would put their magic on show by one means or another, and the only matter in question was who would begin. Since the point of the conversation was the order of turns and nothing else, permitting them to go first was no part of the magic itself.

There was an advantage in it besides. The people could watch the performance to the end, and the sorcerers had all the time they needed to work their craft and to turn their staffs into snakes. Only after that was the staff of Musa to become a serpent and swallow the whole of what they had made, so that the defeat of magic stood out openly in front of everyone. The truth came at the very moment the crowd was waiting for it, and that made it more striking to their hearts than it would have been at the start.

**"So when they did, they deceived the eyes of the people, stunned them, and made a great display of magic"** describes what they produced. The number of things thrown was seventy of the staffs alone. The words say that they cast a spell on the eyes of the people. They frightened and overawed them, and they came out with a mighty sorcery, which in one reading means a plain lie. Ibn Abbas said that they threw thick ropes and long sticks, and that these appeared to be crawling, an illusion that their magic created.

**Where the craft could reach and where it could not.** The verse makes plain that the display was a bewitching of the eyes of the onlookers. The people were made to see the staffs and the strings as snakes leaping on the ground, while the things themselves did not change in their nature. It was a form of influence on the minds of those watching. The fear that Musa felt at that moment is recorded in the Book, together with the answer given to him. He was told not to fear. He would have the upper hand. He was to throw what was in his right hand, and it would swallow up what they had made. What they had made was only the trick of a magician, and no magician is successful however much skill he may reach (20:67-69).

None of that settles the question of what magic can do in general. The account here does not prove that sorcery is confined to the deceiving of eyes, and there is no proof against the other forms either. Many kinds of magic are taken to be real in their effects. The words magic and sorcery are applied to all acts that appear to happen in an unusual way. Sleight of hand belongs to that list, and so does an influence on a distant mind, and the holding of a gaze. The change of one thing into another by such means may be possible, and no valid evidence has been produced either for it or against it.

### Why the display was allowed to run its course

The whole scene had been arranged so that the contrast could be seen. The sorcerers were given the festival day, the assembled people, and the time to do everything their art could do. Their craft was the pride of Egypt at that time, and the minds of the people were held by it. That is why the miracle Musa was given was of that same field, so that the master of it could not be mistaken for the truth. The sticks and the ropes were turned into what looked like snakes before the eyes of a nation, and then a real serpent opened its mouth and swallowed them on the ground. What the people saw with their own eyes in that hour settled what no argument could have settled, and the men who had been bought with a court place were the first to bow.

### In short

- Musa told them to throw first, and his courtesy towards them was among the things that later brought them to the faith.
- His permission had nothing to do with the magic itself, since the contest was settled and the only question was the order of turns.
- Their display came first so that the defeat of their craft would be open and unmistakable in front of the whole nation.
- What they did was a bewitching of the eyes, since the staffs and ropes only appeared to be snakes, and Ibn Abbas described them as thick ropes and long sticks made to look as though they crawled.
- Fear came over Musa at the sight, and he was told not to fear, that what they had made was a trick, and that no magician succeeds, however great his skill (20:67-69).
- The passage does not decide how far sorcery can really go, and the kinds of it that are taken to have real effects are left undecided for lack of proof either way.

117.text:
The moment that separated the two comes now. "Then We inspired Moses, “Throw down your staff,” and—behold!—it devoured the objects of their illusion"

### Phrase by phrase

**"Then We inspired Moses, “Throw down your staff"** gives the instruction at the height of the contest. It was a tremendous moment, and it was the moment in which Allah set the truth apart from the falsehood. The revelation came to His servant and messenger with the order to throw the staff he was holding in his right hand.

**"and—behold!—it devoured the objects of their illusion"** is what happened when he threw it. The staff swallowed straight away everything they had put on show, which was the magic they had used to make their trick appear real when it had no reality in it at all. The account here begins with verse 117 of this surah.

**What the reports add to the scene.** Ibn Abbas said that the staff of Musa swallowed all the ropes and the sticks that the magicians had thrown. Muhammad bin Ishaq described the way it happened, that the staff followed the ropes and the sticks one after another, until nothing the sorcerers had thrown was left. Then Musa took it in his hand, and it turned back into a stick as it was at the first.

Al-Qasim bin Abi Bazzah gave the same event with more of its detail. He said that when Musa threw the staff it became a huge serpent, plain for all to see, and it opened its mouth and swallowed the ropes and sticks of the magicians. It was at that point that the magicians went down in prostration, and they did not raise their heads until they had been shown the Garden, the Fire, and the recompense that belongs to the people of each. Thousands of staffs and ropes had been turned into snakes leaping across the ground, and the crowd stood stunned and bewildered at the sight, and within no time at all the great snake had eaten every one of them.

### In short

- The order came by revelation at the height of the contest, and it was the moment that set truth apart from falsehood.
- The staff swallowed the whole of the illusion the magicians had put on show.
- Ibn Abbas said the staff took all the ropes and sticks, and Ibn Ishaq that it followed them one after another until nothing remained.
- The report of Al-Qasim bin Abi Bazzah adds that it became a huge serpent that opened its mouth and swallowed what they had thrown.
- The magicians went down in prostration at that sight, and the crowd stood stunned as the last of the snakes was eaten.

118.text:
The verdict of the contest is stated in one sentence. "So the truth prevailed and their illusions failed"

### Phrase by phrase

**"So the truth prevailed"** says that the case was settled in its favour. Another reading of the words gives the sense that the matter became clear, that Musa was in the right, and that what he had said was shown to be true by what the people had seen with their own eyes.

**"and their illusions failed"** gives the other side of it. Their sorcery came to nothing, and the work they had done with such confidence turned out to have no weight at all. The word used here carries the sense of a thing that fizzles away and leaves nothing behind.

**Why the two halves belong together.** The contest had been arranged so that the difference could be seen rather than argued. What the magicians had done was an illusion laid over the eyes of the crowd, and the thing itself stayed as it was. What Musa was given was a real change in the creature, and when the two met in the same field of sight, one of them ate the other. There was nothing left for argument afterwards. The truth was confirmed by the event itself, and the craft that had been the pride of the land stood empty in front of everybody.

### In short

- The words state that the truth came out clear and established, and that Musa was shown to be in the right.
- The sorcery of the magicians was made vain and came to nothing.
- What they had done was an illusion over the eyes, while what Musa was given was a real change in the creature.
- When the two were set side by side in the same field, the illusion was swallowed whole.
- The case was settled by what the people saw, and the craft of the land stood empty in front of them.

119.text:
The outcome for the court is named. "So Pharaoh and his people were defeated right there and put to shame"

### Phrase by phrase

**"So Pharaoh and his people were defeated right there"** fixes the place of the defeat. It happened in the assembly, in the open place where the meeting had been set, and the word has the sense of being overcome on the spot without any room to recover.

**"and put to shame"** gives the second half of the sentence. It is not enough to lose a contest. The loss here carried humiliation with it, since the whole weight of the kingdom and the whole of its pride in the craft had been put into the gathering, and it was the king's own men who went down.

The defeat was also the defeat of the magicians, who had come to the assembly sure of themselves and sure of the reward Musa would never give them. They were beaten and humbled in front of the nation they had been brought to impress, and the king who hired them was humbled with them, since the two had staked everything on the same plan. So the verse gathers both parties into one sentence, since the plan had been made in one place, and it was broken in one place.

### In short

- The defeat came on the spot, in the assembly where the contest had been arranged.
- The humiliation is named alongside the loss, since the whole of the kingdom's pride had been placed in that gathering.
- The magicians were beaten in front of the nation they had been brought to impress.
- The king who hired them was humbled with them, and both are gathered into the one sentence.

120.text:
The men who had been bought with a court place do the opposite of what was asked of them. "And the magicians fell down, prostrating"

### Phrase by phrase

**"And the magicians fell down, prostrating"** records what they did at the sight. One reading of the words is that they went down so quickly that it looked as though they had fallen rather than lowered themselves, and the sense of it is a surrender that could not wait.

**What brought them down.** When they saw the greatness of the power of Allah and the clear signs in front of them, they had nothing left to do but go down before Him. Their own position in the matter was the one that made the sight decisive. Theirs was the craft of Egypt, and they were the masters of it, so they knew better than anyone where its limits lay. Since the work of Musa was outside every one of those limits, they understood that what they were watching was not magic at all. It was prophethood, and the difference was plain to the men who had spent their lives in the trade.

The account also carries another sense, that the prostration was a favour placed in them at the very hour they were expected to fight.

### What the defeat of magic did to the whole picture

The men who had come for a reward had known of the message of Musa beforehand. His calling in Egypt went on for about forty years, and this contest came in the last stage of it, so the name was not new to them. What had not yet gone was the veil over their eyes, and when they saw his superiority in the very field they had made their own, that veil was torn away at once.

What they saw in that hour was how small human devices are, even at their most complete, and how great God is. From then on Pharaoh and all his authority counted for nothing with them. The men who had asked for a reward before the contest treated the threat of the worst punishment afterwards as a thing of no account.

### In short

- The magicians went down at once, and one reading has them falling rather than lowering themselves in the usual way.
- They knew the limits of their own craft, and the work of Musa stood outside every one of them, so they recognized prophethood and not magic.
- On one reading the prostration itself was a favour placed in them by Allah at that hour.
- The calling of Musa in Egypt had lasted about forty years before this contest, so the message was not new to them.
- What the sight did was to show them the smallness of human devices and the greatness of God, and after that Pharaoh and his authority counted for nothing with them.

121.text:
The confession of the gathered sorcerers is reported in their own words. "They declared, “We ˹now˺ believe in the Lord of all worlds—"

### Phrase by phrase

**"They declared, “We ˹now˺ believe in the Lord of all worlds"** is the declaration they made as they came up from the prostration. The words were spoken in front of the king and in front of the nation, and they were spoken by the men who had been hired to defeat the messenger.

The confession is also a statement about whom they were leaving. In one report Pharaoh heard the words and shot back a question at them, asking whether they were referring to him. He had presented himself to the people as their lord, and the craft that had been hired for his sake was now raising a claim about who owned the worlds, so the question came out of him before anything else did.

The reason the words carried that force is set out plainly in another place. Those men knew that what they had witnessed with the staff could not have been done by sorcery. Every kind of trick in their field had just been eaten in front of them, and the conclusion was not a matter of argument any more. What they had seen was a sign from the Lord of everything, and the first thing to do was to say so out loud.

### In short

- The declaration was made openly before the king and the nation, by the men who had been hired to defeat Musa.
- Their belief was in the Lord of all worlds, which set them against every claim of the king beside him.
- Pharaoh heard the words and asked whether they meant him, since he had set himself up as the lord of the people.
- The magicians knew that what they had seen with the staff was beyond the whole of their craft.
- What they witnessed left nothing to argue about, and their first act was to say plainly what they believed.

122.text:
The last words of their declaration name the two men in front of them. "the Lord of Moses and Aaron.”"

### Phrase by phrase

**"the Lord of Moses and Aaron"** is added after the words about the Lord of all worlds, and the addition has a purpose. It makes it clear that the Lord worshipped by Musa and by Harun is in fact the Lord of the universe. The words also mark the difference between them and the king. Pharaoh had pretended to be the lord of his people, and the magicians named the two men whom he had set himself against as the servants of the true Lord.

**Aaron in the account.** His name comes here beside his brother's, as it does in the account of the mission and in the answer to the call. The two of them stood before the king together, and the confession of the magicians names them together, which is the plain way to make a statement about who sent them and whom they serve.

**What the verse settles.** The men who make this declaration had come for a reward and left with their prostrations. What they said in these two verses outlasted everything the court could do afterwards. Their words also mark the end of the ground the king had built on. He had claimed the lordship of the land, and his own hired men now named the Lord of all worlds, the Lord of Musa and of Aaron, in front of the whole nation. The rest of the account reports what he did about it, and how little it moved them.

### In short

- The name of Aaron is joined to that of Musa, so the Lord they worship is named as the Lord of both.
- The addition makes plain that the Lord of the two men is the Lord of the whole universe.
- The words mark the break with the king, who had pretended to be the lord of his people.
- The men who had come for a reward left the ground with their declaration of faith, and it outlasted everything the court did afterwards.
- The king's own hired men named the Lord of all worlds before the whole nation, and the account goes on to show how little his answer moved them.

123.text:
The king answers the prostration with a threat, and he dresses the whole thing up as a plot. "Pharaoh threatened, “How dare you believe in him before I give you permission? This must be a conspiracy you devised in the city to drive out its people, but soon you will see"

### Phrase by phrase

**"Pharaoh threatened, “How dare you believe in him before I give you permission?"** is his opening charge. The whole of the matter stood differently in the two minds. To the king, the acceptance of the messenger was a thing that needed his leave, and the belief of the magicians was an act of disobedience to him personally. To the magicians, it was a sign that had reached them from their Lord, and it was not his to give or to withhold. It is always the way of a proud man in power, that his own opinion is put above the arguments and the proofs, and such people are never moved to accept the truth.

**"This must be a conspiracy you devised in the city to drive out its people"** is the charge he built on it. He proclaimed to the people that the defeat of the magicians had come about because they had plotted with Musa and agreed to it together. He said of Musa in another place that he was their chief who had taught them magic (20:71). The claim was a lie, and the king and every man of sense in that court knew it was a lie. Musa had come back from Madyan and was a stranger in Egypt, the magicians had been gathered from the towns of the land at the king's own command, they had been promised rewards by him, and Musa had never seen or met any of them before the day of the contest. He knew all of that, and he said what he said to deceive the ordinary people of the kingdom.

The Book describes him as a man who fooled his people and found them obedient (43:54). A people who accepted his word when he said that he was their lord, the most high (79:24), are among the most ignorant and the most misguided of the creatures of Allah.

What the words about driving out its people were meant to accomplish is plain. The charge was that the magicians and Musa had joined hands to gain influence and power, so that the chiefs and the masters of the land would be replaced by them, and the rule of the state would pass into their hands. Nothing of that had ever been said by Musa. He had asked for one thing only, which was that the Children of Israel be allowed to go with him.

**"but soon you will see"** ends the sentence with the thing he did not yet name. It is an indefinite threat, and the next verse spells it out.

### What the reports say about how it began

As-Suddi reported that Ibn Mas'ud and Ibn Abbas and several other Companions said the following. Musa met the leader of the magicians and asked him whether he would believe in him and bear witness that what he had brought was the truth, if Musa defeated him. The man answered that on the next day he would produce a kind of magic that could not be beaten by any other magic, and he swore that if Musa defeated him he would believe in him and testify to his truth. Pharaoh was watching the two of them, and that is why he said what he said about a plot.

**What the declaration did to the country.** Some historical reports say that after the magicians declared their faith, six hundred thousand more people followed them and declared their belief in Allah. Before the open contest there had been only two individuals in the land who believed. So a great number of people entered the faith in a single day, and the position of the king became an awkward one from the moment it happened.

He handled it the way a clever politician handles such things. He hid what he felt from the people and turned the ground under himself into firm footing again by putting the charge of conspiracy and rebellion on the magicians. In one stroke the contest became a plot, the miracle became a scheme, and the men who had stood in front of the nation as their own were presented as traitors who had conspired with Musa and Harun to bring disorder into the country. His aim was to keep the people in the ignorance they were in, and by the claim that the whole thing had been arranged beforehand, to rob the miracle of its weight and the conversion of its plainness.

### Why the threat came out of pride

To give up one's life for the truth is the last and fullest testimony a person can bear to it, and the magicians were enabled to make that offering. By putting themselves in front of the worst punishment the king could threaten, they proved that their belief in Musa was not an arrangement and not a conspiracy, but a plain acknowledgement of the truth.

That action stung the pride of Pharaoh. To side with Musa against him was to insult him in front of the whole community, and a haughty man in his position answers an insult with force. Both sides had been defeated in the field of argument, and the difference is what each did afterwards. The magicians admitted the defeat and became entitled to the reward of God, while the king made it a matter of prestige and took it out on the people who loved the truth. What he could not do was undo the argument, so he turned to power, and for that the price was his own eternal punishment.

### In short

- The king treated the belief of the magicians as an act needing his permission, while to them it was a sign from their Lord.
- He called the contest a conspiracy between Musa and the magicians to drive the people out and take the rule.
- The magicians had been gathered by his own order and paid by his own promise, and Musa had never met them before, so the charge was false and he knew it.
- The Book describes him as a man who fooled his people, and a people who accepted the claim that he was their lord the most high (79:24) are among the most misguided.
- The reports say six hundred thousand followed the magicians into the faith, where only two individuals had believed before, and the day left the king exposed.
- He answered it by turning the matter into a plot, and his pride, once wounded, chose force over truth.

124.text:
The undefined threat is now made precise. "I will certainly cut off your hands and feet on opposite sides, then crucify you all.”"

### Phrase by phrase

**"I will certainly cut off your hands and feet on opposite sides"** is the first part of the sentence he passed. The meaning of the words is the right hand and the left leg of every one of them, so that the body is left altogether disabled, and the same words are reported in another place with the crucifying named on the trunks of the date palms (20:71). The cutting from opposite sides was the part that made the punishment a lasting injury even for those who survived it.

**"then crucify you all"** is the second part, and together the two make a punishment that is meant to be seen. One reading places the crosses on the river bank, where the traffic of the people would pass them. Pharaoh ordered that they be made an example, so that whoever looked at them would be frightened away from the same step.

Ibn Abbas said that Pharaoh was the first to crucify people and to cut off hands and legs on opposite sides. The whole of the sentence was delivered to men who had just bowed to the Lord of the worlds, and it was delivered in front of the nation, which is part of what the answer in the next verse was measured against.

### In short

- Verse 124 of this surah names the punishment. It is the cutting of the right hand and the left leg, the opposite sides of the body, so that the person is left crippled for life.
- The same sentence is reported in another place with the crosses on the trunks of the date palms (20:71).
- The crucifying was to be done publicly, on one reading along the river bank where the people would pass.
- The purpose was to make an example of them, so that the sight would frighten anyone who thought of following them.
- Ibn Abbas said that Pharaoh was the first to inflict both parts of that punishment.

125.text:
The answer of the magicians is short and steady. "They responded, “Surely to our Lord we will ˹all˺ return"

### Phrase by phrase

**"They responded, “Surely to our Lord we will ˹all˺ return"** is the whole of their reply to the sentence that Pharaoh had passed on them. The words are an affirmation about the end of every person. One reading gives the sense plainly, that they would be restored to their Lord after death, however that death should come about.

**What had changed in them.** A few hours before they had been the followers of the king's religion, and Iman is a power that makes such a change possible. When it enters a heart, a person finds in himself enough to stand against the whole world and all the forces that have been gathered against him. The men who said these words had been hired to defend a throne. They were now saying to the king's face that they were going back to their Lord. What the words also show is their whole indifference to the life of this world. The promises that had brought them to the contest were gone from their minds in that hour, and what the words say is that they had another end in view.

### What they said besides

Another passage reports more of their answer to him. He should decide whatever he wished to decree, since he could only decide for the life of this world. They had believed in their Lord so that He might forgive them their faults, and the magic to which he had compelled them, and Allah is better to reward and more lasting in punishment. The same passage names the two ends. Whoever comes to his Lord as a criminal has the Fire, where he neither dies nor lives. Whoever comes to Him as a believer who has done good deeds has the high ranks (20:72-75). So the magicians spoke to the king about what outlasts a king, and they left the sentence in his hands.

### In short

- Their answer to the threat was that every person returns to his Lord, whenever and however death comes.
- The change in them in a few hours shows what Iman does when it enters a heart, since a person then finds strength against the whole world.
- Their words show how little the life of this world weighed with them after that, since the rewards they had come for were already forgotten.
- They told the king to decree whatever he wished, since his decree reached only this life (20:72-75).
- The passage names the two ends, the Fire for the criminal and the high ranks for the believer who does good.

126.text:
The last thing they say is a statement of their crime and a prayer. "Your rage towards us is only because we believed in the signs of our Lord when they came to us. Our Lord! Shower us with perseverance, and let us die while submitting ˹to You˺.”"

### Phrase by phrase

**"Your rage towards us is only because we believed in the signs of our Lord when they came to us"** names the fault the king was punishing. They had found fault in them for nothing except the faith itself, and the words put the charge on the table plainly. The signs of their Lord had come to them, and they had believed them, and if that was the crime, then they stood by it.

**"Our Lord! Shower us with perseverance"** is the first half of the prayer, and it asks for firmness at the very point where the punishment was going to fall. The word carries the sense of being honoured with steadfastness when the crucifying and the cutting came, and the point of the asking was that they should not go back to disbelief under it. So they asked for strength at the exact place where strength would be needed, which is the way a servant asks when he knows his own limits.

**"and let us die while submitting ˹to You˺"** is the second half, and it is the sum of what a believer wants from the whole of his life. They asked to be taken while they were surrendered to Him, sincere in it, and following the religion of Musa.

### Where that prayer came from

The change in their thought and their action was the fruit of the faith that had entered them. Beyond that, their faith opened the door of knowledge and wisdom in them, and their prayer at that hour is one of the marks of it. The prayer was also the best way out of the difficulty they were in. Perseverance and patience are the keys to victory over an enemy, and the hardest minutes a person spends are the ones where he must simply stand still and hold on.

The proof of what patience does belongs to the field as much as to the cell. The report of the commission formed to investigate the causes and effects of the World War found that the Muslims who have faith in Allah and in the Hereafter are the bravest of men in battle and the most patient in hardship, because of that faith. The lesson was clear enough to the German military officials whose speciality was the science of war. They urged that honesty, and a sense of accountability in the Hereafter, be planted among their soldiers, since those are among the great sources of strength and courage.

### The change itself was a sign

The instant and complete turning of the magicians was no less a miracle than the staff that ate the snakes. Men who had spent their whole lives in disbelief and ignorance became, in one hour, among the most knowing and the truest of people. They were ready to give their lives for what they had come to see. The pity of the matter is that the Muslims and the Muslim states try every other means to make themselves strong. They pay no heed to the thing from which that strength comes, which is faith, perseverance and patience. Ibn Abbas, Ubayd bin Umayr, Qatadah and Ibn Jurayj all said of these men that they began the day as sorcerers and ended it as martyrs.

The prayer itself carried a surrender that has its own answer. When a servant of God gives himself body and soul to his Lord, he comes so near that he begins to receive what is special from Him. The words he speaks at such a moment are inspired in the full sense. What the magicians said came to this, that they had surrendered entirely, that they had done what was in their power, and that they left the rest to Him.

### In short

- They put the charge in plain words, that the king was punishing them for believing the signs of their Lord when the signs came.
- Their prayer asked for perseverance at the exact point where the punishment would fall, and that they be taken while surrendered to Him.
- Faith had opened knowledge and wisdom in them, and the prayer was both a mark of it and the best way out of their difficulty.
- Perseverance and patience are the keys to victory over an enemy, and the report on the World War found the believers strongest in battle and steadiest in hardship, because of their faith in Allah and the Hereafter.
- The instant change in the magicians was itself a miracle, and what it shows is that the strength of a people is drawn from faith, perseverance and patience.
- Their prayer was a full surrender, and the account treats it as words that were placed in them at that hour.

127.text:
The court turns its attention from the magicians to the nation, and the king answers with a policy. "The chiefs of Pharaoh’s people protested, “Are you going to leave Moses and his people free to spread corruption in the land and abandon you and your gods?” He responded, “We will kill their sons and keep their women. We will completely dominate them.”"

### Phrase by phrase

**"The chiefs of Pharaoh’s people protested"** records the pressure that came on the king from his own court. They put the question to him in front of one another, since something about his conduct had begun to look strange to them. His fury and his rage had fallen on the magicians alone, and against Musa and Harun, who were the real opponents, he had not dared to say a word. His own leading men noticed it, and they came to him with the question the verse reports.

**"Are you going to leave Moses and his people free to spread corruption in the land"** is the charge. What they meant by corruption was that Musa and his people were spreading unrest among the subjects and calling them to worship their Lord instead of the king. The wonder of it is that these very men were the corrupters of the land, and they did not see it in themselves.

**"and abandon you and your gods?"** is the second half of the charge, and it gives away something about the king himself. He had set small idols for his people to worship, and he had told them that he was their lord and the lord of their fathers. So a man who claimed to be a god for his people was being asked to protect the gods he kept beside himself. The complaint also lets it be seen that the king had claimed lordship while worshipping others, and that is the contradiction his own chiefs were pressing on him.

**"He responded, “We will kill their sons and keep their women. We will completely dominate them.”"** is his answer, and it is a policy rather than a reply. He had no convincing word to the question, so he returned to the measure he had used before. By killing the males and leaving the women alive he meant to bring the whole people to an end within a period of time, and the women were to be spared to serve his people as servants. His words about power over them were a claim of complete dominance and supremacy.

**"your gods", and whose calf it was.** The idols the chiefs spoke of were, in the report that As-Suddi gave from Ibn Abbas, cows. Whenever the king saw a beautiful cow, he would command the people to worship it. That is the same calf that As-Samiri later made for the Children of Israel, a statue that seemed to moo, and the report shows where his idea came from.

**What the king was afraid of.** The whole answer was the speech of a frightened man. He had seen the staff turned into a serpent and the hand come out shining, and after that he could threaten the whole tribe of the Israelites while keeping silent about the two men who stood in front of him. Maulana Rumi put the law of it in a line. The one who takes up taqwa and holds Allah in awe is himself held in awe by every human being, and by the spirits as well.

### What the policy shows about the king

The order to kill the males and spare the women was not new. It had been put into force once before, in the years before the birth of Musa, so that he would never be born, and the king was looking at the wreck of his own plan while he spoke. The crowd of the Israelites standing in front of him at that moment was the evidence that the first version of the policy had failed. The one he was sent to destroy was raised in the king's own house and stood before his throne as the messenger of the Lord of all worlds.

There is a rule in that. When Allah intends to bring disgrace on a people, everything they contrive turns into nothing but disaster for them. The law that was meant to end the people of Israel served to bring their deliverer into the world, and the second attempt at the same law was answered by the destruction of the king and his army in the sea.

### In short

- The chiefs of the court pressed the king, since his anger had gone no further than the magicians and he had not dared to threaten Musa and Harun.
- The charge they brought was that Musa was spreading corruption and leading the people away from the king and his gods.
- The ones who were really corrupting the land were the men bringing the charge.
- His answer had no argument in it, and he returned to the old law of killing the sons and sparing the women, to end the people in time and keep the women as servants.
- The gods the chiefs named were the cows the king set up for worship, and the same calf was later set up for the Children of Israel by As-Samiri.
- The first round of that law had already failed, since the one it was meant to prevent was standing in front of the king, and a people whose ruin is intended finds every plan of theirs turning to disaster.

128.text:
The messenger turns to his own people with the answer that holds for every generation under a tyrant. "Moses reassured his people, “Seek Allah’s help and be patient. Indeed, the earth belongs to Allah ˹alone˺. He grants it to whoever He chooses of His servants. The ultimate outcome belongs ˹only˺ to the righteous.”"

### Phrase by phrase

**"Moses reassured his people"** is the setting of the instruction. The law had just been laid on them once more, and they were badly alarmed by what they had gone through before the coming of Musa and by what was now beginning again.

**"Seek Allah’s help and be patient"** gives the two wise remedies he placed in front of them. The first was to ask Allah alone for help to remove the hardship and to bring good, and the second was to hold themselves steady under the trial until matters turned in their favour. The two together are the sovereign cure that does not fail against any difficulty.

Seeking help is the essence of the remedy, and the reason is plain. If the Creator of the universe comes to a person's help, then who is there to stop Him? Maulana Rumi put the same truth in a couplet, that the earth, the air, the water and the fire are all servants of Allah, and that they are dead to us while they are full of life to Him. There is a tradition that says when Allah wills a thing to be done, everything turns in favour of that purpose. So nothing is more powerful against an enemy than to seek the help of Allah with a sincere heart, and the mere uttering of a formula is not what is meant.

Patience is the second ingredient, and the word used for it, sabr, means to keep oneself under control when things go against a person. Everybody knows that nothing significant is achieved without difficulty, and the one who prepares himself ahead of time to meet hardship is the one who reaches what he aims at. The Prophet ﷺ said in a tradition that no greater blessing has been given to anyone other than patience, and the report is carried by Abu Dawud.

**"Indeed, the earth belongs to Allah, He grants it to whoever He chooses of His servants"** is the ground of the whole instruction. The earth spoken of here is the land of Egypt, and the point is that it belongs to Allah alone. It does not belong to Pharaoh or to any other person to do with as he pleases. It is Allah who turns it over to one people and then to another as He wills. So a people who keep taqwa and act on the two instructions would come in the end to rule the whole country.

**"The ultimate outcome belongs only to the righteous"** names the end of the matter. The good end, and in one reading the Garden itself, is for those who keep their duty to Him and turn away from disbelief, from the worship of partners, and from shameful deeds.

### The difference between a prophet and a politician

The Israelites had brought the problem of the rule of Pharaoh to their prophet and asked him to solve it for them, and the solution he gave was that they should turn to God. That is the difference between the way of the worldly leader and the way of the prophet in the face of a communal problem. The worldly leader looks for the answer at the level of the government, either by making terms with it or by coming to blows with it.
