What the prophet offered here was that whatever was happening should be borne, and that the help of God be sought, without expecting anything from the powers of the day.

What the people said back to him is recorded in the verse that follows, and the answer he gave to that is the plainest statement of where power comes from and what it is for.

### In short

- The instruction came at a moment when the old law had been renewed and the people were frightened.
- The two remedies are seeking the help of Allah and holding steady under the trial, and the two together do not fail against any difficulty.
- The tradition carried by Abu Dawud says that no greater blessing has been given to a person than patience.
- The earth belongs to Allah alone, and He gives the rule of it to whichever of His servants He chooses.
- The good end belongs to those who keep their duty to Him, and in one reading the good end means the Garden.
- A prophet meets a communal problem by turning the people to God, while the worldly leader looks for the answer in a bargain or a fight with the government.

129.text:
The people answer with a complaint about their whole history. "They complained, “We have always been oppressed—before and after you came to us ˹with the message˺.”" The reply comes back in the same verse. "He replied, “Perhaps your Lord will destroy your enemy and make you successors in the land to see what you will do.”"

### Phrase by phrase

**"They complained, “We have always been oppressed—before and after you came to us ˹with the message˺.”"** gives the objection that the Children of Israel raised with Moses. They had been tormented by the killing of their sons, by the seizure of their women, and by the labour laid on them, and they said that the persecution had gone on both before the messenger came and since he came. The words carry the difficulty they had with the instruction they had just been given, since they could not see how patience by itself was going to free them from the punishment of the king or bring them success against him.

**"He replied,"** opens the answer of Musa. The word rendered as perhaps sounds open, and on the tongue of a man it would carry uncertainty. Spoken of Allah it conveys certainty. The promise given there was that the adversary of the Israelites would be destroyed.

**"and make you successors in the land"** is the second part, and it was fulfilled in the plainest way. Their enemy was destroyed, and they were made the ones in authority in the land of Egypt, and in the broader sense they were given the earth as an inheritance.

**"to see what you will do"** is where the promise turns into something weightier than a promise. The words encourage them to value what Allah gives when affliction is lifted and replaced with bounty, and then they put the question of conduct in front of them. That is the point the whole account is making. Power and rule are a test for those who hold them, given so that it may be seen how far they fulfil the duty of establishing peace and justice and make the good prevail over the evil.

### The report about the verse

Abu Hayyan included the following in his commentary, Al-Bahr Al-Muhit. Amr ibn Ubaid visited Mansur, the second of the Abbasid caliphs, before he came to the caliphate, and recited this verse, that it may be that Allah will destroy your enemy and make you a successor in the earth. The reciting was taken as a prediction that the man before him would come to the throne. Soon afterwards Mansur did succeed and became the caliph, and Amr ibn Ubaid came to him again. The caliph reminded him of what he had said, and Amr ibn Ubaid answered at once that the first part had come true and the man had become caliph, while the second part remained, since the verse goes on to say that He will see how you act. He meant that gaining power is no ground for pride by itself, since the acts of those in authority are judged afterwards, and the way they use what was put in their trust is seen.

### Where power comes from

Moses explained to the Israelites why he was offering them a solution that went against the ordinary way of thinking. The troubles had come from the ruling authority, and by any ordinary reckoning that authority was the only thing that could resolve them. What the people had not weighed was how power comes to be held in the first place. Nobody holds power merely by the working of strategies, since power is conferred and taken away directly by God, and if that is so then the resolution of the problem lies with God as well. Another verse covers the same ground, that Allah gives dominion to whom He wills (3:26), and the Israelites were being taught to look past Pharaoh to the One who had set him over them.

### What power is for

Power in the hands of any people is a test, and being powerless is a test of its own kind. If a person has been given power, it is because he is being tried on whether he turns haughty and tyrannical or behaves with justice and modesty. If the empowerment goes to somebody else, the purpose is still to test. When a group loses power because of its own incompetence and another group takes it, the second group is put to the same examination, and if it proves incompetent in turn the power will be taken from it and given to a third. The prosperity and the standing that a person craves in this world are things that can only be held in the real sense in the Hereafter. In this world they are given out for the test, and in the Hereafter they will be given to the righteous as their reward.

### In short

- The people complained that the oppression had gone on both before the messenger came and after, and they could not see how patience would change it.
- The promise given back to them was certain, that their enemy would be destroyed and that they would be made the ones in authority in the land.
- The last words of the verse make conduct the point of the whole promise, since power is given so that it may be seen how those who hold it behave.
- Abu Hayyan records the report of Amr ibn Ubaid before Mansur, who was told that the first half of the verse had come true and that the second half still stood over him.
- Power is conferred and removed by God alone, and for that reason the answer to the problem of a ruling authority also lies with Him.
- Rule is a test for whoever holds it, and the prosperity people crave in this world is only held in the real sense in the Hereafter.

130.text:
The punishments begin, and the first of them comes from the sky. "Indeed, We afflicted Pharaoh’s people with famine and shortage of crops so they might come back ˹to their senses˺"

### Phrase by phrase

**"Indeed, We afflicted Pharaoh’s people"** introduces the sequence of events that carried that people to their end. The words mean that they were tested and tried, and what follows is the first of the heavenly punishments sent to them.

**"with famine and shortage of crops"** names the two things taken from them. The first is the years of drought and want, the famine that follows a poor yield, and the second is the loss of the fruits, which is the lighter of the two. Historical reports put the famine at seven years.

The two are distributed in one account. Ibn Abbas and the commentator Qatadah said that the drought fell on the people of the countryside, while those living in the cities and the towns were punished by the loss of the fruits. The scarcity was remembered long afterwards. It was reported from Raja' bin Haywah that in those years the date palm produced a single date.

**"so they might come back ˹to their senses˺"** gives the purpose. The famine was sent so that they would remember, take heed of the warning, and turn back to their Lord in repentance. That is the shape of the whole series. Each punishment came as a warning before the final one, and the door of return was left open for as long as they refused to walk through it.

### Where this falls in the account

The historical reports say that Musa spent twenty years in the land of Egypt. He called the people through that time and delivered to them the message of his Lord. He was given nine miracles during that stay, and those signs stood as warnings to the people of Pharaoh. The Book refers to them in the words about the nine miracles given to him.

Two of the nine were performed in front of Pharaoh and his people at the outset, which were the staff and the hand. The third was the famine reported in this verse. The verses that follow report the remaining six, and the account moves through them one after another.

### In short

- The people of Pharaoh were tested with years of drought and with the loss of their fruits.
- One account puts the famine at seven years, and the date palm was reported to have produced a single date in that time.
- The drought is said to have fallen on the countryside and the loss of fruit on the towns and cities.
- The purpose was to bring them back to their senses and to return them to their Lord in repentance.
- The famine was the third of the nine signs given to Musa, after the staff and the hand, and it came during the twenty years he spent calling them in Egypt.

131.text:
The way the people read their own fortunes is laid out for the record. "In times of prosperity, they said, “This is what we deserve,” but in adversity, they blamed it on Moses and those with him, the Children of Israel among them,. Surely all is destined by Allah. Yet most of them did not know"

### Phrase by phrase

**"In times of prosperity, they said, “This is what we deserve,”"** gives their reading of the good things. When a fertile season came, and provision, and land that gave its yield, they said that the thing was theirs by right. They took the good as a payment owed to them for what they were, and no thanks went to the One who had sent it.

**"but in adversity, they blamed it on Moses and those with him"** gives their reading of the bad. When drought came, and want, and hardship, they laid the whole of it on the messenger and on the believers who were with him, and said that the trouble had come because of those people and what they had done.

The word used for the bad omen carries the sense of a bird. The Arabs before Islam held a superstition that a bird coming down on the right or on the left foretold a good or a bad fate, and the verse takes their practice up and turns it on its head.

**"Surely all is destined by Allah"** is the correction. Good and bad come from Allah, and everything in this world happens under His will. There is no creature that brings good or bad fortune to anyone, and it is plain ignorance to hold such a belief and to build one's affairs on assumptions of that kind. Ibn Abbas said of the words that the afflictions of those people were with Allah and from Him.

**"Yet most of them did not know"** states the reason for the mistake. When a people come under the anger of Allah, they lose the faculty that tells right from wrong. The people of Pharaoh had lost it. They did not take the lesson from the warning, and they read the most plain of events backwards.

### In short

- Good seasons were taken by them as a right they had earned, with no thanks given for them.
- Bad seasons were blamed on Musa and the believers who were with him.
- The word for a bad omen carries the sense of a bird, which recalls the old superstition about birds and fate.
- The correction is that everything is from Allah, and no creature brings good or ill to another.
- A people who fall under the wrath of Allah lose the faculty that separates right from wrong, and most of them did not know.

132.text:
The refusal is put into words that shut the door on every sign in advance. "They said, “No matter what sign you may bring to deceive us, we will never believe in you.”"

### Phrase by phrase

**"They said, “No matter what sign you may bring"** answers the signs before they see them. What the words mean is that whatever miracle, proof or evidence he brought them, they would not take it from him.

**"to deceive us"** is how they named the signs. Their claim was that the wonders were brought to work a magic on them and to dazzle their eyes, and the whole of the proof was thus dismissed as a deception in advance.

**"we will never believe in you"** is the conclusion they held to. The refusal covers both the man and what he had come with, and the decision had been taken before the evidence was in. It was after this that Musa prayed against them, and the punishments of the following verse came as the answer to that supplication.

### What their words show about a person and the truth

Words have to be used to call a thing right or wrong, and to name a man innocent or guilty. The one who uses them is a human being, and in this world of trial he has been given the power to use them in whatever way he pleases. The most critical part of that freedom is the ability to call the truth a falsehood and the falsehood a truth. A person can name as magic what is plainly a miracle worked by a prophet, and then set it aside. If God gives him a blessing, he can put it in words that make it appear to be the fruit of his own ability and effort. If God sends him a warning for the truth he has ignored, he is free to say that it came because of the unlucky presence of the very worshippers of God whom he has ill-treated.

Everything flows from God, and all of it is sent so that a person may learn from it. What he does with words is to give the opposite meaning to every admonition, and so he stays cut off from the lesson that was inside it. The statement of Pharaoh here is the plain example of it. The truth was clear in a perfect shape in front of him, and he refused it.

What follows from that is a rule about people and the truth. The reality of the truth reveals itself to the person who is serious about it, the one who has the inclination and the willingness to receive it wherever it comes from and in whatever form. The person who is not serious about it, and whose mind is content with the state he is already in, cannot see it as the truth and so cannot accept it. To be happy with the condition a man is in makes him unaware of everything outside himself, and he becomes ignorant in spite of his knowledge and deaf in spite of his ears. A man will certainly find the truth when his mind is free of the thinking that has been conditioned into it, and most people are held by such conditioning, which is why the truth eludes them.

### In short

- Their refusal was made in advance, covering every sign Musa might bring.
- They named the signs as a deception worked on their eyes, and dismissed the proof before it arrived.
- Musa prayed against them after that, and the punishments that follow came as the answer.
- A person is free to use words to call the truth a lie and a lie the truth, and that is the most dangerous part of the freedom he has been given.
- The truth reveals itself to the one who is serious about it and open to receive it, while the one who is content with his own condition stays deaf to it.

133.text:
The five remaining signs are named in one verse. "So We plagued them with floods, locusts, lice, frogs, and blood—all as clear signs, but they persisted in arrogance and were a wicked people"

### Phrase by phrase

**"So We plagued them with floods"** names the first. The word used for it means a continuous rain, falling day and night, and in one account from Saturday to Saturday. According to the greater commentators it was a flood that filled the lands and the houses of the people of Pharaoh, leaving them no place to farm and no room to live in their own homes.

**"locusts"** is the second, the well-known insect, and it ate everything the earth produced, both the vegetation and the fruit. In the account of what happened, the locusts consumed the trees and even the nails on their doors, until the doors fell away from the houses. In one description they ate the wood and left the nails.

The locust is also a food, and the reports about it are worth setting down. In the Two Sahihs there is a report that Abu Ya'fur put a question to Abdullah bin Abi Awfa about the locust. The answer was that the companions had fought seven battles beside the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, and that locusts were among the things they ate. Ash-Shafi'i, Ahmad bin Hanbal and Ibn Majah all carried a report from Abdur-Rahman bin Zayd bin Aslam, from his father, from Ibn Umar, that the Prophet ﷺ named two kinds of dead animal and two kinds of blood as lawful. They are the fish, the locust, the kidney and the spleen.

**"lice"** is the third. The word used here was explained in more than one way. Ibn Abbas said it is the grain bug, and in another report from him the small locusts that have no wings. Mujahid, Ikrimah and Qatadah were reported with the same view. Al-Hasan, together with Sa'id bin Jubayr, held that they are small insects of a black colour. One account has Musa commanded to strike a mound with his staff. He did so, and the pests poured out of it in such numbers that they covered the houses and the stores of food, and robbed the people of sleep and of rest.

**"frogs"** is the fourth, and the reports describe how far they went. Musa once heard the croaking of a frog while he was with Pharaoh and asked him what he and his people would suffer from it, and Pharaoh asked what a frog could do. By that night a man would be sitting among frogs that came up to his chin. He could not open his mouth to speak, since a frog would jump into it. They filled the houses, the food and the cooking pots, and one of them could not lift a piece of clothing or uncover food without finding frogs in it.

**"and blood"** is the fifth. The waters of the people of Pharaoh turned to blood. The rivers and the wells and the containers they kept in their houses all gave blood, and any water they collected from a well or a river or a vessel turned to blood. One report describes the strangeness of it, that whenever an Egyptian and an Israelite sat down to eat together, the morsel taken by the Egyptian turned to blood while the one taken by the Israelite did not change.

Abu Ja'far bin Jarir recorded from Sa'id bin Jubayr the whole sequence of it. The rain came and they feared it as a torment and asked Musa to pray, and they promised faith and the release of the Children of Israel. He prayed and the rain was lifted, and they broke the word. Then the locusts came and ate the grass, and they made the same promise, and Musa prayed, and they broke it again. The grain pests followed, and then the frogs, and then the blood, and each time the words of the promise say the same thing and the result was the same. What the reports say of that first rain is that the crops of that year grew as they had never grown before, and one of them would take ten bags of grain to the mill and come away with three small ones. A report cited by al-Baghawi from Ibn Abbas adds that the first relief was granted after they asked Musa to pray for them, and that they did not keep the promise they had made.

**"all as clear signs"** describes the whole series, and it is verse 133 of this surah. Each punishment was a plain sign in itself, distinct from the others, and they came one after another with a fixed interval between them. Muhammad bin Ishaq bin Yasar gave the whole series in order, with the locusts eating the trees and the nails of the doors. A report cited by al-Mundhir from Ibn Abbas gives each punishment a length of seven days, beginning with Saturday, and gives the people three weeks of relief between one and the next. The like of that account was attributed to Ibn Abbas, to As-Suddi, to Qatadah, and to several others among the salaf. What those reports say is that the signs came in order, and that the promises were made and broken with each one.

**"but they persisted in arrogance and were a wicked people"** gives the answer of the people to all five. They were too proud to have faith in Allah and too set in their ways to accept what Musa had brought. They were a people who committed wrongs. They would not give up the falsehood they were on, and they were not guided to the truth.

### How the divine protection showed in the middle of it

One thread runs through the reports of the whole series, and it is worth following on its own. The punishments fell on the Egyptians and stopped at the door of the Israelites. When the flood filled the land and the houses of the people of Pharaoh, the lands and the houses of the Children of Israel were not touched by the water. When the locusts ate up the crops and the fruit, they did no harm to the houses or the fields of the Israelites, and those fields were close by. The bread of the Egyptian turned to blood at the table while the bread of the Israelite beside him stayed as it was.

So the series of punishments was also a series of signs for the people of the messenger, and it taught them where their safety lay while the whole land around them was being struck. The two peoples were living in the same country, working the same soil, and eating at the same tables, and the difference between them in those years was the difference between belief and denial.

### The mission of Musa and where the signs belong in it

The prophetic work of Musa in the land of Egypt had two parts. The first was to carry the message of the oneness of God to Pharaoh. The second was to take the Children of Israel out of Egypt, settle them in the desert of Sinai, and give them their religious training in that clean air. One account gives the length of the stay as twenty years, and another as about forty. The Children of Israel, who were the progeny of Joseph, were at that time in the grip of the Copt ruler, and the Copts used them as labourers in their fields and in their building works. That is why the rulers of the Copts did not want them to leave the land.

At the beginning, when Musa asked Pharaoh to let the Children of Israel go with him, the king and his courtiers gave the request a political colour and accused him of intending to drive the Copts out of Egypt (7:110). The charge made no sense, since the plan of Musa was to take himself and his people out of the land rather than to remove anyone else. At that stage the people of Pharaoh had a swollen opinion of their own power, and that is why they saw even a straightforward proposal as something crooked.

In the later stage the matter stood differently. Allah set the king and his community under every kind of affliction. For many years there were famines one after another. There were heavy storms with thunder and lightning. The locusts invaded the country and ate the crops and the gardens and left the greenery bare. The lice multiplied until clothes and beds were infested with them. In the houses and on the roads the frogs were everywhere. The water of the rivers and the lakes turned to blood. When the people of Pharaoh began to suffer under these things, they asked Musa to pray to his Lord to relieve them, and they promised that they would then let the Children of Israel leave with him. So the demand that had once looked to the Copts like a political plot to drive them out now appeared to them as what it was, a migration of the Children of Israel themselves.

### In short

- The five signs were the flood, the locusts, the lice, the frogs and the blood, and each came as a clear sign on its own.
- The flood filled the land and the houses, the locusts ate the crops and even the wood and nails of the doors, the lice consumed what was left, the frogs filled the houses and the food, and the water turned to blood.
- The locust is lawful as food, and the reports in the Two Sahihs and from Ibn Majah carry that ruling.
- Ibn Abbas said each punishment lasted seven days from Saturday, with three weeks of relief before the next, and the same was reported from As-Suddi, Qatadah and others among the salaf.
- The Israelites were protected through the whole series, since the water, the locusts and the blood passed over them while they lived and ate beside the Egyptians.
- The people persisted in arrogance through all of it and remained a people of wrong, and the signs came during the forty years of the mission, whose second part was the migration of the Children of Israel out of Egypt.

134.text:
Under the weight of it the people make promises they have no intention of keeping. "When tormented, they pleaded, “O Moses! Pray to your Lord on our behalf, by virtue of the covenant He made with you." Then comes the bargain. "If you help remove this torment from us, we will certainly believe in you and let the Children of Israel go with you.”"

### Phrase by phrase

**"When tormented, they pleaded"** sets the condition under which the promises were made. The words describe each occasion when one of the punishments fell on them, whether that was the flood, the locusts, the lice, the frogs or the blood. What moved them was the pain, and not the proof.

**"O Moses! Pray to your Lord on our behalf"** is the request itself. The same men who had refused to believe him whatever sign he brought now asked him to stand between them and their Lord, which is the plainest admission of where the power over the punishment lay.

**"by virtue of the covenant He made with you"** is the argument they used. In one reading the sense is that they were appealing to what Allah had commanded him to do, and in another it is the favour of prophethood that had been given to him, with the promise that came with it, that the torment would be lifted when they turned back. They had no claim of their own, so they asked him to plead the standing he had been given.

**"If you help remove this torment from us, we will certainly believe in you and let the Children of Israel go with you"** is the bargain. The promise had two halves, and the second was the thing he had come to ask for from the very beginning, that he be allowed to take his people out of the land, releasing them from the captivity they were in. The first half is the harder of the two to understand, since they had already seen the signs and refused them, and belief had been made a thing of the tongue only.

### The whole thing, five times over

The account of the series shows the pattern repeating. The rain came and they feared, and they said that they would believe and send the Children of Israel with him. Musa prayed, and the affliction was lifted, and they did not believe and did not send them. The locusts came and they made the same promise, and the same thing happened. Then the grain pests, then the frogs, then the blood, each with the same words and the same result. By the time the promise was made for the fifth time, the whole of the court knew what the promise was worth.

### In short

- The promises were made under the pressure of the punishment, not out of any acceptance of the proof.
- They asked Musa to pray for them, which was in itself an admission of where the power over their affliction lay.
- They appealed to the covenant and the standing he had been given, having no claim of their own.
- The bargain promised belief and the release of the Children of Israel, which was the thing he had asked for from the start.
- The same promise was made and broken five times over, and the record of the series is a record of one broken word after another.

135.text:
The last word on those promises closes the passage. "But as soon as We removed the torment from them—until they met their inevitable fate—they broke their promise"

### Phrase by phrase

**"But as soon as We removed the torment from them"** records the other side of the bargain. The relief came through the supplication of the messenger, who prayed for them each time the punishment had done its work of warning.

**"until they met their inevitable fate"** sets the limit of the respite. The relief they were given was only for a fixed term, and there was a day appointed that they were bound to reach. The term named in the account is the drowning, when the whole matter came to its end in the sea.

**"they broke their promise"** states what they did with the bargain. The word carries the sense of reneging, of going back on what had been given. Immediately after the relief they were already breaking it. In one reading the sense is that they went on with their disbelief and refused to send the Israelites with him, holding to what they were on and giving the messenger nothing of what they had promised.

### Where the whole matter came to rest

So the passage ends as it began. The people had the plainest of signs in front of them, and what the words say is that they read every one of them as something to be escaped rather than as something to be answered. The proof had come to them in nine forms, the door of return had been held open through the whole of it, and the end of the story was the sea.

### In short

- The relief came each time through the supplication of Musa, and each time it was thrown back at him.
- The respite had a limit fixed for it, and the day they were bound to reach was the day of the drowning.
- Their breaking of the word is put in the past continuous sense in the text, since they were already reneging as the relief arrived.
- They held to their disbelief and refused to let the Children of Israel go with him.
- The passage closes with a people who turned the signs into things to be escaped, and with the end of the account waiting in the sea.

136.text:
The end of the people of Pharaoh comes in one sentence. "So We inflicted punishment upon them, drowning them in the sea for denying Our signs and being heedless of them"

### Phrase by phrase

**"So We inflicted punishment upon them"** says that the retribution was taken from them once and for all. They had rebelled and gone past every limit, and the signs had been set in front of them one after another without any effect on them. When the appointed time for their destruction came, the punishment was released on them and there was nothing left to hold it back.

**"drowning them in the sea"** names the punishment. The sea spoken of here is the salt water, and it was the same water that Musa split by the power of Allah, so that he and the Children of Israel walked through it dry. The people of Pharaoh followed them into the parted water. When the whole of the army was inside, the sea closed over them and every one of them drowned.

Before that end, one sign had come to them that was heavier than the rest. The sixth punishment is given in the Book as the rijz, which means plague or pestilence, and the number of the Egyptians who died in it is put at more than seventy thousand. They were relieved of it through the prayer of Musa, and they broke the promise they had made as they had broken every promise before it. When it was clear that nothing would bring them to their senses, the final punishment arrived, which was death. They left their lands and their houses and everything they owned behind them and rode out after Musa and his people, and they were drowned in the sea.

**"for denying Our signs and being heedless of them"** gives the reason. They called the nine signs a lie, and they were heedless, in the sense that they never turned the matter over in their minds. The signs of Allah had passed in front of their eyes and they took no lesson from any of them.

### What this end tells the reader

The passage closes the account of a people who were given more warning than any other people in the surah, since they had nine signs of the clearest kind, and the door of return was held open for them through every one. What was left at the end was the sea, and what the verse establishes is that the punishment follows on the denial and not on anything else. The people themselves had read their own troubles as a bad omen of the messenger, and the last of their troubles was the answer to the prayer he had made against them.

### In short

- The punishment was taken from them once and for all at the appointed time.
- The sea was the same water Musa had split by the power of Allah, and it closed over the people of Pharaoh while the Israelites watched.
- Before it came the plague, in which more than seventy thousand of them died, and the promise they made at its lifting was broken like the others.
- Their lands and their possessions were left behind when they rode out after the messenger.
- The reason given is the denial of the signs and the heedlessness that kept them from reflecting on them.

137.text:
The other side of the same event is now told, and the promise that stood behind it. "And ˹so˺ We made the oppressed people successors of the eastern and western lands, which We had showered with blessings. ˹In this way˺ the noble Word of your Lord was fulfilled for the Children of Israel for what they had endured. And We destroyed what Pharaoh and his people constructed and what they established"

### Phrase by phrase

**"And ˹so˺ We made the oppressed people successors"** names the people who came out of the whole affair with the land. The words describe them as those who were taken to be weak, and not as the weak. The difference carries a point of its own. A people whose support is Allah are never weak in the real sense. Their outward condition may look otherwise for a time, and the end of the matter makes the truth of it plain to everyone. Dignity and honour belong to Allah, and He gives them to whom He wills.

**"successors of the eastern and western lands"** describes what they were given. The word used here for succession is the word for inheritance. The choice is deliberate, since an heir takes what comes to him by right. The point of it is that the Israelites were the real inheritors of the land and the wealth of the people of Pharaoh, just as a son is the inheritor of what his father left. The east and the west are put in the plural, which may be a way of naming the points of sunrise and sunset as they shift through the winter and the summer. Verse 137 of this surah opens on that sentence. Experts in the explanation of the Book say that the land meant is the land of Jerusalem, Palestine, Jordan and Egypt. These came under the rule of the Israelites after the people of Pharaoh and the Amalekites were destroyed.

**"which We had showered with blessings"** names what the land itself was. The blessing spoken of is barakah, and the blessing was in the water and in what grew, the fields and the trees. The Book calls Syria a land of blessing, and Egypt is named as blessed in a number of traditions. The Caliph Umar ibn al-Khattab called the Nile the prince of all rivers. Abdullah ibn Umar said that Egypt carries nine parts of blessing out of ten, and that the tenth part was divided out over the whole earth. The report is carried in Al-Bahr Al-Muhit.

So the verse says in the end that a people who had been counted weak and abject were given the rule of lands that had been held by men of arrogance. The promise of Allah and His messengers came out true, as it always does.

**"In this way the noble Word of your Lord was fulfilled for the Children of Israel for what they had endured"** names the promise and the reason.

The promise meant here is either the one Musa had spoken to his people in verse 129, that their Lord would destroy their enemy and make them successors in the land. Or it is the promise given to the Israelites in Surat Al-Qasas. There Allah says that He wished to show favour to those who were oppressed in the land. He would make them leaders and inheritors, and establish them in the land, and let Pharaoh and Haman and their hosts receive from them the very thing they feared (28:5-6). The two are one and the same in substance, since the promise Musa gave to his people was drawn from the promise of Allah.

The favour was the reward of their patience, which is why the verse says that it was for what they had endured. Patience in distress is what brought it. There is an indication inside that, that any people or any person who follows the same example, at any time and in any place, will receive the same reward.

**What patience does when a person is outmatched.** Al-Hasan Al-Basri drew a lesson out of the verse. When a person is not strong enough to defend himself against an enemy, the way to success is to hold steady. If a man who has been wronged tries to take his revenge with his own hand, and does wrong to his opponent in return, Allah leaves him to himself. The affair then ends in success or in failure as it happens. When he asks Allah for help against the wrong done to him instead, and waits, Allah opens the door of success on him.

### The same promise for the community of Muhammad ﷺ

The promise of rule over the land was fulfilled for the Israelites. A promise of the same kind was given to the community of the Prophet ﷺ in Surat Al-Nur. The Book says there that Allah has promised those of them who believe and do good deeds that He will give them succession in the earth, as He gave it to those before them (24:55). As the Israelites saw the word of Allah come true in their sovereignty over the land, the Muslim ummah saw it come true in sovereignty over a great part of the earth. That reading is recorded in Ruh al-Bayan.

### A note on the complaint of the Israelites

It is not right to say that the Israelites did not observe patience. When Musa asked them to hold steady, they said that they had been persecuted before he came to them and after he came. Their patience under the constant persecution of the people of Pharaoh is a proven fact. The words in that place may have been an expression of grief rather than a complaint.

**"And We destroyed what Pharaoh and his people constructed and what they established"** returns to the other side. What they produced is what they built, such as their agriculture and their buildings, and in one reading the words cover the designs and the schemes they worked out against Musa. What they established is what they raised high, which is read as their mansions and their trees. Ibn Jarir, Mujahid and Ibn Abbas said that the word means what they built. Qatadah said of the whole sentence that what they produced came to nothing, and what they had raised was left standing empty. Al-Hasan Al-Basri said of the same words that the buildings and the works of a people who oppose a messenger do not outlast the messenger. So the verse ends with the houses and the crops of the great ones of the earth brought down. The tents of the people who had been counted weak are set up in their place.

### Why the passage is placed here

The events told up to this point have been about the destruction of Pharaoh and his people. The verses that follow describe the victory and the success of the Israelites, and then their insolence in the face of everything Allah had given them. The whole passage also carries a comfort for the Prophet ﷺ in the face of the stubbornness of the people who refused him. It shows how the messengers before him were treated by their own peoples, and what came of it in the end.

### What the denial of signs comes to

The punishment fell on the communities that denied the signs of God. The believers were given a special help from Him instead, on account of their patience under the provocations of the people around them, and their standing firm on the path of God.

The word for signs carries the sense of the arguments that establish the truth as truth. What holds a person back from them is his own pride. Instead of giving his full attention to the argument in front of him, he turns his attention to the man who is presenting it. He cannot answer the argument. The person making it is not a figure of established standing, and he carries no worldly glory. So the easiest road for the proud man is to make fun of the presenter rather than the proof. He tells himself that to sit and listen would make his own status lower than that of the preacher. To keep his rank, he refuses to admit the superiority of the truth.

That is the real point at which a human being is being tested. In this world God makes Himself known indirectly, through signs and through reason, while in the Hereafter He will make His being known directly, and then no one will dare to deny Him. Only that faith has value which comes from a person's own discovery of the truth while God is as yet unseen.

### In short

- The people who were treated as weak were made the inheritors of the eastern and western lands that had been blessed.
- They are called those taken as weak rather than the weak, since a people with Allah as their support are not weak in the real sense.
- The word used is inheritance, which makes them the true inheritors of the land and wealth of the people of Pharaoh, and the land meant is Egypt and Syria.
- The promise was fulfilled for them because of their patience, and the same promise was given to the community of Muhammad ﷺ in Surat Al-Nur (24:55).
- What the people of Pharaoh built, planted and raised high was destroyed, and the word of the Lord stood for the people who had endured (28:5-6).
- The denial of the signs comes from pride, which turns a person's attention from the proof to the man who brings it. Only the faith of a person's own discovery, while God is unseen, has value.

138.text:
The people are on the far shore with the sea behind them, and the first thing they ask for is an idol. "We brought the Children of Israel across the sea and they came upon a people devoted to idols." Then the request and the answer come. "They demanded, “O Moses! Make for us a god like their gods.” He replied, “Indeed, you are a people acting ignorantly"

### Phrase by phrase

**"We brought the Children of Israel across the sea"** recalls the crossing that had just been told. They went over the northern end of the sea and came to the peninsula of Sinai, and then they travelled south along the bank.

**"and they came upon a people devoted to idols"** describes what they saw on the way. The people in question are said by some of those who explained the Book to have been from Canaan, and by others to have been of the tribe of Lakhm. In one account they are called al-Raqim, and are described as a remnant of the people of Abraham. What they were given to was the worship of idols, and they stayed near them in devotion.

Ibn Jarir commented on this place that the people were worshipping idols they had made in the shape of cows, and that this is what influenced the Children of Israel afterwards, when they worshipped the calf. So the request made here was the seed of what came later, and the verse records where it was planted.

**"They demanded, “O Moses! Make for us a god like their gods.”"** is the request itself. It came from the ignorant among the Children of Israel, and it came after they had crossed the sea and seen the signs of Allah and His great power with their own eyes. What they wanted was a god they could see, since the God they had been brought to is not seen with the eye.

**"He replied, “Indeed, you are a people acting ignorantly”"** is the answer of Musa. What he was telling them was that they did not know the greatness and the majesty of Allah, nor His freedom from any partner and from anything that resembles Him. In another reading the sense is that they were ignorant of what was due to Him alone in His oneness, and of what may not be ascribed to Him. It was their repayment of His favour to them that brought the words out of the messenger.

### What was behind the request

The people of Israel had come out of the greatest victory of their history and had entered a life of ease and comfort, and then they began to show the marks of ignorance, in the way that people who are given wealth and luxury begin to show them. The first impertinent request they made was this one, that a god be made for them like the gods of the people they had seen being worshipped along the road.

There is a weakness of the human being underneath it, and it is worth naming. A person attaches importance to appearances, and because of that he cannot give his attention to the God who is not seen. He cannot detach himself from the things that the eye can take in. The unenlightened bow down before gods of stone and of metal, while people who count themselves advanced give their devotion to a personality, or a community, or a structure of culture. The form changes with the times, and the devotion stays where it was.

### The report of the lote tree

A report carried by Ibn Jarir from Abu Waqid Al-Laythi puts the whole verse in front of the community of the Prophet ﷺ. He said that they had left Makkah for the battle of Hunayn in the company of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ. Some of the disbelievers had a lote tree whose shade they used to stay in, and on which they would hang their weapons, and the tree was called Dhat Al-Anwat. So when the companions passed by a large green lote tree, they said to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ that he should appoint for them a Dhat Al-Anwat like the one the others had.

He said, by the One in whose hand my soul is, that they had said just what the people of Musa said to him, and he repeated their words, that he should make for them a god as the others had gods, and that his answer had been that they were an ignorant people and that what the others followed was doomed and their deeds were in vain.

The report is a mirror held up to the ummah that had the Messenger of Allah among them, and it shows that the inclination recorded in this verse is not a thing confined to one nation or to one age.

### In short

- The Children of Israel crossed to the peninsula of Sinai and travelled south along the bank of the sea.
- On the way they came upon a people given to idols, said to be from Canaan, or from Lakhm, or named al-Raqim as a remnant of the people of Abraham.
- Ibn Jarir said the idols were shaped like cows, and that this is what influenced the Children of Israel later in the affair of the calf.
- They asked for a god they could see, after they had watched the signs of Allah and His power at the sea.
- Musa answered that they were ignorant of the greatness of Allah and of His freedom from every partner.
- The report of Abu Waqid Al-Laythi at Hunayn shows the same inclination in the companions' question about the lote tree called Dhat Al-Anwat, and the Prophet ﷺ answered it with this very verse.

139.text:
The messenger finishes his answer with the fate of the people they admired. "What they follow is certainly doomed to destruction and their deeds are in vain.”"

### Phrase by phrase

**"What they follow is certainly doomed to destruction"** is a sentence about the end of the people themselves. The way they were on was going to be destroyed, and the destruction meant here is of the religion they held and of the community that held it.

**"and their deeds are in vain"** speaks to the work they had done. Everything they had put into that worship was error, and no part of it stayed with them as a gain. In one reading the words say plainly that what they were doing was a waste and a losing of themselves.

**Why the messenger said it in that order.** He had already told his people that they were ignorant, and the next thing was to show them what sort of thing they were asking to be given. If he had refused the request and said nothing else, the desire would have stayed in them. What he did was to name the end of the very people they wanted to copy, and there is no argument against a model that is on its way to ruin.

The words also turn the attention of the Children of Israel back on themselves, since they were being asked to look at a nation whose worship was about to be extinguished, and to want for themselves what was already lost.

### In short

- He told them plainly that the way of the people they admired was going to be destroyed.
- Everything those people had done in that worship was error, and none of it stayed with them.
- The answer turns them away from the model by naming the end of that model.
- The request is refused with a reason, so that the desire behind it is uprooted rather than simply denied.

140.text:
He puts the question to them in a form that answers itself. "He added, “Shall I seek for you a god other than Allah, while He has honoured you above the others?”"

### Phrase by phrase

**"Shall I seek for you a god other than Allah"** is put as a question with an answer already built into it, and in another reading the sense is whether he should command them to worship another lord. The thing they were asking of him was the one thing a messenger cannot do, since a messenger comes to turn people from the worship of the created to the worship of the Creator.

**"while He has honoured you above the others?"** is the argument that closes the matter. In one report the words mean that they had been preferred over the peoples of their own time, and the token of it was the destruction of their enemy and their being made leaders in the land and established in it. Moses put the question to them so that the contrast between what they had and what they were asking for would stand out on its own.

**How the honour is understood.** The superiority spoken of here is not a thing of race or of birth. What it refers to is the mission. The Book speaks of a community as the best community raised up for people, and that is the office meant here as well. The way of God with these things is to choose a community to carry His Book, and then to use that community to carry His message to the other nations. In the ages before, that office was held by the Children of Israel, and after the coming of the last Prophet ﷺ the same mission was given to the Muslim ummah. So the honour was a trust placed on their shoulders, and what they were doing on the road beside the sea was spending it.

### In short

- The question is put so that its own answer stands in it, since a messenger cannot call people to any god but Allah.
- The reason follows at once, that Allah had given them honour above the other peoples of their time.
- One report names the tokens of it as the destruction of their enemy and their establishment in the land.
- The honour meant is the mission and not race or birth, and the Book speaks in the same sense when it calls a community the best community raised up for people.
- That office was carried by the Children of Israel before, and after the coming of the last Prophet ﷺ it was given to the Muslim community.

141.text:
The place they had been brought out of is put in front of them once more. "And ˹remember˺ when We rescued you from the people of Pharaoh, who afflicted you with dreadful torment—killing your sons and keeping your women. That was a severe test from your Lord"

### Phrase by phrase

**"And ˹remember˺ when We rescued you from the people of Pharaoh"** calls them back to the shame they had been brought out of. They had been under the tyranny of the king and his people, and had gone through humiliation and disgrace at their hands. They had also watched their enemy being destroyed in front of them and meeting that end in the water.

**"who afflicted you with dreadful torment"** names what the torment was in the plainest terms. The worst of the chastisement laid on them was the killing of their sons. Their women were kept alive, and the purpose of that was service, since they were made to serve the Egyptians as servants. The sons here are the small children.

**"That was a severe test from your Lord"** names what the whole experience had been. In one reading the words mean that the rescue itself was a tremendous favour from their Lord, and in another that there was a great trial in the punishment itself. The two readings belong together. What the people went through was a test, and the rescue that followed was a favour, and both of them came from the same hand.

The sense of the trial is set out in one report, that being saved from the people of Pharaoh was a great test from their Lord, to see whether they would be thankful. That is the use the verse puts the memory to. The people had been rescued from slaying and from servitude, and they were now free on the far shore of the sea. They were being reminded of what had come before, so that the memory would put the request they had just made in its true light.

### What the years of oppression were for

The opportunity the king had of oppressing the Children of Israel was itself a test for them, and not a punishment. Believers are put through such things so that they may be shaken and woken up. It then becomes clear who among them turns away from the religion of God because the circumstances have become hard, and who holds on to it by patience when the days are dark. The same subject was set out in the explanation of Al-Baqarah, the second surah of the Book. The story of the Israelites is told there at length, and the same reminder is given to them.

### Where the passage is going

Musa had found the Children of Israel on the far side of the sea asking for a god they could see. The account of the reminder given to them in Al-Baqarah carries the same lesson. The reminder given here takes them back over the years of the sons they had lost, and the years of service they had been made to give. It sets all of that against the thing they were now asking their Lord for. The verses after these go on to the account of the mountain, where the same people are given more of the signs and the same inclinations appear again.

### In short

- The Israelites are sent back to the memory of the years they spent under the tyranny of the people of Pharaoh.
- The worst of the torment named is the killing of their sons and the keeping of their women as servants.
- What they went through was a severe test, and in one reading the rescue itself was the great favour from their Lord.
- The trial was to see whether they would be thankful, and the reminder of it is set against the request they had just made.
- The oppression they suffered was a test for them and not a punishment, and believers are tried in that way so that it may be seen who holds on with patience.

142.text:
The account moves from the sea to the mountain, and the law is given over forty nights. "We appointed for Moses thirty nights then added another ten—completing his Lord’s term of forty nights. Moses commanded his brother Aaron, “Take my place among my people, do what is right, and do not follow the way of the corruptors.”"

### Phrase by phrase

**"We appointed for Moses thirty nights"** records the promise made to him. The word used here in the Book is read in two ways, wa'ada and wa-'adnā, and it carries the sense of making an offer of something good, so that what was promised was that Allah would speak to him directly and give him the guidance for his people. The promise was that he should go to the mount and spend thirty nights there in devotion.

**"then added another ten—completing his Lord’s term of forty nights"** gives the rest of it. The thirty were followed by ten more, and the whole of the term appointed by his Lord came to forty nights.

**"Moses commanded his brother Aaron, “Take my place among my people”"** is what he said before he left. He set his brother over the people in his absence and gave him charge of their affair until he came back to them. The account notes in this place that Allah was reminding the Children of Israel of the guidance He had sent to them, by speaking to Musa directly and giving the Torah to him. That book contained their law and the details of their legislation, and the promise of those forty nights was the beginning of it.

**"do what is right"** is the first instruction. Its object is not named in the words, and that may be deliberate, so that it stands as a general command covering the whole conduct of the people and of the deputy himself.

**"and do not follow the way of the corruptors"** is the second. Since Harun was himself a prophet of Allah, the command cannot be taken as a warning against committing corruption in his own person. What it means is that he was not to do anything that would help or encourage the people of corruption. That command was tested soon enough. When the people were taken up by the calf that Samiri made for them, Harun stood against the deed and warned Samiri, and the account of it later shows Musa calling his brother to account over what had happened, since he took it for a failure of diligence. The verse leaves a lesson in that for a community that confuses negligence with piety.

### Why thirty nights and then ten

The term was fixed at forty nights in the will of Allah, and the question of why the first part was thirty and the rest was added afterwards has been taken up by those who explained the Book. No one has access to the whole of the wisdom in the acts of Allah, and what they have offered are explanations by way of likely reasoning.

One of them is that the wisdom behind the arrangement was the gradual enjoining of the law, so that it would be easier for the people to put into practice. Another is that those who are in authority are being taught to give their subordinates time when the work is not finished by the day it was set for. That is what happened here. The spiritual readiness that was being sought was not reached within the thirty nights, so ten more were added, and the time needed for that perfection was given to him. The Book recalls the same appointment in another place, where it says that Allah delivered them from their enemy and made a covenant with them on the right side of the Mount (20:80).

The reports of what he did in those days are also given in detail. Musa fasted through the thirty days and nights without breaking the fast. When the thirty came to an end he took his meal, cleaned his teeth with a twig, and presented himself at the appointed place on the mount. Then Allah told him of the odour that the fasting mouth carries, and that it is dear to Him. Since the cleaning had taken the odour away, he was told to fast for ten more days, so that the odour would be there again.

That report about the odour is not a proof that cleaning the teeth during a fast is forbidden or disliked. The report is quoted without a chain of narrators, and even where it is sound it may be a command that belonged to Musa alone, or to the people of the Torah. The permission to clean the teeth while fasting is established by the practice of the Prophet ﷺ. Al-Baihaqi carried the tradition from Aishah that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said that the best act of one who is fasting is the cleaning of the teeth with the miswak, and Al-Jami' Al-Saghir records the status of that report as hasan, which is a grade of authentic tradition.

### The two journeys of Musa

A question was raised about a difference in the accounts. Musa spent thirty days fasting through the night without breaking his fast at all, while on the journey he made to visit Khizr, of which the story is told in another surah, he could not hold out even half a day. He said there, give us our food, since this journey of ours has left us tired (18:62). Ruh al-Bayan explained the difference through the nature of the two journeys. The journey after knowledge was a journey of one created being to another created being, and it was a journey of teaching courtesy and of hardship. In it he was carrying himself along, he was aware of his own suffering, and he saw the marks of hunger because he was still with himself. The thirty nights on the mount were different in kind. That was a journey for the Creator, made by a devoted servant who had cut himself off from the creation in the search for his Lord. In a journey of that kind, the vigour of the body's demands for food and drink is weakened, and a person becomes able to fast through the days and the nights together.

The inner reading of the whole passage is put in a way that suits the subject. It was said of these verses that the promises of lovers, even when they are put off, show intimacy. In the matter of ordinary dealings, adding days to a promised meeting is no part of good faith, and the rule does not hold in the way it does between friends. What the Lord of the worlds did with Musa is taken as the illustration. He promised him thirty days, and when they passed He added ten more, and the addition was made because Musa was pleased with it. He counted the thirty as the capital and the ten as the profit, since the speech of his Lord was heard a second time in the extra nights. In that journey he waited thirty days without recalling food or drink and without being aware of hunger, carried along as he was by the journey of generosity, while on the other journey he was still in the road of creatures.

### The nights and the months

Another point is drawn from the wording. In the laws given to the prophets, the date turned over at night, and that is why the verse says thirty nights and not thirty days. The lunar month begins with the sighting of the moon, and the moon can only be sighted at night, so the dates in that calendar turn over at sunset. Al-Qurtubi carried the saying of Ibn al-Arabi on this, that the solar calendar serves the benefits of worldly affairs while the lunar calendar serves the acts of religion.

The particular months are named in the reports. Ibn Abbas said that the thirty nights were the nights of Dhul-Qa'dah, the eleventh month of the lunar calendar, and that the ten nights added to them were the first ten of Dhū’l-Hijja. On that reckoning the Torah was given to Musa on the day of Eid al-Adha, and the report is carried by Al-Qurtubi.

### The number forty and the practice of doing things by degrees

The number forty is taken as having an effect of its own in the correction of the heart. It is reported from the Prophet ﷺ that the one who worships Allah for forty days with sincerity of heart is given wisdom as a spring in his heart, and the report is given in Ruh al-Bayan.

The verse also teaches the people to fix a period for the thing they are working for, and to come at their aims by stages. That is the way Allah does things. Haste and hurry in affairs are not approved by Him, and the creation of the universe in six days, when He had the power to create it in a single moment, is the plainest instruction in the principle. The Torah was not given to Musa in one moment either, and the period fixed for it was a way of stressing the same practice.

It was by ignoring that principle that the Children of Israel lost their footing. When Musa left for the mount he told them that he would be away for thirty days, and when he did not come back in that time, since he had been kept ten days longer, they grew impatient and said that he had been lost somewhere and that they should choose another leader. So they fell in with Samiri and began to worship the calf. Had they been a people of patience, and had they understood that things come by degrees, they would not have fallen into that error.

### The deputy and the weight of the trust

The appointment of Harun carries two lessons of religious importance.

The first is that a person who holds a responsible office should appoint somebody to take care of the work while he is away. Musa made a point of this before he went up the mount. The Prophet ﷺ used to appoint a deputy whenever he left Madinah, and Ali and Abdullah ibn Umm Maktum were given that trust on different occasions. The report is carried by Al-Qurtubi.

The second is that the person leaving should set out instructions for the one who is to take his place. Musa gave two. The general one was that his brother should put things right, and the specific one was that he was not to follow the path of those who work corruption. Both of them belong to the handing over of a trust, and both of them were in place before he left.

### What the community needed to be told

There is an order in the commands of the religion, and this verse marks a stage in it. This passage speaks of the time that followed the destruction of the Pharaoh and his people. What Musa carried in Egypt was the call, while the laws were given to him after he reached the desert of Sinai. In ordinary conditions, what is asked of believers is that they put their own lives right and live as true servants of God, and that they invite others to the oneness of God and to a life directed towards the Hereafter. Once believers have become a community with a standing of their own and have the freedom to order themselves, as the Israelites did in the desert, it becomes binding on them to build their social life on the basis of the sacred law.

When Musa set Aaron over the Israelites in his absence, he said to him to take his place among the people, to act rightly, and not to follow the way of those who spread corruption. That is the basic principle of carrying responsibility at the head of a community, and the verse gives it in the words of one prophet to another.

### In short

- Allah promised Musa thirty nights on the mount and completed the term with ten more, so that the appointed time came to forty nights.
- The promise was the beginning of the revelation of the Torah, which carried the law of the Children of Israel and the details of their legislation.
- Musa fasted the term, and the reports explain the addition of ten through the odour that Allah loves in the mouth of one who fasts, while the permission to clean the teeth while fasting stays established by the practice of the Prophet ﷺ.
- The nights were the month of Dhul-Qa'dah with the first ten of Dhul-Hijjah, which places the giving of the Torah on the day of Eid al-Adha, and the counting of dates at night is why the verse speaks of nights rather than days.
- Musa set his brother Aaron over the people with two instructions, to put things right and not to follow the people of corruption, and the verse teaches both the appointment of a deputy and the giving of instructions to him.
